NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, Sze, A rabbit with tasks has been caught at Ota.nteu, New Zealand. Merionethibiro and the whole Principality were startled a few days ago by the intelligence that 118 mountain sheep, stolen from oft a sheepwalk near Maenturg, Merionethshire, were exhibited and found purchasers in Oswestry Smithfield. The French Minister of Agriculture, with the unanimous approval of the Budget Committee, has placed at the dis- pesal of M. Pasteur a tardier sum of 50,000 francs, to enable him to continue his researches into the causes and nature of contagions diseases among animals. This is the third sum granted to this distinguished chemist with the same object, 50,000 hence having been given in 1880 and 40,000 francs in 1881. A lecture on the Guernsey cow delivered by Mr. W. Ledyard has be2n published by the Guernsey Star, from which the following particulars are taken :—la 1798 a law was passed by the insular legislature forbidding the importa- tion of any cow, heifer, bull, and calf, under a penalty of 200 livree, and the forfeiture of the boat and :tackle which should bring them, and a farther penalty of 50 livres on any sailor on board who should fail to inform of the importation. Since that date it is probable that the cattle of the island of Cratern.sey have remained as absolutely pure as any breed that is known. THE REPEAL or THE MALT TAIL—The unfairness of those gentlemen who are now abusing the Government for acced- ing to their own request, and transferring the malt tax to beer, reminds me of a little boy of my acquaintance who was told by his mother to leave off playing under a chair, or he would knock his head. The boy kept on playing there, and presently he did knock his head, whereupon he became very wrathful. "I told you you would hurt yourself if you played there," said the mother. "But why did you let me," PM the rejoinder of Young Hopeful in a towering passion.—Man of Mark-lane. ABERDEEN Carrnx.—Here are a few things worth gene- ral attention! Within eighteen months, above 500 of this variety have been exported to America' raising the value of alt breeding animals 50 per cent. A three-year-old bull had to be slaughtered, and sold by weight. He weighed 132 stone. One of the early prize-taking cows was 21 years old when e:-:hibited. These are, of course, email maxima com- pared with those of the famous Berner Old Grannie, who had twenty-five calves, and died in her 35th year, having bred until she was 29. One breeder, whose herd experience extends over forty years, has had but thirteen bulls daring that period, and nine of these traced to Old Grannie. WEBBS' BULB CATALOGUE, which is jest issued, is excel- lently printed and contains a very large number of first- class engravings of the various varieties of flowers which are described in its pages. The catalogue gives directions for the cultivation of hyacinths, in glasses, pots, and beds, as well as information respecting tulips, crocuses, jonquils, and other winter and spring flowers. Messrs. Webb describe many new and beautiful varieties, and the collections of bulbs which they offer may be relied upon as containing the bast for both outdoor or indoor decorations. All classes of growers appeer to have been attended to, for the varicus collections range from A at 10s. 61., and containing 127 selected balks, to J at £5 Sc., containing 2,659 bulbs. Messrs. Webb are to be large exhibitors at the Royal Man- chester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Show, at Preston, neat week, and their stand, No. 168 (The Royal Museum of Seeds, Grasses, dra.) will be well worth a visit from their numeroue customers and friends in this district. SUTTON'S BULB CATALOGUE.—This, as is usual with Messrs. Sutton's catalogues, is handsomely decorated both inside and outside, and its issue in the autumn is appro- priate from its suggestions for the use of bulbs for winter and spring flowering. The catalogue is unusually iateresting, and contains very ample cultural directions for the hya- cinth, with shorter directions for crocas,ltulip, and other bulbs. Daring the last few years increased attention has been given to the cultivation :of bulbous flower roots, and visiting, as Messrs. Satton do, the leading growers in Hol- land when the bulb are in full bloom, they are able to select the best kinds. Special reference is this year made to the new Freesia, which is a very beautiful novelty ; and also to the " inimitable " hyacinths for bedding. Nothing is more beautiful than a bed of hyacinths in bloom all at once, and scarcely anything is more difficult to obtain. Messrs. Sutton have, however, succeeded in making up collections which will produce this desirable result. Messrs. Sutton are mak- ing large preparations on their stand at the show on Moor Park, Preston, nkt week, and, no doubt, would be glad to see all interested in either agriculture or horticulture ; whilst a visit to it cannet fell to be both interesting and instructive. WEIGHING MACHINES.—My cattle are weighed once every week, and the sheep as near so as can be managed. Sometimes, however, rain prevents this ; even a slight shower will make a material difference in their weight, as the fleece very easily retains moisture. I once weighed a lot of sheep after rain and again when dry, and was sur- prised at the difference. It is certainly true that these ma- chines vary slightly in wet or dry weather; and I always balance mine when there is any doubt. It takes about 90. b to balance the platform and this is accomplished simply by placing bricks round the edge of the weighing board, which allows plenty of room for the weights. I use stout hempen cords (1 inch diameter), which are hooked on to the Iron beam above to support the platform and weighing board. The former platform is kept from rising above six inches by means of wooden blocks at each corner, which are fixed to the oak floor. Thus all danger of swinging is averted, and even if any of the ropes were to break, the accident would be a very slight one. When sheep are weighed, they are enclosed by strong wire netting, which, however, is re- moved for cattle, as I find the latter stand best en the plain boards. It is a good plan to take these machines down every six months or so, and pat them into thorough repair. I often wonder that farmers do not possess these common weighing machines. A really good one can easily be started for .f.:10 or £l2, and there is practically no limit to their true value. I calculate that mine must make fully £5O a' year gain to the stock account; besides which, it has been the means of making many useful experiments.—A. .F. P. FASHION IN CATTLF.—" The Channel Island cow stands at the heal as a producer of butter,excelling both in quality and quantity of Product. Ayrshire and Duch cows excel as deep milkers. The Hereford ox is a superior beef animal. The polled cattle of Scotland have long been esteemed for their hardiness and for the quality of their flesh. All these are merits of substance. They are worth money in the mar- ket. They relate to quantity, quality, and economy. For more than a hundred years the shorthorns have been dis- tinguished for the possession of the varied excellencies that make useful cattle. The product at the pail was satisfac- tory, being of good quality, and of large quantity. The beef was of the best (?) quality, the animal matured early, the carcase mat well on the block, giving a large percentage of the best parts. Taken as a breed, there was nothing known to ,be its equal for the shambles and the dairy combined. Now, with all the merits of these various breeds, with so much of real excellence to begin with, with so many incen- tives to excel in economical production in the dairy and on the block, is is not singular that the efforts of breeding have been turned toward the production of fancy colours and other elements without absolute value? But such is the potency of fashion, that thousands of dollars have been paid with enthusiasm for Mee thinze which the highest art of the dairyman and butcher would fail, to discover. Some of these things are uediecoverable except to those who delve in musty records; others are as open to the eye and hand of one man as to those of another, but are only known to the initiated, or the infatuated. Though making no pretence to the skill of the prophet, my belief is that the time is not dis- tant when the test of production will take the place of fancy points, and that a pedigree on that basis—a basis that all can understand—wig be the test of value as it is of merit." —Cot. Scott, in "lowa Homestead." CANADIAN AGRICULTDRE.—The report of the Canadian Minister of Agriculture, which has ja t been issued, shows that the farmers of the Dominion are in a flourishing con- dition, and their prospects for the future very bright. The Minister points out that the attention of cattle importers is now being given to the importation of the best pedigreed animals that can be procured, the value of which in laying a good foundation for the country cannot be over-estimated. Then follow the statistics. These show that the total num- ber of cattle imported during the year' from Britain for im- proving the home breeds was 751, besides 1,179 pure bred sheep and 53 pigs. There hah been a falling off in the ex- ports of cattle and sheep during the year, the numbers being 45,535 of the former and 62,401 of the latter, in addition to '7,05S rattle and 9_465 sheen ,sbinned from ports of .08 United States. The number of immigrants who arrived in Cantle as settlers last year was 47,991, of whom about 28.600 went into Manitoba and the North-West Territory, 3,742 of that number sailing from Glasgow. During the present year 500 additional miles- of railway will be con- structed west of the Red River, which will afford further facilities for settlers in the North-West; and as it will make the distance to Liverpool 600 miles shorter thanl from the American grain•growing provinces, the Canadians evil be placed on a better footing for competing with-their neigh- bours in the European markets. An additionaltlarge area of accessible land for settlement will also be opened up, and the North• West Territory will be more easily reached than hitherto. The reports from the different agents of Canada in Great Britain speak hopefully of a great increase in the number of emigraute to the Dominion during the present year, a.ericultariste generally manifesting more interest in all that relates to the new country. Some delegates from Germanv were invited out by the Government last year, and on their return gave a very flattering account of what they had seen, which has induced considerable numbers from the Fatherland to cross the Atlantic for a new home where they will be beyond the reach of military despotism and in a land of political freedom. Mr. Thomas Graham, Glasgow, the agent for Scotland, emhodies in his report a letter from Messrs. John Swan and Sons, Edinburgh, on the Canadian cattle supply to this country, in which they im- press upon the Dominion Government the necessity of im- proving the 'existing breeds of both cattle and sheep by judicious crossing, there being, they say, a wide outlet here for cattle for winter feeding and early fattening.

DUTCH DVEZSTICITY.—A housewifely duty which seems strange to our EeglLh eyes, but is always performed by Dutch ladies of all ranks, is the walling up of cups and saucers. After lunch and tea, a silver bowl i 3 brought in, and the cups and saucers are daintily washed and carefully dried with a delicately fine liron napkin, usually beautifully marked in white embroidery with the initials of the family, surmounted by the cenet'e or baron's or baron's coronet, if the family be noble. This time-honoured custom is now, I think, retained rather as a cherished observance of an old national peculiarity, dating, no doubt, from the days when ladies in all countries took the personal supervision of their linen and china closeta—Caseell's Family Magazine. SaatzTaiNG ABOUT VEGETABLES.—Vegetables are of great we in correcting the stimulating effect of a meat diet, this being especially the case where the meat has been salted, it having been found that when much salt meat is taken, and but little vegetables, that scurvy and various cutaneous diseaeee were very prevalent The various kinds of cab- bage are of much use as articles of diet. They are better suited for persons in robust health, than for the weak. In the latter, they ire apt to produce various disorders of the stomaeh. Ceutflewers and broccoli are both more tender and more easily digested than cabbage, savor greens, or kale. Spinaeh, although an agreeable article Of food, deer nal; contain so much nourishment as cabbage or cauliflower. Parsnip contains much nourishment, although, perhaps, not quite so much as carrot. It is an anti-scorbutic, and pre- vents the ill effects that result from living on a salt diet. The carrot is a root which contains much sugar, and is very nutritious, but by some authorities Is not considered so digestible as the turnip. Endive is wholesome, either boiled, or eaten raw with slid. It contains a bitter principle, and is slightly narcotic. Beans, although both wholesome and nutritious, especially when young, yet are beet suite for those persons who take much exercieeionf a thesteapeenntaariry h . They are rather apt to disagree with persons The tough coat that covers the bean is found to be very in- digestible. Beaus are usually eaten with bacon, in which case the fat of the meat tends to counteract many of the ill :effects of the bean. In week stomachs they are apt to produce indieeetion and heartburn. The kidney, or French beana, when eaten young (as they usually arc), are very digestible, and are more easily acted on by the stomach than any of the oth?r legumes. Peas contain much DOW iehment. According to Sir R. Davy, they consist of more than half of nutritious matter. The watercress is cooling and antiscnrbu. ate, and promotes digeolon. Seet-root is very nutritious, and Is a good antiscorbutie ; but, probably from the large quantity of sugar it contains, is so apt to Caine flatulence, Meat it is rarely employed as food for man. Much of the Nagar used abroad is obtained from this root. It i 3 found NW one pound of sugar can be obtained from fourteen ]po nds of beet-root- This vegetable makes an excellent j Plekle.—Cassell's Household Guide.

'itfA
THE STATE OF IRELAND.
Applications tinder the nerr measure are coming in daily to the Land Commission in Dublin from landlords and tenants.

The military at Limerick have been strengthened by 100 men, in anticipation of disturbances on the occasion of the execution of Hynes. Lord Spencer has refused to b°Twit a reprieve to the young man Hynes, who was convicted of the murder at Ennis. The execution will take place on Monday. Ten of the prisoners arrested for the murder of ::the Joyce family, at Miamtrasna, were on Wednesdaylevening-com- mittea for trial at the next Special Commission in Dublin. Captain Blake has intimated his intention of contesting Ennis, vacant by the resignation of Mr. Finigan, on Land League and advanced Nationalists principles. Captain Vake will issue his address in a few days. Two farmers, named Horan, were waylaid and shot at on Sanday night, near Parsonstown, by a man named Barne- well. They disarmed him, belaboured him severely, and left him. He was found by the police patrol, and his deposi- tions having been taken, the Horans were arrested. The Freeman's Journal mentions that the freedom of six places have been conferred on Mr. Gray M.P., sine- his imprisonment, and accepts it as a protest from the Irish people against the system under which he was sentenced, and a pronouncement in favour of an unfettered Press. Mr. E. D. Gray, M.P., in a communication to the Town Council of Cork, has intimated that he cannot think of en- tering into the securities required by the decision of Mr. Justice Lawson. In that event he will remain in prison till February next, unless previously released by the Lord- Lieutenant.

On Wednesday afternoon, at the Dublin Police Court, William Terrie, Richard Terrie, and William Terrie, junr, , were sent for trial on a charge of having wilfully murdered Ellen Terrie, the wife of the former and mother of the two latter prisoners. It is alleged that the accused kicked the deceased to death in the course of a drunken row. Mvlimn.— Information was received on Wednesday afternoon by the Athlone constabulary of the murder of a man named Thomas Quinn, at Edenderry, King's County, some miles from the town. Quinn was in the employ of a man named Gill, and was driving along in his cart, drawn by an ass, when shots were fired with fatal effect, the man being killed at once, and the donkey also being shot dead. As far as is known at present, no cause can be assigned for the outrage. Tuesday night'sDubl in Gazettecontains a return of the num- ber of agrarian outrages reported to the constabulary last month. There are 8 cases from Ulster,29 from Leinster, 39 from Connaught, and 89 from Munster—total 165. The offences are classed as follows :—Murder 1, firing at 7, aggravated assaults 2, assaults endar.gering life 1, incendiary fires 16, robbery 1, killing and maiming cattle 11, riots 1, threatening letters 83, intimidating 10, injury to property 26, firing into dwellings 1.

The Orangemen of the district of Armagh, in the neigh- bourhood of Portadown, have held a demonstration to inau- gurate the Pertadown Orange Hall. Mr. E. W. Verner presided, and a resolution was passed in which the Orange- men expressed sentiments of horror and indignation at the d sgrace brought upon Ireland by the murders and outrages committed by a disloyal section of the community in other counties, and pledged themselves to uphold law and order to the utmost of their power, and to resist any attempt to sever the union between Great Britain and Ireland.

At a meeting held in Saintfield, county Down, on associa- tion has been formed to be called the Saintfield Farmers' Union, the object of which is to secure to the people gene- rally the utmost possible benefit from the Land Act, to protect farmers from excessive legal costs, to aid farmers in putting their cases before the Courts, and to seek such further reforms in the Land Law as will make the farmers owners of their farms on such terms as will be mutually advantageous to themselves and to the country. All the police constables who have been dismissed were on Wednesday afternoon summoned to the Riding School, Dublin Castle, at three o'clock. Over Dv attended. The men were marched one by one from the Lower Castle Yard up to the archway leading to the Upper Castle Yard, and here each man advanced and was interrogated by Captain Hamilton, secretary to the Lord Lieutenant, and Mr. Jenkin- son, inspector of the new Detection of Crime Department, as to their names, numbers, and whether they had attended any of the meetings. They were then dismissed and in- formed that their case would be considered.

THE PERENIX PARK MURDERS.—The man Westgate, who has accused himself of the murders of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke, has been removed to a jail in Jamaica, be- caue3 of the Fantome having been ordered to Barbacloes. He still maintains that his confession is true.. He is closely watched, because of his having threatened to commit suicide. He is troubled with fearful dreams, and wakes raving. The doctors say he is suffering from intense excitement. West- gate states that after the murderous affray he went back and stabbed Lord Cavendish in the back.

AMERICAN CITIZENS IN IRELAND.—Acting under instruc- tions, Mr. Stephen Joseph Mear.ey has taken steps to test the legality of his arrest. On Wednesday he served upon Mr. Purcell, resident magistrate in Ennis, who had bound him over to keep the peace for six months, a notice intimating that as an American citizen he can no longer carry with him the stigma of the British bondsman, and, unaccused or un- convicted, continue the confession-of lawlessness involved by the existence of the bonds for his good behaviour. He accordingly places himself in the position occupied by him prior to the execution of his recognisances, and awaits further magisterial action. MURDER IN LOUGHREA. A terrible murder has been committed in Loughrea dis- trict by a returned Irish-American, named Walsh. He had been at a friend's house, and on his way to his own residence entered the house of a man named Kelly, where he remained seated for a time. Mrs. Kelly was en- gaged with a. hatchet splitting wood, when he suddenly seized the hatchet and clove her skull with it. Later on Walsh was arrested at his own residence, but made no state- ment. It appears that after Walsh's return from America he was sentenced to a shoat imprisonment for some offence, bet on the recommendation of a gentleman in the vicinity he was released before the expiration of his sentence. The husband of the murdered woman is said to be missing since the murder. •

div.head: PRESTON GUILD.
div.p: THE PRESTON GUILD.

The Preston Guild was proclaimed for the last time on Saturday. The Earl of Lathom, who was present, announced that the Duke of Cambridge would take the place of the Duke of Albany in the ceremonies and festivities of this week. The announcement was received with cheers. _

On Sunday morning the Guild Mayor, accompanied by Lord Winmarleigh and a body of county gentlemen, pro- ceeded in state to the parish church, escorted by rifle and artillery volunteers. Among those in the procession were the Bishop of. Manchester and the Bishop of Carlile, Mr. Ecroyd, M.P., and Mr. Raikes, M.P. In the morning the Bishop of Manchester preached a sermon appropriate to the event. Speaking of guilds, he said they had served their purpose, and did not exist as org,aniz ttions, but the pageantry reminded them of their operations. They were institutions of monopoly, protection, and privilege—words which were fast becoming obsolete. As a remedy for the democratic spirit he propounded a spirit of absolute justice in all our institutions. The sun of England's glory was not set. There was a bright long day before her still. There were better times coming. There were unexampled signs of progress in directions which all would admit were sound, true, right, and healthy. In the evening the Bishop of Manchester preached at St. Peter's Church, and the Bishop of Carlisle preached at the Parish Church.

The festivities In connection with the Guild began on Monday. The town was crowded with visitors. At ten o'clock the Mayor opened the Guild Court in the Guild Hall. Among the guests present were the Earls and Countesses of Derby and Sefton, the Bishops of Manchester and Carlisle, Lord Winmarleigh, Sir Richard Cross, M.P., Mr. W. Ecroyd, M.P., the Right Hon. Cecil Raikes, M.P., and the mayors of the principal Lancashire boroughs. The Guild Mayor afterwards proceeded to the parish church in state; and high mass was sung at all the Roman Catholic churches. The proceedings throughout the day were exceedingly imposing, and the town wore its gayest aspect. The Duke of Cambridge arrived at Ormskirk, en route to Preston, and had a hearty reception from the in- habitants. His Royal Highness was the guest of the Earl of Lithom,

. 1 Tuesday's festivities in connection with the Guild were to a certain extent spoiled by the unfavourable weather. Rain fell during a considerable portion of the day, much to the discomfort of the thousands who had aesembled in the streets to witness the outdoor proceedings. At ten o'clock, amidst a drenching shower, a procession, consisting entirely of friendlysocieties,marched through the principal streets, and finally dispersed in North Road. The Duke of Cambridge, accompanied by his host and hostess (Earl and Countess of , Lathom), and other distinguished guests, arrived at Preston ' station by special train from Ormskirk at eleven o'clock, and was received by the Guild Mayor. At the Guild Hall, in the presence of a considerable gathering of nobility and gentry and burgesses of the ancient borough, an address was presented to His Royal Highness by the Mayor and Cor- poration. A special grand lodge of Freemasons was held in the Free Library of the Town Hall prior to the ceremony of laying the foundation stone of the Harris Free Public Library and Museum. The stone was laid by Lord Lathom, Pro- vincial Grand Master of West Lancashire, with masonic rites. These proceedings were followed by a luncheon in the Corn Exchange. Preston enjoyed the greatest day of its carnival on Wed- nesday, when thousands of workpeople, representing the tex- tile and other trades of the country, formed an almost inter- minable procession through the town, which was crowded with visitors to its fullest cipacity. The procession em- braced about five thousand persons and forty lurries, repre- senting the various processes of cotton preparing, spinning, and manufacture, all in full operation. Crom?ton's original spinning mule, 92 years old, lent by Messrs. Dobson and Barlow, Bolton, was working, apparently as well as ever, under the charge of Robert Ainsworth, 78 years of age, the oldest spinner in Preston. Another interesting feature was a hand-loom a hundred years old with wheel and swifts, both working under the direction of the oldest weaver and winder in the town. Some of the more modern looms were weaving fancy pocket handkerchiefs hearing devices commemorative of the Guild, which were sold in large numbers to the visitors. The amalgamated trades procession embraced between twenty and thirty different branches of induetry, all of which were shown in operation, and some of the processes were exceedingly interesting. The processions were witnessed by the Duke of Cambridge, , the Earl of Sefton, and Lord Lethom. Now and then, as , particular portione of the procession CATIIe opposite the place ' occupied by his Royal Highness a short stoppage was made, and explanations of the machinery and productions given. Early in the afternoon the Duke of Cambridge and party went to the show of the Manchester, Liverpool, and North r Lancashire Agriculture' Society. They were escorted by a number of the sth Dragoon Guards, and were received by Lord Winmarleigh, the president for this year of the society. The depot of the North Lancashire Regiment furnished a guard of honoar at the perk, where the band of the Royal Marines played. A luncheon was held on the show ground, :,Lord Winmarleigh presiding. Speeches were delivered by the Duke of Cambridge, Lord Derby, and Lord Wininarleigh, who referred to the importance of the society and the excellence of its objects. After luncheon the duke and party returned to the town, escorted by the \Dragoon Guards. Between three and four in the afternoon the Countess of Derby awarded the prizes in connection with the Preston Floral and Horticultural Society's show. At half. past tour o'clock a miscellaneous concert took place in the new hall at the Corn Exchange, at which the Earl of Lathom was present; and in the evening a grand fancy dress ball was held in the same building. The weather was fortunately fine all day, and the town was never so full of visitors. The scenes at the railway stations of holiday people crowding into the trains were exciting and in most places , confusing, owing to the extraordinary pressure of traffic. The celebration of the Guild Merchant was continued on Thursday. The main attrction was a procession of Catholic Guilds through the town. Cardinal Manning, accompanied by the Bishop of Salford, and other dignitaries of the Roman Catholic Church, was present, and after witnessing the procession his Eminence was presented with an address from St. Augnstine's Guild. Mr. Pyne, organist, Manchester Cathedral, gave a recital on the organ presented to the town by the Dewhurst colliery proprietors. There was a banquet and conversazione of the amalgamated friendly societies in Moorbrook Mill, a miscellaneous concert in the new Public Hall, and finally a display of fireworks in Avenham Park. The morning trains carried crowds of visitors to Preston, but the traffic was by no means so heavy as on Wednesday.

div.head: TM: STRIKE IN THE IRISH POLICE
div.p: TM: STRIKE IN THE IRISH POLICE

FORCF. SERIOUS RIOTING. The wholesale dismissal of members of the Dublin Metro- politan police on Friday, followed by the resignatioa of nearly the whole of the force of the city, induced a very serious state of affairs in the Irish capital. A proclamation, as we briefly stated last week, was issued from the Castle, calling upon all loyal and well-disposed citizens to come forward and undertake the duty of special constables. To this appeal there was a large response on the pert of a number of clerks, 'solicitors, and persons belonging to the official classes, but the conditions—seven days' enrolment and the non-membership of any secret society obliged the Executive to dispense with the services of many applicants. Late on Friday evening between 300 and 400 special constables had been sworn in, and the military were called out, but in spite of these precautions the capital was literally in the bands of the mob. No organised disturb- bance of the peace, however, took place. the feelings of the people being relieved by the smashing of windows at I different places and hooting the specials." Communications between the Castle authorities and their late servants were passing on Saturday, and.the men were told that if they drew up a memorial expressing regret for their disobedience, they might probably be allowed to resume duty. One of their demands was, however, that the dis- charged men should be reinstated before any general resumption of office took place, and as the Lord Lieutenant refused to make any such promise, the negotiations for the time ended. During the afternoon the Lord Lieutenant addressed 250 special constables who were paraded before him. His Excellency explained and justified the dismissal of the mutineers, and appealed to the amateur force to assist the authorities in preserving peace and order. The specisl constables were on duty on Saturday evening, but were viewed with little favour by the people, and con- fined their duties to marching round with the military wh;oh rqllv ha,l nharcrp nf tha doil-r Several eis- turbances occurred during the evening, and the military bid to clear the streets by repeated charges with the bayonet. In one of these affrays eight persons received wounds more or less serious, one of the sufferers being a reporter for a Dublin newspaper, who was surveying the riot for purposes of description Later in the night the city became more tranquil. On Sunday afternoon a lamentable affray took place in Capel-street. Large numbers of Orangemen had been sworn as special constables, and towards them the hostility of the people was most pronounced. Irritated beyond endurance by the jeers of a rough crowd one of the specials, who was armed with a revolver, fired two or three shots amongst his termentors, wounding severely two men. In retaliation the crowd set upon and brutally maltreated the Orangeman, who was, on being rescued by his comrades, taken into custody. The wounded men and their assailant, himself badly hurt, were taken to Jervis-street Hospital, where other cases of injury arising from the tumults in the streets were also received. The special constables hastily enrolled or. Saturday proved, in many instances, unable to manage the crowds, and in fact their presence only served to create irritation, they being generally recognised as ultra-loyalists. On Mon- day the Lord Mayor (Mr. Dawson, M.P.) waited upon the Lord Lieutenant, and urged the desirability of swearing in as special constables men of known character and position in the city, such as shopkeepers and others, who he believed would meet with more co-operation from the mob in the work of preserving peace and order. To this representation his Excellency replied by stating that the full number of " specials " required had already been obtained, and that no more were required. , Two hundred of the dismissed police on Monday signed a memorial to the Chief Commissioner (Captain Talbot), in which they stated their regret at having cemmitted a "gross breach of discipline " in attending a meeting contrary to orders, and beg to apologise for having done so, trusting at the sanie time that the Lord Lieutenant will take their cases into his favourable consideration with a view to their rein- statement. The Dublin police courts were on Monday chiefly engaged in disposing of cases arising out of Sunday's riots. Among the prisoners was special constable Anderson, who fired at an 3 wounded a man named Smith, the latter in turn being

div.head: FOREIGN I N DILIGENCE.
div.p: FOREIGN I N DILIGENCE.

Considerable excitement has been caused in South Africa by the discovery of new gold fields in the Transvaal, and large numbers are flocking to the diggings from Natal, Kimberley, and the Cape Colony. The cholera epidemic is cominitting fearful ravages in the Philippine Islands. At Yloilo alone there have been, it is reported, 4,550 deaths within the past fortnight, A fresh insurgent outbreak is reported from Tunis. Four hundred horsemen have made their appearance before Kairouan, and troops have been despatched from various points with the object of surrounding them. Aleko Pasha, the governor-general of Eastern Roumelia, who is making a tour of the province, is meeting at every stage of his journey with an enthusiastic reception, both from the t,hristian and Mussulman population. The India Office has thought it desirable to issue a state- ment correcting reports which have been published of the prevalence of cholera at Aden and in India. The substance of this statement is that there have been no cases of cholera at Aden since October last, and that there is no epidemic cholera in India.

DUEL BETWEEN EDITORS.—A desperate duel with swords has been fought between two French journalists who had differed as to the proper representative of Bonapartism. Few people may think this a matter worth fighting about, but these two gentlemen fought to the death, one, after being wounded three times, piercing the other through the heart. The report that the Emperor of Germany had been injdred by falling as he was getting into his carriage is declared to be absolutely unfound:d. The venerable monarch is in the enjoyment of perfect health, conducts his ordinary business, Days visits, and takes daily drives in the park of Babalsberg. Yesterday, the Emperor left Berlin for Breslau to attend the autumn military mancoures. The hostilities on the Turko-Greek frontier are said to have been brought to an end by diplomatic communications between Constantinople and Athens by which the status quo gnte- has been established. The points under dispute are to be settled by Said Pasha and M. Condouriotis, acting as the plenipotentiaries of their respective Governments. The Porte, of course, claims to have beaten the Greeks in all the encounters which have taken place. According to the Nottoya Vremya, the Rev. Mr. Lansdell, en Etp6ll3ll clorgymau, who otariod ocycral woeke ago from St. Petersburg on a missionary tour in Siberia, was arrested and brought back, the police having taken the bibles he dis- tributed for Nihilist literature. After some considerable difficulty, however, the reverend gentleman got himself set free again, though whether he proceeded on his journey is not stated.

The views of John Dunn on the "situation" in Zululand have been transmitted to the Earl:of Kimberley. He thinks that Cetevrays will coalesce with the Dutch, and that he is imbued with (requine contempt for the British power. He now denies the report that he is prepared to welcome the ex-King, and while he reiterates his belief as to the disas- trous consequences of Cetewayo's restoration, he recognises the futility of resisting the Government. SERIOUS RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN GERMANY: 54 PERSONS KILLED.—A very serious railway accident has occurred on a German railway, near Hugstettin, by which, it is said, no fewer than fifty-four persons have been killed, and eighty-six injured. Accaunts . as to the cause of the accident are conflicting—one statingl that the embankment gave way, and another that a tele- graph pdle had been thrown across the line during a thunder- storm. Be that as it may, the train, which contained about 1,200 excursionists, and was on its homeward journey, was thrown off the line, and over twenty carriages, it is said, were smashed. If this be so, the loss of life is small compared to the amount of wrechage. EDUCATION IN THE CENTRAL PROVINCES OF TNDIA..— An interesting statement on the enormous development of education in the central provinces of India has been made at Jubbulpore by Mr. Hunter, who, in replying to an address from the public bodies to the Education Commission, stated that in twenty years education in Ill'Oso provinces had , multiplied nearly fivefold. Iteferrinq° to the demands of the ' provinces for a collego teaching up to' the B.A. standard, Mr. Hunter appealed to the wealthy natives to take the matter into their own bands, and promised that a college would be established if they secured a thousand rupees monthly. We are warned that a Franco-Malagasv question which will seriously affect British interests in the Mauritius has been prepared in Madagascar and is approaching our shores. A special embassy has left Antananarivo, the chief of which reloices in the oxiv: of Ravoninalli.tvkniarivo. Ttui 11).bm-

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.
Consequent on the refusal of the bammermen at Siemen's steel works, Swansea, to agree to a reduction amounting to 33 per cent., the works are at a standstill, rendering 1,500 men idle.

BLACK Courrrwr NAILERS.—It was reported at a meetinA of nailers at Halesoien on Tuesday that trucking existed to an alarming extent in the Black Country district, the result being that an average nailer could not earn more than ss. .a week. An anti-truck league will be formed, and, if neces- sary, evidence will be brought in order to proceed against the numerous offenders.

The Board of Trade returns, issued on Thursday, shosi that the imports for August increased £424,07, and the exports increased £378,323, as against the corresponding month of last year. For the first eight months of the year the imports increased £10.807,701, and the exports increased £10,293467, as compared with the first eight months of 1881.

A statement has been issued by the Government of India inviting the attention of capitalists to the importance of developing the iron industry in our great dependency. The supply, it is remarked, of cast iron, wrought iron, and steel could be produced remuneratively on a strictly commercial ,basis, but private enterprise should. be on a largo scale and not confined to one locality. The Cleveland ironmasters' returns for August appeared on Mond fy, and show a reduction in stocks in excise of anticipation, namely, of 21,842 tons, leaving a total stock of Cleveland iron in milers' hands, or in warrants, of 309,494 tons, of which 147,818 tons wtre Cleveland and the re- mainder hematite and other classes of iron. There are 120 furnaces in blast, of which _Bl are on Cleveland iron and 39 on hematite.

Bua.s or SALE AND FAILIIRES.—In the week ending September 2, 1532, there were 742 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 183 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 179, a decrease of 16. The totals for portion to September 2,1832, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 32,560, a decrease of 1,346; the failures gazetted number 7,261, a decrease of 725.—Stubbs' Mercantile Gazette. WAGES DISPUTE IN THE IRON TRAI:E.— It has been resolved by the operatives in the manufactured iron trade of the north of England to claim 711 per cant, advance at the end of October, when Sir J. W. Pease's award terminates. The employers have given notice of a reduction from the same period. The men base their claim on the generally improved prospects of the finished iron trade, and because the returns of the Board of Arbitration, made by Mr. Waterhouse, the accountant, giving the net average prices of iron, were higher than those upon which Sir J. W. Pease based his award. THE LABOUR MARKET. The labour market is again somewhat more unsettled than it has been for some time past. In the north the ironworkers are again considering an advance, and at the recent Miners' Conference suggestions for a general strike were offered by some of the delegates. Several sections of workers, notably the bottle makers of Sunderlani, are still on strike. Owing to heavy rains har- vesting operations have been retarded in several districts ; otherwise agricultural prospects seem fairly good. In Kent hop picking will probably commence next week, but there will be only a very email demand for migrant pickers. At Birmingham the nardware branches are somewhat brisker, and at Sheffield the saw trade, which has been very dull for a long time past, shows a revival. The boot and shoe trade is again better at Leicester, Leeds and Norwich. At Stafford it remains somewhat dull. Signs of increased organisation in the pottery district may be noted. Many large railway, dock, and other undertakings are still in want of navvies and first-class labourers; meanwhile building contracts are somewhat falling cff as the year advances, and there is a good deal of miscellaneous unemployed labour in the metropolis. The letter carriers throughout the country are moving for further consideration of their claims by the Postmaster General, and some sections of the police are also unsettled. Recent receipts from the United States, and also the north-western territory of Canada, are satisfactory so far , as recent immigration is concerned. In the Transvaal the ' new gold fields are attracting much attention. A significant arrival of German joiners on the Clyde may be noted.— Labour News. THE WEATHER AND THE Come TRADE.—The Mark Lane Eapress says :—" Broken harvest weather has continued during the past week, and enough rain has now fallen every- where to make matters look rather serious in the first week of September. In the earlier districts of the southern and south-eastern counties of England the greater portion of the wheat crop, possibly one-half of the barley crop, and a fair proportion of the other grain and pulse, may be assumed to I have been ingathered, but in the remainder of the English counties the bulk of all the crops remains outstanding and has received more or less injury. In Scotland the harvest is only just cemmencing, and there the weather during the , past week has been very rough and unfavourable. A similar state of affairs exists in the northern counties of England and parts of Ireland. Farmers' deliveries now consist mainly , of new wheat which has been stacked, and the condition of native offerings continues very unsatisfactory. Prices in provincial markets again show a shilling to three shillings decline during the week, whilst in London on Friday new English wheat was not saleable except at a reduction of one or two shillings from Monday's shilling decline. From samples of barley yet to hand it would appear that fine malt- ' ing barleys will not be very plentiful, and for such prices may rule comparatively high. Foreign wheat off stands in ! London continues inanimate." The Farmer says :—" The arrival of several fresh wheat cargoes off the coast and the improvement in the weather keep buyers reserved. English wheat irregular in condition and is. per quarter cheaper. ' Foreign wheat also is. lower, except for special sorts. Flour neglected, and country branis 61 reduced from last Monday. ! Maize, beans, and peas are unchanged. Barley quiet for i malting samples; foreign feeding, dd. cheaper. Oats largely offered; sold fairly at nearly old quotations. Tone of the market keeps depressed."

THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADE: MANCHESTER, WEDNESDAY.—The absence of any real pressure to sell et the part of makers who are still kept busy with deliveries on account of work in hand keeps up a steady tone in the iron market. There is, however, very little new business in the marlret, end so far as there is any indication of the course of the market it is in favour of buyers. Lancashire makers of pig iron are still sending away good deliveries against con- tracts; in district brands of pig iron the business doing lia! been of a very restricted character. In finished iron the home demand is only moderate. For delivery equal to Man- chester the prices are about as under:—Lancashire pig iron, 461; Lincolnshire, 47s to 48s 61; and Derbyshire, 48s to 493 6d per ton less 21; bars, £0 7s 7d per ton. Engineers, although still busy, report a filling off in the number of new inquiries, and workmen are not in such pressing demand se they were a short time back. Ths coal trade of the dis- trict cbntinues dull. Any zinproveiaiem iu the aeivaua is confined to the increased requirements for house-fire pur- poses usual to the season of the year. Prices are still kept down by the excessive production not only throughout this but other districts, and now that the strike at the St. Helens collieries is at an end any little assistance which the with- drawal of the output of the above district might have given to the market will now be removed. Manufacturing require- ments for the commoner classes of round coal for iron making and steam purposes continua fairly good; burgy, however, only meets with a slow sale, and although some firms in the Manchester district show a tendency to stiffen in their prices for slack this elas3 of fuel generally seems to be getting mere plentiful. Present prices at the pit mouth remairt about as under :—Best coal, 8,3 to Ss 61; seconds, 6s to 7s • common round coal, 5s to 5s 61; burgy, 4s to 48 ; good slack, 336 d to 3s 9d; and inferior sorts, 2s 9d to 3s 3-1 per ton. Shipping has shown rather a falling off, and both at Garston and Liverpool prices continue very low.

A CURIOUS INSTRIIMaNT, THE MOSOCHORD.—Another popular inetrament with the people from the thirteenth to the fifteenth centuries was the Trumscheit, called by the theorists of the romantic south the Monochord. It con- sisted of a long narrow box made out of three planks', and tapering towards the top. When standing upright it was taller than a man. One of the planks acted as a sounding. board, one strong string of gut extending the whole length of the box. The monochord was played with a wellTesined bow made of horse hair. Sometimes a string, half the length of the original one, was added for the production of the cctave. It is very presumable that an incessant dron- ing buss was all that could be produced from the mono- &lord, or at the very outside the tonic and dominant. An illustration and description of the monochord by Pristorius will be given later on in the work, and will show that even such a rude instrument underwent a kind of development.— The History of Music. This may be easily detected, for if Cocoa thickens in the cup it proves the addition of starch. &CORY OF REVOLTING CIIVELTIr.—A story of revolting cruelty, to which it would be difficult to find a parallel, comes from the West Coast of Africa, where two men named John and Williams, agents and schoolmasters of the Church Missionary Society, and their wives were charged with the murder of a girl under circumstances of incredible barbarity. Two ransomed girls were, it seems, guilty of running away from the mission station at Onitsha, on the Niger, in 1877, bat were captured and taken to Williams's house, where after being stripped, they were tied together back to back, and brutally flogged by Williams and Jahn, while their wives stood by and laughed. Then at their command some natives flogged the girls with whips, canes, ropes, and other instruments of torture, after which pepper was rubbed into their wounds, and they were left suffering tortures in the burning sun. When mid-day Came a number of school boys were ordered to flog them again, and again pepper was rubbed into their wounds. Night coming on, they were untied, and the girl who has died was lashe 1 to a tree in an exhausted condition. Three days afterwards she was seen lying on the ground with a fresh wound on her head, and Mrs. John was standing over her with a stick. Next day she died. These and other details of sickening cruelty were stated before a court of inquiry on the 11th August, and the prisoners were then ordered to tase their trial for murder on the 21st of that month.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

In an article on "Trade and Finance," which appeared in Tuesday's Daily News, there is the following reference to the Manchester Ship Canal :—"The necessity of 'central markets, if trade is to be conducted without waste of power, grows clearer every year. Liverpool is a great port, but essentially an out-port. Manchester would be a better centre for many operations, and the proposed canal aims at making it a complete centre. It is at present dependent on foreign countries for its entire supply of cotton ; it is also dependent on foreign custom for the sale of the greater part of its pro- ducts; but it leans ore Liverpool, or rather it lies immured like a worker in a prison, and Livepool hands its supplies in through the window. Lumbering barges, it is true, wind slowly up the Mersey with goods. A ship canai—a scientific Thames—with wharves and docks and ship yards, would open it to direct trade with the world. The cost would be enormous, the return probably larger in proportion. The loss of power Involved in discharging goods at Liverpool, repacking and forwarding inland, would be saved; the further loss of energy to merchants in travelling to Liver- pool to buy cottony which might more conve- niently be bought on the spot-, would also be prevented. As an instance of the centralising tendencies in trade, the serious attention now given to the projected Manchester ship-canal is itself worth notice. When a large retail shop which supplies all sorts—one from which customers may furnish a house or merely buy a reel of cotton—can under- sell small shops not so well situated i we may be sure that a convenient centre of operations saves friction, unnecessary loss of power, and therefore needless expenditure. Co- operative stores probably owe much of their success to the fact of their accumulating wide variety of goods under the same roof. And what applies to retail business must have some application to large trade—the "grand commerce." In fine, method springs from science, as does knowledge of forces. The scientific man of business will always have the advantage not only in knowing thoroughly with what he is dealing, but also in being able to apply his advanced knowledge by the best methods. He will be best able to avoid wake of material and power, whether his business be of the producing or distributing kind. Such men, including those who advocate the Manchester ship-canal, duly appreciate the value of scientific- communication."
CHURCH WORK IN MID-CHESHIRE.

A three days' bazaar was opened at Alsager on Wednes- day by Mr. G. Palmer, M.P. for Reading (who was assisted by Mr. Craig, M.P., and Mr. Henry Bristowe. Vice-Chancel- lor of the Duchy of Lancaster), for the purpose of raising funds towards the cost of a new church. The circumstances of the parish are rather remarkable. Many years ago the chapel of Alsager was built by a -private family, who ob- tained a private Act of Parliament securing to them distinc- tive privileges in connection with it. Some time afterwards the Ecclesiastical Commissioners made a scheme conferring upon the people of Meager certain rights in that chapel, but on subsequent examination this scheme was found to be in- valid, for in the Act by which the powers of the Church Commissioners were instituted there was an express proviso that no scheme made by them should have power to over-ride a private Act of Parliament. A number of marriages had taken place in the chapel referred to, and only last year the Archbishop of York had to introduce a bill to legalise them When the present incumbent came to Barthomley, he found this great anomaly existing in Meager—that there was a number of people living in a growing place (almost a town), and they were neither in his parish nor out of it. Neither was the incumbent of Alsager under any obligation to look after their spiritual interests, although they resided in the neighbourhood of his church. The Archbishop of York was asked to procure a new scheme dealing with those people, and attaching them or some of them to the church at Alsager; but the law officers of the Crown gave a decided opinion that no scheme could be made, seeing that Alsager was fenced round by a private act of Parliament. As there were many proprietory rights in connection with the chapel, and the number of free seats was very small, the incumbent of Barthomley determined to build a new church, and to give his services and labour amongst the people as far as possible. The bazaar opened on Wednesday, therefore, was aid of the building fund. Mr. Palmer, M.P., referring to the growth of education, said that the advancement in the range of thought, both political, religious, and social, within the last 50 years, had rendered theory and practice so inter- dependent that these subjects could not but come within the soope of public teaching. The introduction of fresh methods of teaching called for new efforts in ether directions than those which during the last half-century had been the orthodox mode of teaching the people in their own towns and villages. He agreed with the writer in one of the periodicals lately published, when he said, addressing the members of his church, "Get out of the ruts." It was time they got out of the ruts, and laid hold of the people who were at present be- yond their reach. He was not a Churchman himself, hut he concurred in the remark that churchmen by their superior enlightenment, and the Church of England by its superior training, were well fitted to lay hold of the people, and to use such means as might be suggested to them by what was being done—and, in some cases, done very successfully— by other bodies arouud them.—Mr. Craig, M.P., followed, and explained the peculiar circumstances of the parish as above related, and said he heartily supported the Rector of Barthomley in his labonrs.—Mr. Bristowe (vice-chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster) also gave an address.

A FIGHT ON THE PILAIRIE.—From natural enemies Buffa- loes have little to fear. The wolves that skulk in and out among the herds are always on the outlook for the sick, the aged, and the young, but they never attack the strong. and healthy animals of which the vast droves are composed. Indeed, (ha only creature at all able to cope with the gigan- tic strength of the bison is the grizzly bear' and even it will seldom assume the aggressive unless there be no help for it. ' Should it be possible for it to shirk the combat, it will assuredly prefer flight. Sometimes, however, means of escape are cut off, or the grizzly may be a she-bear accom- panied by her cubs, which she will never desert. Anxiety for their safety will, therefore, compel her to offer battle. Facing each other for A few moments, the bison, its smali eyes flashing fire, speedily charges the bear with sudden and furious onslaught. And such a charge! Few anim'als c mid stand up against it, for with a well-directed blo'fy of its heavy head it will hurl the grizzly savagely to the ground. Should the bear succeed in avoiding the assault, , and grip the bison, then it is:the latter's turn to quake, for the embrace of the grizzly is almost invariably fatal. As soon as they are at close quarters there is littlr hope for the buffalo, which is hugged graduAlly q death.—" Little Folks" lfeegazir.e
