div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 9, 1882. THE WAR IN EGYPT.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 9, 1882. THE WAR IN EGYPT.

On Tuesday two sons of Mayor Hinchcliffe were out in Appledore Pool, North Devon, shooting wild fowl, when the gun of the elder brother accidentally went off, the shot lodging in the legs of the younger who died in four hours.

Mr. Bradlaugh, in a letter to a Welsh correspondent, reiterates his intention of presenting himself at the table of the House of Commons, without notice, whenever the in- terest of Northampton will be best served by his taking such action.

Walter Robert Garland, described as a "retired gentleman," was on Tuesday committed for trial by the Stipendiary Magistrate of Manchester for obtaining various sums of money from intending emigrants and others, on the alleged false pretence that he was an agent of "The Grand National Emigration Union." The new annexe to the Manchester Warehousemen and Clerks' Orphan Schools at Cheadle Hulme, which has been erected at a cost of £4,000 in commemoration of the 25th anniversary of the foundation of the institution, was form- ally opened on Saturday by the Bishop of Manchester. Addresses were delivered by the Bishop, Mr. John Slagg, M.P., Mr. J. Broome. and others. The liquidation of the City of Glasgow Bank proceeds in a satisfactory manner, and the end of the tragic story of this concern will be reached at the annual meeting ot the shareholders, which takes place in a few weeks. It will be remembered that the amount due to outside creditors was £47,000, and the whole sum has now been claimed except £lO,OOO, on which, in accordance with the official intima- tion, interest will be given. The Birmingham magistrates, on Tues lay, committed to the assizes Alfred Whittingham, a postman of Wilton-road, Birmingham, for stealing two letters containing 160 stamps. Several letters having been missed,the London postal authori- ties were communicated with, the result being that two test letters, which ought to have been delivered, were found at the prisoner's house, as also were several hundred postage stamps. DEATH OF A COLLIER FROM A GUNPOWDER EXPLOSION. —An inquest was held on Tuesday, at Quarry Bank, Dud- ley, on James Hampton, a collier. Deceased was employed on the celebrated Nine Locks Pit, Brierley Hill, and, whilst plugging a hole with gurpowder, a spark dropped in his can. The explosion so injured Hampton that he died shortly afterwards. The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death," but recommended that in future colliers should only use cartridges instead of loose powder. SUBMARINE MINE EXPERIMENTS.—SOMe U 1 portant ex- periments with submarine mines have taken place at Chat- ham. The experiments were to aFcertain whether the explosion of a large mine submerged in the water, in the centre of a chain of other mines, would cause the explosion of the others. A mine of 5001bs. of gun cotton was exploded, but the surrounding mines were not injured. The force of the explosion was felt a distance of two miles. ESCAPE. FROM A CONVENT.—At Bristol, on Tuesday, a girl of 15, named Geraldine Duncan Evans, was charged with wandering about. It transpired that she had escaped from Amos Vale Convent by scaling the wall and exchang- ing her convent clothes for others shich she stole. She now said that she would go back to the convent until they found her a situation, but if detained beyond a fortnight she would again escape. The magistrates discharged the girl on the understanding that she was at liberty to go where she pleased, and she left the court in company with a sister from the convent.

THE VICAR'S RATE AGITATION A.T COTENTRY.—SEIZURE OF GOODS.—Great excitement prevails in consequence of numerous seizures of Nonconformists' goods under distress warrants for the non-payment of vicar's rates in Trinity parish. The warrants were ordered last Wednesday. On Tuesday morning police officers, with an auctioneer, com- menced work, seizing at one place a quantity of flannel, at others boots, books, furniture, and miscellaneous trade and domestic properties, which were removed in trucks. All the persons so spoliated are Nonconformists, and are offering a passive resistance to the rate on pi inciple. The Rev. A. J. J. Cachemaille, vicar of Oldham, has taken the Salvation Army very decidedly under his protection. He has " General" Booth as his guest during the present week, and on Monday evening he attended a mass meeting of the Army at the Skating Rink, where he gave utterance to words of encouragement and congratulation at the work already performed by the organisation. The Church of England, he said, was never more active or successful than at present, but she had failed to secure the masses of the people, and he welcomed the Salvation Army, which had succeeded in attaining that end. CouarrY COURTS.—The Act to amend the law relating to costs and salaries in county courts was issued on Thursday. It is now enacted that no person other than a solicitor of the 'Supreme Court shall be entitled to have or recover any fee or reward for appearing or acting on behalf of any other party in any proceeding in a county court. The right of a barrister is not to be affected, nor the right of a •solicitor to receive costs in respect of a barrister appearing. Amend- ments are made as to ether Acts, and power is given to a judge of-a county court to award costs on the higher scale to a plaintiff on any amount recovered, or to a defendant, provided the judge certify that the actions involved some novel or difficult point, or that the question litigated was of general or public interest. AN ELOPEDlENT.—Considerable commotion was caused in Nottingham on Saturday, on its being reported that the wife of a well-known tradesman in the town had eloped with a gentleman forming one of the " Pirates of Penzance" Company, which has occupied the boards of the Theatre Royal during the week. It appears that for a few days pre- ceding the departure, the errant wife and the actor bad been living together, and it is stated that the husband received information of the intimacy, and took the rather singular means of engaging the services of one or two ex-prize righters: The aid of these gentlemen, however, was not called into requisition, as the husband arrived too late to see the train by which the couple departed. The. matter has been placed in the hands of a local solicitor. RENEWAL OF THE LAND AGITATION IN SKYE. A Portree correspondent says :—As the crofters at the Braes still persist in sending their stock to graze on Benlee, two officers from Inverness, along mith a ground officer, pre,- ceeded to the Braes, on Saturday, to serve notices of inter- dict on behalf of the landlord. They were able to serve a few in the nearest disaffected portion of the Gedintailer district, but the object of their visit becoming known the women and children turned out en masse, and compelled the officers of the law to beat an ignominious retreat. The officers were pursued for nearly two miles by the crowd, who spared neither missile nor hard word. Action by the authorities is waited with some anxiety, as the men are now returning from the fishing, and are as determined as ever respecting their alleged right to the grazing ground in. dispute.

NATIONAL TEMPERANCE JIIBILEE.—NearIy 50,000 persons assembled at the Crystal Palace on Tuesday, to celebrate the jubilee of the total abstinence movement. The fête was organised by the National Temperance League, and among those, who joined in it were thousands of members of the temperance societies, brought by special excursion trains, in many cases from distant towns. The pleasure of the out-door proceedings was greatly marred by unfavourable weather, rain falling with little interruption till night. The fete began with a conference to commemorate the signing of the first teetotal pledge by the seven men of Preston on the Ist September, 1832. Among those who read papers were Mr. Wm. Livesey, eldest son of Mr. Joseph Liyesey, one of the original band of teetotalers. Two crowded public meetings were afterwards held, addressed by Mr. Francis Murphy r.nd Mr. Booth, leaders of the Blue Ribban movement, also by foreign delegates. Two effective concerts were also given, the first by 5,000 children, and the second by almost as many adults, all abstainers. The programme included an extensive procession in which the Good Teraplars and Blue Ribbon Army made a large display of coloured sashes, medals, and showy banners. THE RATING ON FREE LlnnenrEs.—A public meeting was held on Monday night at the South Lcndon Free Library and Art Gallery, in Upper Kennington-lane, to con- sider the action of the parochial authorities in Lambeth in enforcing by distraint the payment of rates on accouat of the premises occupied for the purposes of the library and gallery. Mr. Hill presided, in the unavoidable absence of Mr. Cohen, M.P. (vice-president of the cannel!), Over a very small meeting. Mr. Rossiter, the treasurer, gave a brief account of the origin and progress of the library, which was established in 1878, and has, depended entirely upon volun- tary contributions. There was, he said, an Act of Parlia- ment which freed from rating every institution, whether public or private, which was exclusively set apart for pur- poses connected with the arts, sciences, and literature. Among such institutions he would instance the Landon Library. The only conclusion which he could draw from what bad transpired in connection with the library was that there was no public spirit in the south of London in favour of the maintenance of institutions of a kind likely to promote the intellectual well-being of the inhabitants of Lambeth. Mr. Barker, clerk to the churchwardens and over- seers, contended that the exemption claimed in the present case was not authorised by law. After a discussion it was resolved that proceedings against Mr. Rossiter should be delayed until the opinion of Mr. Ludlow, the registrar who signed the certificate of exemption, could be ascertained as to whether in his view such certificate remains in force.

A BEMARKABLE GAME OF CHESS.—The announcement that a clergyman in the North of England is about to play a game of chess on his lawn with living pieces supolied from the children of his parish, recalls one of the most amusing of the "Contes Eccentriques," of Adrien Robert. The Thugs, according to the French writer, who wished to have it all their own way in India, having made five attempts to stab, poison, and blow up the Governor of the East India Company, attributed their want of success- to a talisman in the shape of his grey felt hat, unknown till then in India. His passion was chess, and it was determined by the chief of the sect to challenge him at that game. The stake was the Governor's hat on one side, and the surrender of the ring- leaders of the Thugs on the other. On the plains of Bar- rackpore a chessboard one hundred yards square was marked out. There were elephants for the castles and knights in armour and living pawns. The Governor's men were sup- plied at £25 a piece by his rival. The game lasted all day, for all the piece S were killed as they were taken. Just as the Thug Queen was in danger, having taken the White Queen, the imperturable Governor adjourned to lunch, where he stayed two hours. His rival was in anguish, for the Queen was his own wife. On the return of the Governor the white King advanced to take her, but the magnanimity of the Englishman stepped in, and he took her prisoner. This generosity so demoralised his opponent that in a few more moves the game was over, the conspirators handed over to the mercies of John Company, and India saved from perish- ing. The story is not found- in the histories, no doubt, but it is quite as veracious as most of the special telegrams from the seat of war to be found in the columns of the Figaro.— Pall Hall Gazette.

The tourist season is proving such a failure in Ireland that it is said very few hotel proprietors there will be in a position this year to pay income tax. As a porter on the Cambrian Railway was shutting a carriage door of a train at Mactlynlleth station, on Wednes- day night, he was knocked under the wheels and instan- taneously killed. _ _ _ _

The Birmingham Musical Festival donations which have been received this week increases the total receipts to about £15,200, with one exception the highest amount ever received at a Birmingham festival. Mr. Marriott, M.P., sends from Homburg a letter over'a column and a half long, defending his opposition to the closure by bare majority. The Times, in publishing this lengthy epistle, declares that Mr. Marriott seems to be a politician of one idea, and to be still suffering from "bare majority on the brain." On Thursday morning, at Burnley, John Entwistle was remanded on charges of uttering base coin. The prisoner lived in Burnley, and, it is stated, has carried on for 50 years the practice of making coonterfeit coin. He has been con- victed at Burnley no fewer than 11 times for the offence, and has served a term of six years' penal servitude. Thursday was the anniversary of the battle of Boro- dino, which was fought on September 7, 1812, between the French, under Napoleon Bonaparte, and the Russians, under Kutusoff ; 240,000 men were engaged in the fighting, and a great number were killed on both sides. The Russians re- treated, leaving Moscow, which the. French entered on Sep- tember 14.

At Bolton, on Thursday, a miner, named Henry Cooke, was charged with defrAuding the Worsley Miners' Provi- dent Society. Prisoner, who had acted as secretary to the society, presented a note to the treasurer demanding payment of £7 funeral allowance to the wife of a deceased member. He was paid the money and kept it. An examination of the books subsequently showed that he had embezzled £45. He was remanded.

At the Sheffield Town Hall, on Thursday, James Dillon and Charles Woodhouse were each sent to gaol for two months for molesting two fellow-workmen employed by Messrs. Andrews, steel manufacturers. The prisoners kicked the men because they consented at the firm's desire to go on piece-work. Dillon, Woodhouse, and others, who declined to do so had created such terror in the minds of the workmen, that they were afraid to go to their shops. An extraordinary scene occurred in the licensing court at Liverpool on Thursday. A man named De Silva, who was out of court when his case was disposed of, returned, and, entering the witness-box, shouted that he was ruined and would be heard. The stipendiary ordered him to be quiet, but he would not, and continued to shout that he had not had justice. This be reiterated several times, and ultimately a detective went into the box and brought De Silva out protesting. THE FULHAM TRAGEDY.—An order was made by Mr. Justice Day on Wednesday afternoon, by which the trustees of the will of a Mr. Sykes, were directed to pay £2 a week to Mrs. Sykes, in whose house the Fulham murder was com- mitted last Oaks day, and £2 weekly to her second husband, whose position has altered from that of a student at Harrow and candidate for holy orders to a railway porter. Be has commeneed a divorce suit against his wife. On Thursday morning a vestry meeting was held at Hey- wood to elect three members of the Burial Board. It was announced that the chairman of the board (Mr. Samuel Smith) declined re-election in consequence of irregularities at funerals caused by the neglect of clergymen and dissent- ing ministers to attend on several occasions. The Clerk said the registrar had officiated on the consecrated side, thus laying himself open to an action at law. He would have acted like the registrar.

„ A large contingent from the Local Regiment of the Blue Ribbon Army appeared at the Birmingham annual licsnsing meeting on Thursday to oppose the granting of new licenses. The "captain” claimed his right to be beard on behalf of the Army on the ground that he was a burgess and a rate- payer. The magistrates ignored the claims, stating that the "captain" was not a professional man, and had not given notice. The " ciptain " replied that be bad been studying the licensing laws, and found that be had a right to oppose, and he should consequently appeal to a superior court.

On Thursday the Board of Trade inquiry respecting the stranding of the screw steamer Newhan, of Newcastle, on Shabali reef, while proceeding from Bombay to Marseilles, concluded at North Shields. The court, in giving judgment, considered that the stranding of the steamer was caused by careless navigation; no bearings were taken to ascertain the ship's true position, and the proper course was not set previous to the clonally. The court found the captain, Williant Lewis Grant, in default, and suspended his certi- cate for six months; the chief mate, John William Scrunger, was censured.

NEW Ac r ow "FRACTIONS OF A. PENNY."—Among the last acts passed in the session was one relating to the revenue. It recites that "fractions of a penny" have never been paid by the Bank of England on account of dividends on the National Debt, and the fractions so accumulated unpaid have exceeded £140,000. The Bank of England are new required, when directed by the Treasury, to certify the amount in band arising from "fractions of a penny" not paid on account of dividends, and the Treasury may by warrant order the same to be paid into the Exchequer. By a schedule to the act it appears that up to March 31 last, the "fractions of a penny" have amounted to £143,272 118.2 d. A CLERGYMAN AND THE LODGING-11017SE KEEPER.— Mrs. E. Davies, lodging-house keeper, Colwyn Bay, sued the Rev. Carson Carr, who resides in Derbyshire, for £2B 7s, being for three weeks' use of rooms in her house. Mr. Louis appeared for plaintiff, and Mr. Merrivale, Bangor, was for the defendant. It appeared that the defendant engaged rooms for his wife from the Ist of September, but, on taking possesion of them, Mrs. Carr (lid not find them to her satis- faction, and left the house two days after her arrival, arranging to give £lO to the landlady by way of settlement. An agreement was subsequently drawn up and sig-ned by Mrs. Carr and a friend named Mrs. Leek, but Mr. Carr re- fused to pay the amount, on the ground that he had gone to the wrong house. He, however, offered £4 as recompense for the landlady's loss in not obtaining visitors to take the rooms, but this was not accepted. Judgment was given in favour of plaintiff for £5 to settle the dispute. DARING BURGLARY IN LONDON. —A burglar of apparently high position in his "profession" has fallen into the clutches of justice, and it is not unlikely that he will have to answer a capital charge. He was surprised in an attempt which he was making on Tuesday night upon Hightield House, Stamford Hill, and being surrounded he threatened to murder anyone who laid hands upon him. At length he discharged a couple of revolvers, and Richard Howe, the groom at the house, received such injury that there is little hope of his recovery. The burglar's violence was in vain, for he was secured and disarmed. He gives the name of John Saunders. A search in his house has led to the re- covery of a large quantity of valuables, the proceeds of burglaries in the north of London. Saunders was brought up at the Clerkenwell Police Court, on Wednesday, when the story of a fearful struggle was told, and a remand for a week was ordered. THE CUTLERS' FEAST AT SHEFFIELD. The Cutlers Feast was held at Sheffield on Thursday night, Mr. Albert A. Jowett being Master Cutler for the corning yeac. Respond- ing to the toast of "Her Majesty's Government," Sir Thos. Brassey paid a high tribute to the conduct of offic,rs, seamer, and marines during the recent operations in Egypt. They were skilful as they were brave. The diplomatic difficulties in the adjustment of the Egyptian ques;ion would be great, and they would be best overcome by our showing ourselves strong in arms and magnanimous in council. In eland he cherished the hope that what the Government had done would not be labour in vain.—Mr. Jas. Lowther, responding for the House of Commons, said that institution had been styled the grand inquest of the nation; but recently a great deal of deterioration had been going on. The question to ' be decided now was whether the nation wished it to be merely a law-making machine or the faithful reflex of the varied opinions of all classes and interests of the community. In his opinion the ventilation of the grievances of the subject and the careful scrutiny of supply was a duty far superior to the mere passing of laws such as they were told was the sole duty of the House.

PRESENT POSITION OF WESLEYAN METIIODISAL—The minutes of the Wesleyan Methodist Conference for 1882-83 are printed, and present at a glance the present position of the parent branch :—Wesleyan Methodists in Great Britain, full and accredited church members, 393,754; on trial for church membership, 40,653; ordained ministers, 1,549 • on probation, 81; supernumeraries, 279. In Ireland and Irish missions, full and accredited church members, 24,475; on trial, 776 ;ordained ministers, 200; on probation' 18; super- numeraries, 43. In foreign missions full and accredited church members, 89,369 ; on trial, 12,934 ; ordained ministers, 398 ; on probation, 198 • supernumeraries, 18. French Conference, full and accredited church members, 1,769; on trial, 126; ordained ministers, 27 ; on probation, 1, supernumeraries, 3. Tot ds : Church members, 509,367; on trial for church membership, 54,489; ordained ministers, 2,124; on probation, 298; supernumeraries, 341. The num- ber of ministers and members in the Australian Wesleyan Methodist Church and the Methodist Church of Canada are given in the minutes of their respective confererces. Ninety- three young ministers have recently been recAved into full connection with the Wesleyan Conference—viz , 67 in Great Britain, 4 in Ireland, and 24 in foreign missions.

FOREIGN OFFICE PAPERS RELATING TO THE SUEZ CANAL —Papers were issued on 'Thursday relative to the affairs of the Suez Canal. They extend from January, 1881, to July,• 1882, and deal mainly with questions of purely commercial interest respecting the passage of vessels through the Canal, such as the obligation of masters of ships to show their manifests at Egyptian ports. Canal surcharges, Sze. It also includes a memorial from the Chamber of Shipping of the United Kingdom to Earl Granville, complaining that British shipr,wners have for some years past suffered, and are still suffering very grievdusly, from the Heavy Canal dues and pilDtage charges imposed upon vessels passing through the Cana), and asking his lordship to endeavour to secure a large reduction, in pilotage dues especially, pilotage being held to be altogether unnecessary. To this memorial Earl Granville replied in May last that the pilotage charges were fixed by an inter- national commission, and that discontinuance of the pilot service through the Canal was out of the question. To de- mand a reduction of the Canal dues would be an intolerable interference with a private concern, though the day might arrive when the company might deem it advisable to reduce those dues, or when, in the interests of the public, it may be doirable that it should be reduced by means not incom- patible with the vested interests of shareholders. A table is included amongst the papers, showing that from 1869, when the Canal was opened, to December, 1880, the number of British vepsels passing through the Canal rose from nine vessels, of 6,286 tons, to 1,592 vessels, of 2,500,000 tons. The total number of vessels of other nationalities during the same period was 434, of 64,400 tons.

MILITARY SITUATION. There is little change to record in the military situation. The best news from Ismailia is that two engines are now at work on the railway between Ismailia and Kassasin Lock, and that, consequently, both men and horses are again enjoying the luxury of having enough to eat. Four loco- motives from Suez and two from Port Said are expected at Ismailia daily. Arabi has made a new, but not altogether unexpected move. He has formed an entrenched camp at Es-Salihiyeh, from whence he can threaten both the Suez Canal and the right flank of Sir Garnet Wolseley's force advancing upon Tel-el-Kebir. This position is well chosen by Arabi, as it is peculiarly adapted to serve the purposes of a base for a counter attack. It is on the road from Zagazig to Kantara, and is the terminus of the railway which runa from the former place about two-thirds of the whole way. At this point he is about equidistant from Kassasin Lock to the south and from the nearest point on the Suez Canal to the east. In both directions the desert stretches, but fifteen miles of sand would prove but a slight obstacle to the operations of the Bedouin irregulars, who might be brought up by railway to Es-Salihiyeh in order to make a smart dash on the Canal. The General is said to have been pre- pared for this manceuvre, which will necessitate the careful guarding of the Canal between Kantara and Ismailia, and the avoidance of a too great extension of the British force on the march to Tel-el-Kebir. Supplies continue to be pushed forward to Kassasin with all possible speed, which, however' is at a rate which almost recalls the snail- like progress of the Commissariat in Zulu- land at the time when the country was impatiently await- ing Lord Chelmsford's advance on Ulundi. The difficulty of conveying food and other supplies to the front has so retarded the progress of the army that it is very question- able whether delay at the outset until the transport arrange- ments were in a more advanced state would not have con- duced more to the speedy success of Sir Garnet's march upon Cairo than his hasty and unprepared advance has done. The first blows in the advance from Ismailia achieved brilliant results, but these only rendered it the more im- perative to pursue and completely overthrow the enemy before be could recover from his flight and take up new offensive or defensive positions. Had the allied army in the Crimea marched upon Sebastopol immediately after the rout of the Russians on the Alma, it is well known that Sebasto- pol would have fallen into their bands without further struggle, but delay, though it was brief, gave the Muscovites time to take courage, and the chance of seizing Sebastopol was lost. So, in the present case, an immediate pursuit of Arabi's routed forces would have given Tel-el-Kebir into Sir Garnet Wolseley's hands, but now the Egyptians have re- covered from their panic, have thrown up entrenchments at Es-Salihiyeh, which, as we have said, threaten noth the Suez Canal and the British right flank, and have added to tbe previously formidable defences of Tel-el-Kebir. Already the result is seen in the British operations at Kassasin. Supplies, as has been stated, are being collected there as a sort of advanced base, and an entrenched camp is being; formed for their protection, so that if, when Sir Garnet ad- vances upon Tel-el-Kebir, the Egyptians make a counter attack from Es-Salitaiyeh, a small force at Kassasin will be able to hold the camp. It may be, of course, that the British Commander will not advance upon Tel-el-Kebir until tae rebels have been dislodged from Es-Salihiyeh, in which case the Kassasin camp may have to sustain an attack from Tel- el-Kebir. In either case the unfortunate result of the unavoidable delay in the British advance is equally clear, and shows that,the advantage of Sir Garnet's brilliant successes has been lost. Tel-el-Kebir is nearer than Es-Salihiyeh to Kassasin and is moreover on the direct route to Cairo. It is, therefore, likely to be first attacked ; and, as Sir Garnet's forces will be in communication by- railway with both Kassasin and Ismailia while advancing upon the Egyptian strongheld, tl)ere will be much less fear of a flank attack than if the attack was directed against Es- Salihiyeh. All accounts agree in saying that the defences of Tel-el-Kehir are formidable. Major Macdonald, accom- panied by a dozen Bengal Cavalry, has reconnoitred up to the entrenchments. and describes them as very formidable, with one high and strong earthwork, three smaller ones, and a line of trenches at right angles with the railway. The daring officer and his little band had some difficulty in geiting safely back again, but by taking a roundabout route their fleet steeds saved them. Less demoralisation has followed the most recent defeat of the enetny than might have been expected. Very possibly his success in carrying away the eleven guns through which the Guards charged has somewhat revived his courage. Be that as it may, the Egyptians have thrown up entrenchments only a few miles in advance of General Graham's position, and once again the Fresh Water Canal has been tampered with. Its depth is decreasing, and the supposition is that Arabi has thrown another dm across it. Sir Garnet is con- sequently again compelled to advance and fight for posses- sion of the Canal, when, profiting by former experience, the enemy may make a more desperate defence of it than he did before. It is also said that the country round Tel-el-Kebir has been put under water, with a view, no doubt, to prevent- ng a turning movement at that important point. Strongly fortified as it is, a front attack at Tel-el-Kebir will be attended with much difficulty, and if Arabi has succeeded in protect- ing his flanks with water he will have scored a great advan- tage. If the Egyptians stand to their guns at Tel-el-Kebir as they did at the bombardment of Alexandria, to take this position by storm will be no light matter. It will be the first really serious battle of the campaign. Sir Garnet may, therefore, well wait until all is ready for this arduous enter- prise. At Kassassin, on Wednesday, the splendid body of troops now assembled there were drawn up in general parade. The enemy seems to have thought that the review was the pre- liminary to an immediate advance, and a good deal of firing was indulged in on both sides of the Canal. The British at once replied, but the affair was limited to long-distance firing, and the infantry did not become engaged on either side. A general desire is being manifested for another advance, (ho arrangements for which are completed, but one account says a forward movement is not expected before Saturday. The delay appears to be greater than Sir Garnet anticipated, the Highlanders being still on board ship at Ismailia because of the difficulty of conveying food to the front.

Major Genual Drury Lowe His Royal Highness's sense of the admirable arrangements made by him for strengthening General Graham's hands, and of the soldierly devotion dis- played by the officers and men serving under his command. In His Royal Highness's opinion, the action of the 28th ultimo refutes the arguments of those who contend that heavy cavalry are useless in modern warfare.

div.head: POSITION AT ALEXANDRIA.
div.p: THE POSITION AT ALEXANDRIA.

It is still difficult to understand the military situation at Alexandria. There is no room for fear as to the safety of the British Cleo there, but it cannot be supposed that in keeping itself secure it is doing all that is expected of it. Of course it is also guarding Alexandria from attack, and there is little likelihood of Arabi's forces attempting to capture the city while the British are at Meks and Ramleh. Still, the condition of Alexandria is not satisfactory, and much disquietude has been caused by the arrest of a spy, upon vrhom was found a letter addressed to M. Antonopoulo, who has recently been staying at Alexandria. M. Antono- poulo has been arrested, and a plot, in which several Greeks are said to be implicated, is understood to have been dis- covered, its object being to murder Europeans in Alexaudria in case there should be serious fighting at Ramleh. Possibly there may be only a grain of truth in this rumour, but it illustrates the feverish condition of the people, and shOws how dangerous it is to have fanatical natives going about,as they do, exciting the Arabs by saying the Bedouins are coming. For this offence an Arab was flogged on Monday.

THE MILITARY CONVENTION. It is now beyond doebt that the Military Convention be- tween England and Turkey is agreed upon, and the Sultan's proclamation of Arabi as a rebel has also been issued, so that there is now no reason why the stipulated number of Turkish troops should not land at Port Said as speedily as the transport can convey them there. The proclamation of Arabi accuses him of having disturbed the peace of Egypt from motives of personal ambition, of having caused the death of many persona, brapght about foreign intervention, and compelled England to bombard Alexandria. In con- clusion it declares that the Khedive's authority and prestige must be maintained, and that the Porte will protect his pri- vileges. Arabi's reply to the proclamation will be awaited with interest, bat it would be a relief to everybody were Sir Garnet Wolseley to find himself in a position to deal effectually with Arabi before the Turks land. FRENCH STORIES.

The folhwing pessimist despatches, though probably con- cocted on the Boulevards, should, not (the Daily News Paris correspondent thinks) be hidden under a bushel. The Liberte's special correspondent is supposed to telegraph from Port Said that the English greatly suffered at Kassa- sin. Two equadrins of cavalry were decimated. Since this affair the troops have greatly lost heart. Dysentery makes fearful ravages. An epidemic has attacked the horses, and unless it be stopped in a few days it 101 be impossible to find horses for the artillery. The Courrier du Soir, most likely only trying to trump the above, writes:— "Ismailia, September 4.-I'he situation of the English army is most serious in every point of view. It is in a bad situa- tion, which time can only augment. Demoralisation rapidly increases.

div.head: GERMANS AND SIR GARNET.
div.p: GERMANS AND SIR GARNET.

In speaking of coming events in Egypt, the German papers are, generally speaking, reserved, with the exception of the National Zeitung, which says that the confidence the English have hitherto shown in the generalship of Sir Gar- net Wolseley is not justified by the course of the campaign ; and its unfavourable judgments increase from day to day. He is reproached with not having shown due insight and impartiality in the selection of the staff officers and chief commanders, and in having given the preference to those who served with him in the Ashantee War. He is also blamed for negligence in the arrangements of the transport.

div.head: DISCLOSURES BY MAdbIOUD FEHNIY.
div.p: DISCLOSURES BY MAdbIOUD FEHNIY.

_ An Alexandria telegram says that Mahmoud Felimy, Arabi's late chief military adviser, who was sent as a prisoner to A!exandria last week, has revealed in detail Arabi's plans of defenco, describing tbe positions and strength of the enemy. Mahmoud denies that he was captured, and says he gave himself up—a statement which, it is remarked, is confirmed by the British, though this is scarcely recon- cileable with the language of Sir Garnet's despatch reportiug the capture. Mahmoud's revelations as to Arabi's military dispositions are believed to be accurate, and the substance of them has been telegraphed to Sir Garnet Wolseley, but in addition to his military confession be makes serious charges against several persons in the Khedive's Court, accusing Cherif Pasha, amongst others, of having held treasonable communications with Arabi. THE DUKE OF CAMBRIDGE AND GENERAL DRURY LOWE.

The Field Marshall Commanding in Chief has expressed himself in high terms of approval of the conduct of Major General Drury Lowe, C. 8., commanding the cavalry of the Fgyptian expedition, on the occasion of the attack on General Graham's position on the 28th ultimo, and Sir Garnet Wolseley has been instructed to make known to

div.head: AID FOR THE WOUNDED.
div.p: AID FOR THE WOUNDED.

Four trained nurses, with Dr. Herbert Sieveking, left Liverpool on Saturday for Alexandria for duty in the Egyptian hospitals. They carried a large amount of hos- pital stores, supplied partly by subscription and partly by the generosity of such firms as Messrs. Bell and Co., of Lon- don, and Messrs. Richardson and Co., of Leicester. Lady Strangford and others left on Wednesday via Venice to make arrangements; and another party of nurses, with a large Gonsignment of stores, will leave Liverpool to-day (Saturday). Other stores go out by Admhalty transports. Mr. Cookson writes as follows to Lady Strangford:—"Before the first batch of nurses and medical attendants can now reach Egypt most serious bloodshed will have taken place, and for the ease of the Arab wounded at least no adequate provision will have been made after they have received the first attention of the surgeons on the field. Ac soon as the Egyptians are dislodged from their camp near Alexandria and the safety of that city is secured the Arab population will be sure to flock back, and Nyith them crowds of Europeans. I know the Maltese are with difficulty restrained now, and the Greeks also find it so hard to live in their places of refuge that they also will be returning by thousands. Then will begin the real need of your charitable organisation; indeed, it must begin before you can arrive, * * • and all the funds you can get will. I fear, be too small for your purposes. I can testify myself to the complete absence of any means of meeting the distress in the country itself. I say nothing of the admirable moral effect which your mission cannot fail to have on the Arab population, because your aims are strictly practical and outside such considerations. But who can say what disease may not spring up in th, w ace of war, and how can the value of such help as yours b 3 over-esti- mated in combating it? * * My only apprehension is lest your resources, even if larger than they are likely to be, should prove much too small, when the war and the influx of refugees have produced their almost inevitable results."

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS.

The Highland regiments under Sir E. Hamley have joined the main body between Malisameh and Kassassin. Sultan. and Ferrid Pashas are with Sir Garnet, in readi- ness to take charge of the country in rear of the conquering army.
The Freshwater Canal at Ismailia is falling rapidly, and the water company Las reduced the supply at Ismailia and Port Said.

Sir Garnet Wolselev reports that notwithstanding diligent search nothing has been heard of Lieutenant Gribble of the 3rd Dragoon Guards. Three thousand rifles, says a special correspondent at Alexandria, as well as 6,000 bludgeons, have been discovered in a mosque in that city. A somewhat vague telegram from Port Said states that " some "of Arabi's officers from Es-Salihiyeh have given themselves up at Ismailia. Our engineers are busily entrenching the position at Kassasin, so that it may be easily held by a small force when'the main body begins its advance. There is no talk at Ismailia of an immediate advance, and it is believed that Sir Garnet Wolseley intends to get as many men together as possible before attacking the intrench- ments at Tel-el-Kebir.

The last of the Indian contingent, which sailed on Wed- nesday last for Suez, was composed of a portion of the 6th Bengal Cavalry, and the reserve has been further strength- ened by an additional Madras regiment. M. de Lesseps, a Paris correspondent informs us, arrived In Paris on Saturday evening. He protested against English Intervention in Egypt, and said that since the bombardment a genuine national party had been formed which rallied to Arabi.

There is a report that the officer who commands at Tel- el-Kebir intends to desert to the British, but the rumour is extremely improbable. If the officer's intentions were known to Arabi we may be sure that he would not live to execute it. it is stated that the military authority at, home are arranging for making up the 34,000 troops now engaged in the Egyptian expedition to the full army corps of 36,805 men, and for maintainihg them as far as practicable at that strength.

. A correspondent at Alexandria telegraphs that the native carter accused of murdering Mr. Dobson and Mr. Richard- son, is to be executed. The culprit confessed his gnilt,and at the special request of the Khedive he will be hanged and not shot.

In the Punjab a special transport service his been organ- ised for the English divisions of the Indian expedition. It has been placed under the command of Sir P. Bromheal, is to act independently of the general transport, and is consti- tuted to act with a dying column. . .

It is understood that the Government have decided to send oat three additional battalions of ittf,intry to strengthen the force at Al.xanclria to complete the depots of regiments in action to 150 men by sending out 1,000 Reserve men, and to send out drafts for the Guards.

Mahmeud Fehmy has arrived at Alexandria, and has been handed over to the custody of the Khedive'e authorities with the stipulation that he is not to be shot without the British general at Alexandria being first communicated with, a con- dition which Mahmoud will no doubt appreciate. It is announced that the quarantine imposed on all vessels coming through the Suez Canal on account of cholera re- ports has been relaxed in the case of British transports, it having been arranged that British transports from Aden and Bombay shall only undergo 24 hours' observation at Suez.

A correspondent states that the assertions made at Ismailia and elsewhere regarding the wanton destruction of gardens and other property of the natives by British troop are simply gross libels. He had everywhere been struck with the scrupulously honourable manner in which the troops con- ducted themselves in that respect. A Vienna correspondent states with confidence that if any reverse befall the English troops in Egypt the policy of Russia will at once be declared. Complete preparations have been made for a prompt concentration of troops in Bessarabia, and the Russian Government have been asking permission of Roumania for the reconstruction of a railway which was of great service during the late war, but which the Roumanians themselves destroyed on the conclusion of peace. Little is doing at Ramleh. On Monday our gunners opened upon a new redoubt erected by the Egyptians on our advanced left, and some damage is believed to have been done to it. The Arab fire, however, is said to have been very accurate, though, fortunately, it hurt no one. Lieu- tenant Smith-Dorrien, with a small party of the Mounted Infantry, made a dashing reconnaissance of the enemy's position, penetrating further within his lines than has yet been done.

A pleising feature of the war news is the change of tone observable in Italy, as shown by an article published by the Diritto. This organ denies that any antipathy to England has ever been entertained by Italy, and declares that the services rendered to her by the former country remain 'vividly in her recollection. All circumstances, it declares, tend to the maintenance of the friendly ties which unite Italy to Great Britain, " which is justly styled the mistress of civilised peoples. Even though there may be discussions on some questions, these do not partake of the character of hatred, but of the loyalty displayed in the intercourse of friends."

div.head: LATER DETAILS.
div.p: LATER DETAILS.

REPORTED PRO ..,'LA.MATION OF A RELIGIOUS WAR. The following appeared in a second edition of Thursday's Daily News Outposts, Kassasin, Wednesday night.—At midday, es described ln my last telegram, the enemy appeared on the south canal bank, and also on the north side, but towards the west position of the camp. The 19th Hussars having driven the Egyptians from the south, galloped across the canal bridge, and for two miles to the second-named position, to which I accompanied them. We found a force of rebels near, apparently about 400 to 500, comprising infantry and cavalry. The former retired, but the cavalry kept up a brisk fire for nearly a quarter of an hour. Unlike the Hussars, half of whom dismounted, the Egyptians fire from horseback. Their bullets flew thickly past us, but did no damage, the enemy, as usual, firing too high. .The Egyptian loss was considerable, bearing in mind the brief duration of the skirmish. I have counted six dead bodies within a short distance of where I stand. This is by far the most determined demonstration made by the enemy since the battle of Kassasin, and indicates the near approach of a decisive conflict. All our horse with Generals Drury Lowe and Wilkinson have come oat, and the whole position is now watched by mounted rifles, Hus- sars, and ifingal lancers cavalry. The only casualties on our side are Captain Holland, who volunteered from the 15th Hussars, and whose wound appears not to be dangerous; and also a private of the 19th Hussars. Reports have reached the camp that Arabi has been joined by several chiefs' who have proclaimed a religious war against the English, and that the Egyptian force at Tel-el-Kebir numbers at least 60,000. I merely give the report, however, for what it is worth.
RUMOURED SECRET TREATY BETWEEN ENG-

LAND AND TURKEY. A Times Paris telegram says:—The rumour that Eng- land had signed, along with the Military Convention, a secret treaty on the ultimate organisation and administra- tion of Egypt is gaining more and more credit. Men in good position to have informatian believe in the existence of this treaty, and the delay in the negotiations is ascribed to there having been two treaties to negotiate. A Russian to-day assured me that Russia had aide% the understanding between England and Turkey, because Turkey was thus removed from the Austro-German influence; secandly, because, England being satisfied in Egypt and France in Tunis, would show less jealously of Russia in the direction of Constantinople; and because Russia at this moment fears reopening the Eastern question either ty diplomacy or arms, England being in% agreement with the Sultan and the Khedive Europe would have no right to require settlement by Congress. HANGING THE MURDERER OF MEF:SRS. RICHARDSON AND DOBSON. A telegram from Alexandria, dated Thursday, 7-27 a.m., states :—The native carter who was sentenced to ceath for the murder of Messrs. Dobson and Richardson and other Europeans was hanged by men of the native police at seven o'clock this morning. The condemned man was conducted at six o'clock through the town, escorted by a detachment of English troops, who formed a square round the gallows. The murderer walked throughout with an air of defiance. Several hundred Europeans, but only a few natives, wit-

nessed the execution. Only when the English detachment withdrew the Arabs came out in larger numbers. A Central News telegram adds that a detachment of the P6th tnent escorted the prisoner to the place of execation, while the 95th formed a cordon round the spot to prevent rescue. The prisoner bore a placard inscribed, "Atti Hassan, con- demned to death for the murder of Europeans in June." The sentence was carried out in a barbarous fashion by native police. GENERAL ADVANCE OF THE TROOPS. _ _ _

• A telegram from Ismailia dated Thursday, 9-15 a.m., says : —" The troops at Tel-el-Mahuta are going to move up to Kassasin on Saturday, and on the same day the troops at Nefiche will push forward to Tel-el-Mahuta, going to the front on Monday. The troops there will make a forwald move on Saturday. reaching Kassasin on Monday. All the regiments will carry two day's rations. Sir Garnet Wolseley goes to the front on Saturday."

div.head: ANOTHER DISCOURSE ON }TARES AND
div.p: ANOTHER DISCOURSE ON }TARES AND
RABBITS.
REPLY TO "ANGLO-SCOTUS." _

It will, no doubt, relieve the mind of "Anglo-Scotus" to 1 know that we were quite aware that the phrase "First catch your hare" was of doubtful authenticity when we used it, just as we are aware that the "cony "may mean either the cuniculus or the liyrax-Syriacus. In the thirtieth chapter of Proverbs, 26th verse, it is said: "The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks ;" and recent commentators say this passage refers to the Hyrax- Syriacus, or the daman, an animal about the size of our hare, and whose dwelling is emphatically among the rhcks, being seldom, if ever, seen in other places. But some say the rabbit, and others the mountain-mice. Fortunately for our present purpose the question of "Anglo-Scotus " is easily answered by a reference to page 158 of Bishop Wil- kins' Essay, published in folio, in 1688, a somewhat rare book, and not likely to be within the reach of many readers. We, therefore,transcribe the bishop's words for the benefit of readers of The Examiner. He is treating of beasts, which he says may be distinguished by their several shapes, pro- perties, uses, food, their tameness, or wildness, and firstly of "whole-footed beasts," secondly of "cloven-footed beasts," and third of "clawed beasts not rapacious," in which category, after speaking of the baboon, ape, monkey, and sloth, he pioceeds to the " hare-kind, having two long teeth in the lower jaw before, and two others opposite to those (though not quite so long) hi the upper jaw, most of which are counted ruminant, because when they have, by the help of their incisorcs, filled their mouths with meat, they after chew it over again with their molares or grinders, but they are not properly ruminant, because they have but one stomack, out of which they do not fetch up their food being once swallowed. These may be distinguished into the 1 bigger-kind ; whether such as are covered with hair; living • either above ground; being, of all others, the most fearful (3) hare, !eyelet, (Lepus) underground; either tkat with long ears and a short tail; or that with short ears and a long tail, being said to sleep all the winter (4) conny, rabbet, (cuniculus) marmotto, Mus. Alpinus." Giving on the margin a reference to the eleventh chapter of Leviticus, which prescribes what beasts may and what may not be eaten by the children of Israel, and in the sth verse of which the "coney " is forbidden them as the hare is in the 6th verse. Thus proving that the learned bishop meant a rabbit when he spoke of a "cony," in this he was only following other Englishmen who had had occasion to refer to the " cony " in their writings—as we shall see further on. Wedgwood, page 168, Eng. Diet., says: The name is said by Pliny and other writers to be originally Spanish, and through the Latin it seems to have spread to the Germanic and Celtic stocks. In several of the forma cited, the name seems to signify king, or little king, and thus was translated into Bob. Kret/jk, a prince or little king, also a rabbit or coaey (cuniculus)i. " Anglo-Scotus" has given so many interesting references to hares that it may not be uninteresting if we give a few to the cony from a source not so accessible to the general reader. In Eduard Mii•zner's Selections from Early English Literature, now in course of publication, he gives vol. ii., page 467, the following under the diversified heading, " Coning, conning, ,conig, cunig, leonnig, coni, couni(s) ": Old French, connin, or connil ; Dutch, konijn ; Swedish and Danish, kanin, ; Scctch, con- inghis, pl. conil ; Italian, coniglio ; Spanish, conejo ; Portu- guese, coelho ; Latin, cuniculus; New English, cony—with the following illustrations : "We shale do the conyng, ant make roste is loyne. Polit. Sat. p. 191. He coin himself ycharged with conyng and hares. Will, 182. With officers as conyng surveyours. Nuese ,P. p. 9. Hic cuniculas, a conynye. Wr. Voc. p. 220. 231, and connyinge p. 188. Have Iwe nowther conig ne cat That thai ne er etin. Minot p. 37. Ne scat ther boo fou no gra, ne cunig ne ermine. Mor. Ode, st. 182. Cony, cuniculus, Pr. P. p. 90. The while he (se, the raton) caccheth conynges, He coveiteth noght yours caroyne. P. Pl. 384. Sethe welle thy conyngus, Lib. Cur. Coo. p. 8. cf. 20. Connygez in cretoyne colourede. Mort. Arth. 197. Conyys hole, cunus, Pr. P. p. 90. Connics there were also playenge, Ch. R. of R. 1404. Connyngere, or connynge trthe, cunicularium, Pr. P. p. 90. With them that ferett robbe conyngerys, Lydg. M. P. p. 174." This will probably be sufficient to satisfy the curiosity of "Anglo- Scotus " and any other inquirer after the meaning of the word "cony." And now let us say that specimens of the " Belgian bare," a bigger, and, it is said, a better breed, have been introduced here since last" Anglo- Scotus " wrote. So much for hares and rabbits, but what possible good can it do him to ferret out who or what we are? When once we adopt the French fashion of signing our articles he will know all about us, perhaps. Meanwhile it is amusing to find a well-read writer so much at fault in a sporting sense, on account of a simple enallage. If it will help him, let him know, that part of our patronymic was, " Cunningham " (King's house), and that our father was a namesake of one of the forty-two proud possessors of that name, in the county to which he belonged and from whence it sprung (in the time of Malcolm Canmore.) The arms are " pitchfork," and the legend or " motto " " over fork over," many a time as ignorantly called "fork over," as the aforesaid phrase was called first catch your hare. The original owner of the name took "a shake fork" (very like Shakespeare, isn't it) and scattered-hay over Malcolm Can- more when escaping from Macbeth, and the name Cunning- ham was given to him ; the first part of which is exactly the word we have been discussing. In conclusion, we endorse the sentiments of " Anglo-Scotus," and hope be will keep the subject of hares and rabbits before the public both in season and out of season.

div.head: WOUNDING ON THE HIGH SEAS.
div.p: WOUNDING ON THE HIGH SEAS.

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, before Messrs. J. Brundritt, and A. Thomas, Rebabath Robinson, captain of the schooner Caledonia, was charged with wounding a seaman named John Dority, on the high seas' on the 21st July last.—Mr. John Paxton (of the firm of Tyndall and Paxton, Liverpool), prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Trade; and Mr. Lake appeared for the defendant.—The complainant stated that he joined the schooner Caledonia at Plymouth, on the 18th July, as an A. 8., the defendant being master. The vessel sailed the same morning for Hamburg with a cargo of china clay. On the morning of the 21st July, about 8-40 a.m., the crew, with the exception of the man who was left at the wheel, went down into the cabin to breakfast. The master, the mate and his wife sat at the table, and Crabb, another able seaman, and com- plainant, sat on a chest away from the table. Complainant ate his food with a sheath knife, and after he had finished his beef he went to the table to help himself to more. He I picked up a fork which was !vino.' on the table to take a Piece of meat out of the dish, and whilst doing so the ' Icaptain leaned over the table and dealt him a violent blow across the hand with the knife he was using. saying "that's a Greenlander's trade mark," and that in future when he wanted anything he must first ask for it. The captain struck him on the back of his hand with the edge of the knife inflicting a deep wound from the second to the fourth finger. The wound bled very profusely at first, and con- tinned to bleed all day. A man named Henry Osborne, who was in charge of the wheel, bandaged the wound as well as he could with plaister, which the captain provided. After complainant's hand had been ban- daged, the captain came down to the scuttle and said " Johnny, I hope you will look over this; I have never used a knife before." Prosecutor replied that the wound was in- flicted, and it was no use crying over spilt milk. The schooner arrived at a place called Harburg, a few miles from Hamburg, on the 24th July. As soon as they landed he went to the consul, who gave him a letter for the captain, and the latter took him to the hospital, where he remained 16 days. When be came out be declined to return to Eng— land with the schoener as he thought his life was in danger. Since his return to England he had seen Dr. Bagnall, of Runcorn. His third finger was permanently injured. His second finger was also hurt, but he believed it would recover. He left his clothes on the vessel, and had only had 10s. of his wages.—Cross-ex a mined by Mr. Lake, complainant stated that he did not say he would throw his sheath knife at the captain. The captain offered to give him a month's wages and pay his passage hack to England. He had seen men rap each other before, but never with a knife. He was wounded on the same arm when he was 13 years of age, but the wound had not interfered with him in any way.— James Crabb, an able bodied seaman, gave confirmatory evidence. In answer to Mr. Lake, he said he was sure defendant struck complainant with the edge of the knife After the blow had been inflicted the defendant said he was very sorry for what he had done, and that he did not mean to cut Dority. He saw complainant pick up his knife and go on deck. He did not hear him say he would throw it at defendant.—Dr. Rivall said that on Wednesday, the 30th August, he examined Doritv's right hand. The wound, which was then healed, had been arm incised wound running diagonally upwards from the long fidger to the inside of the hand, and was about 21 inches in lergth. The sinew of the third finger must have been cut through, and it would never be better. He did not think the long finger was permanently injured. He did not think the wound could have been made I by the back of the knife without it had been brought down with very great violenee.—Mr. Lake, for the defence, con- tended that the defendant had had great provocation, and that he had no intention of cutting the man's hand.—The defendant reserved his defence, and was bound Over in one surety of £5O and himself in £5O, to app,,ar for trial at the next Knutsford Sessions.

div.head: 1 POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: 1 POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
