div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 9, 1882.

Tem authorities at Dublin Castle are, we think, to be congratulated on the success which has attended their efforts to suppress the spirit of discontent and rebellion in the ranks of the constabulary; and, on the other hand, the insubordinate members of the force are to be commended for the very candid confession they have made of their error, no less than for the very handsome nature of their submission. The dis- turbance, happily, has been checked in the bud, other- wise it might have assumed very alarming proportions, when its suppression would, consequently, have been all the more difficult; but, thanks to the energy, tact, and above all, the firmness displayed by the Lord- Lieutenant, the Chief Secretary, and other lesser oficials of the Irish Executive, a very grave difficulty has been surmounted without that serious injury to life, and especially to property, which was at one time so much feared. We do not for one moment dispute that the men have not grievances which require re- dressing; we doubt net that during the past two years--consequent chiefly upon the Land League, agi- tation—they have, in the discharge of their duty, had to sacrifice many comforts; certainly they have had to encounter many dangers; but it is not to be expected that they can improve their position by flying in the face of all discipline, and that, too, at a time when ' their grievances were actually being inquired into by a Commission. Such conduct is not likely to meet with the sympathy of the public; and it must be dealt with ' as it has been by the powers that be in such a way as to prevent its recurrence at another time. A few facts relating to this excellent force may be read with in- terest at the present time, and they will serve to show what has led up to the dispute. At the outset, it should be statel that the Irish police force has ac- quired an enviable notoriety for its efficiency and its loyalty. In these respects it sets an excellent example to the police forces of other countries; and it would, therefore, have been a pity had its fair fame been sullied by a protracted encounter with authority at a very critical period in the history of the country. Unlike the police forces in England and Scotland, the constabulary of Ireland is under the control of one man, the Inspector-General, and it is more like an army of soldiers than a police force. The members are drilled and trained like an army, they are like soldiers quartered in barracks; and all over the country the men are called upon to perferm identical duties and to submit to identical regulations. The men are not simply, as police officers are in Angland and Scotland, accepted for one city or municipality, but for the whole of Ireland, and they are moved from city to city, from town to town, or village to village, as occasion may require, and just as soldiers would. Ever since, as we have said, the commencement of the Land League agitation, the men have been compelled to submit to much harder work, to endure greater privations, and to often risk their lives in the discharge of their duty; whilst on the other hand there has not been a corresponding allowance made for them in the shape of remuneration. A representation was some time since made to the Executive upon the matter, and it is quite clear the authorities at the Castle had not been unmindful of the claims of the men, for just before the adjournment of Parliament a grant of £lBO,OOO was made for distribution among the con- stabulary to recoup the members for their extra services and their extra expenditure, for not un- frequently were they put to expense. This grant, however, received but a tardy assent from Parlia- ment; whilst a Bill which had for its object the increase of pay of the officers of the force was passed through the House of Commons without much difficulty. The men were not mentioned in it, they

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, SEPTEMBER 9, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, SEPTEMBER 9, 1882.

considered it unfair, they became exasperated, and the agitation for the redress of their grievances com- menced. A few of the men were selected as leaders, communications were opened with the force in sit parts of the country, and various steps were takcn which pointed to insubordination, and was so treated by the ffuthoritiee, who straightway proceeded to extirpate it. Meanwhile a few of the Limerick members of the force were peremptorily dismissed the serviee for refusing, as it afterwards transpired, to share quarters with a few soldiers at New Pallas, but the general bulk of the men were of opinion that it was in consequence of the part these men had taken in the early stages of the agita- tion. Sympathy was aroused in Limerick, Dublin, and other places; some of the colleagues of the men threw off their badges and deserted their beats, , while the others proposed to resign en bloc. A I meeting of the men, however, wes first summoned for last Thursday evening, in Dublin, to decide upon a course of united action, and it was forbidden by the authorities as contrary to the regulations. This only determined the men to be more firm in their resolve, aud the meeting was consequently held, but two hundred and thirty-four members who attended it were on Friday summarily dis- missed. Some of their comrades again deserted, but others took the more straightforward and safe course of tendering their resigna- tions. This, in brief, is the history of the movements; what followed is yet fresh in the recollection ot our readers. An appeal was, under the circumstances, at once made by the Lord Lieutenant for special con- stables, and this was backed up by a proclamation from the Lord Mayor of Dublin calling upon the in- habitants to support the Executive in the pressing emergency, and inviting them to do their utmost to maintain order in the city. To the credit of the people of Dublin, be it recorded, no less than 665 special constables were very soon enrolled; and these gentlemen appear to have discharged their duty with satisfaction to everybody but the Lord Mayor, who proposed to enrol another lot of constables. His questionable intentions have been frustrated by the submission of the constabulary. The members of the force who had in the impulse of the moment deserted their beats returned to their duty on Saturday evening, not as was stated on condition that their comrades should be reinstated, nor indeed upon any condition whatever, except to save themselves from being dismissed on Sunday morning. The Executive could not have accepted them under any other circumstances. It was necessary for the sake of order that the surrender should be most complete, and that it has been. That the dismissed men very soon deeply deplored their insub- ordination is sufficiently proved by the abject memo- rial which nearly 200 of them submitted to the Com- missioners on Monday. In it they say: "We have been guilty of a gross breach of discipline by holding a meeting ccatrary to orders, and beg to apologise for having done so, and hope you may be pleased to recommend our case to his Excellency's favourable consideration for reinstatement in the force." It is gratifying to note that the men in their memorial repudiate all political or disloyal motives, which had been attributed to them, because were there any grounds for such an accusation they would be better out of the force than in it. The Lord Lieutenant seems to have no doubt upon this matter, and strong in the support with which he has been surrounded on all sides he has happily been able to take a very merciful view of the men's behaviour. His Excel- lency can afford to temper justice with mercy. Accordingly, in answer to the appeal of the men, he has announced that he has appointed a careful inquiry to be held into the recent conduct and previous char- acter of each one of the memorialists. He says he will himself personally review the result of the inquiry, and such of the memorialists will be reinstated to the force as appear to be deservini of reinstatement. Such is the position in which the matter now rests. His Excellency's reply, which has given every satis- faction, would seem to mean that the majority of the dismissed men will be restored to their former posts. Of course, there must be one or two ringleaders or black sheep among _them, and these will probably be allowed to remain outside the pale of the constabulary. The men's grievances will also be inquired into and redressed where necessary, and it is to be hoped that the arrangements made for their future comfort will be such as to render the resort to so extreme a course as a strike again unnecessary. Strikes are to be de- precated at all times and under all circumstance, and a protracted strike amongst the members of the Irish constabulary at a moment sueh as the present would have been nothing more nor less than a national calamity productive of untold mischief.

sine for August. His Lordship said that "to carefully con- sider the words So help me God,' meant the renunciation of God's mercy, the invocation of a curse, the assumption that we know better than the Deity how He ought to treat us, that we have the right and the power to direct what that treatment should be." If these words be true, his E.ninence says, are they not equally true of "Forgive us oar trespasses as we forgive them that trespass against us?" Either the latter expression is a presump- tuous sin, or Lord 6berbrooke's interpretation will not stand. The abolition of the oath should not be brought about until the nation is asked to give its opinion in the matter. To do away with the oath would make the people less Christian, and as a result intellectual and moral anarchy would be brought about authority would weaken; the collective will of the nation would shake off all rule, because men would, one by one, break away from all law except his own will. To a people in such a state the words "So help me God" would, no doubt, be a provo- cation, and an oath a contemptible superstition; and his eminence asks "What conscience would there be left in such men ?" There would be no security left; the moral nature would be confounded. After treating the article at con- siderable length the writer concludes thus : "Every enabling Act of Parliament whereby those who refuse to recognise God and His laws shall be admitted to make laws for us, is nothing less than a covert exclusion of 'God from the counsels and commonweal of England. A few men will do this thing, consciously knowing what they do; a malti- tude will do it unconsciously, not knowing and not seeing until too late that they have been used to destroy our ancient and sacred commonwealth, for which many would rather give their lives." This, of course, is all very good, but it is beside the real question at issue—the right of a constituency to elect whom it pleases within certain limits as its representative, and the right of that representative to discharge all the duties which the law has cast upon him.

The news from the seat of war is not this week very eventful; and with the exception of a few skirmishes there have not been any encounters with the enemy. Arabi has, however, recently shown a more offensive attitude, and he seems more determined than ever to impede Sir Garnet Wolseley's advance. How far he will be successful a few days will prove. The transport is now in much better work- ing order, progress has been made with the collection of supplies at Kassasin, and the arrangements for an immediate dash upon Cairo are now almost complete. The Anglo- Turkish Military Convention has been signed, and Turkish troops are immediately to be landed in Egypt, Port Said being the place of debarkation agreed upon. Here they are likely to do less mischief than anywhere else ; and a sharp look-out will doubtless be kept upon their movements by the British forces. At last the Sultan has submitted to a proclamation toeing issued declaring his friend Arabi a rebel, and exhort- ing the people to obey the Khedive. The proclansation states that the decoration conferred on Arabi by the Sultan was bestowed on him, at the instance of Dervish Pasha, in consequence of Arabi' s protestations of fidelity; and it is worth while to note as showing how submissive the Sultan has been that the original draft of the proclamation con- tained no mention af the decoration, The Sultan also declares in the proclamation that the maintenance of the Khedive's authority and the upholding of his prestige are indispensably necessary. How far his Majesty is sincere will be proved by his subsequent actions. The result of the approaching fight at Tel-el-Kebir, where the enemy is very strongly entrenched, will be eagerly awaited. The organ of the medical profession, the Lancet, contained a couple of weeks a)4o an excellent article against the detestable habit of taking "nips" of alcohol between meals, and it has since spoken strongly against the growing practice of smoking cigarettes incessantly. For the benefit of Young smokers and those who indulge freely in cigarettes I quote a few passages from this recent article, because the sooner the injurious habit is abandoned the better. "We have not a word," says the Lancet," to say against smoking at suitable times and in moderation, nor do our remarks at this moment apply to the use of cigars or pipes. It is against the habit of smoking cigarettes in large quantities, with the belief that these miniature doses of nicotine are innocuous, we desire to enter a protest." After pointing out it is owing to the way the tobacco leaf is shredded, coupled with the fact that it is brought into moredirect relation with the mouth and air passages than when smoked in a pipe or cigar, that the free consumption of cigarettes is objection- able, the writer continues :—" It is no uncommon practice for young men who smoke cigirettes habitually to consume from eight to twelve in an hour, and to keep this up for four or five hours daily. The total quantity of tobacco used may not seem large, but beyond question the volume of smoke to which the breath organs ot the smoker are exposed, and the characteristics of that smoke as regards the propor- tion of nicotine introduced into the system, combine to place the organism very fully under the influence of the tobacco. A considerable number of cases have been brought under our rotice during the past few months, in which youths and young men who have not yet completed the full term of physical develepment bare had their health seriously im- paired by the practice of almost incessantly smoking cigarettes. It is well that the fact should be known, as the impression evidently prevails that any number of these little whiffs must needsbe perfectly innocuous, whereas they often do infinite harm." FLACCUS.

WIDNES WESLEYAN OLECITIT. —Well-attended ser- vices were held in Victoria-rcad chapel, Widnes, on Sunday morning and evening, when the Rev. R. Harper, the new superintendent of the circuit, preached his introductory sermons. Collections were made in aid of the trust fund.

USING OBSCENE LANCIIIACtE. —Oa Saturday, at the Runcorn Police Court, a woman named Mary Casey was fined 10s. and 17s. 8,1. costs for having, on the 6th July, used obscene- language in the streets at Runcorn.—Tbomas Morris, a young man, was tined 10t. and costs for having, on the previous day, been guilty of drunkenness and disorderly behaviour in Bridge-street.

CONCERT AT WIDNES.—With the object of aiding a movement which has been started by the Irish Catholics of Widnes for the formation of a "national brass band," a vocal and instrumental concert was given in the Volunteer Hall, on Saturday evening, by the Sarstield brass band. The promoters succeeded in securing a large audience, and a considerable sum will be added to the fund. The songs and selections, which were naturally Irish in sentiment, were well rendered, and greatly appreciated by the audience. THE Clunks's IN RUNCORN WESLRYA.N CIRCUIT. The Rev. E. J. Robinson, who has taken charge of the Run- corn Wesleyan Circuit in place of the Rev. J. Nowell, preached in St. Paul's Chapel for the first time on Sunday morning, and in the evening in Halton-road Chanel. The Rev. Sydney Met% successor to the'Rev. J. Bateman, preached at Halton-road Chapel in the morning, and in St. Paul's Chapel in the evening. There were large congregations at each service, and collections were made in aid of the day schools.

AFtIitTLT, BY A SiTLOR, AT RUNCORN. —A seaman, named William Evans, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. John Brundrit, to answer a charge of assaulting David Davies, captain of the vessel Sarah Davies. The prisoner pleaded guilty. From the statement of the prosecutor it appeared the prisoner went on the vessel Sarah Davies and commenced to quarrel with the men. The prosecutor ordered him ashore' and then entered into conversation with Mr. Thomas, a shipbroker, when the prisoner rushed at him and etruck him a severe blow on the eve, inflicting a wound from which blood flowed freely. Prisoner, who said he had bad some mink, alleged that he was first struck by Davies. Mr. Brundrit sentenced the prisoner to a month's hard labour, remarking that he must be taught that he could not commit an unpro- voked assault with impunity. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.---The usual fort- nightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tues- day, when there were preseLt the Rev. Canon Barclay (chairman), the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. J. Ashton, I'. Norman, Fisher, Whittaker, Baguley, Challoner, Harrison, C. Rigby, Midwood, Weir, Daruyshire, R. Ashton, Walling- ton, Hall, Andrews, Elighfield, and W. IL Linaker (deputy clerk). There was also present Mr. Dansey, the Local Government Board inspector.—The master of the house reported that there were 187 inmates in the house, com- pared with 167 in the corresponding week of last year. The amount of out-door relief paid was £65 17s 4d, agair.st 17s 3d in the corresponding month of last year. A letter was read from the Rev. J. Thompson, of St: Mary's Church, Latchford, Warrington, stating that a few days ago he heard with regret that the Catholic inmates of the Runcorn Union were by some oversight without the assistance of a visiting priest. He had since had. occasion to speak with His Lordship the Bishop of the diocese on the matter, and he had commissioned Mr. Thompson to visit the Union in his name, and attend to the wants of the Catholics who may be inmates of it. He put posed paying a visit on Wednes- day afterooon next, if all was avell.—Mr. Robert Ashton : Let him pay it.—The Chairman: There is no reason why he should not.—This was all the business of public interest.

A BUILDING SOCIETY'S TROUBLES IN WIDNES. —An old wodian named Mary Doyle was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of being in a house in Grenfel-street, belonging to the Warrington Permanent Benefit Building Society, for an unlawful pur- pose, to wit, to steal.—Prisoner said she was guilty of taking a bucket of water.—From the opening statement of Mr. Draper (Messrs. Robert Davies & Co.), who prosecuted, it appeared the society had a number of empty houses in Widnes, and to prevent them from being damaged, the windows were securely boarded up and the doors locked. Notwithstanding these precautions the houses had been broken into, and doors, grates, and other fittings carried away. From the house in question two cupboard doors had le!en carried away, and other damage done. On Monday last, Mr. Marsh, the agent to the society, went to the house, and found the prisoner in the kitchen. She was drawing a bucket full of water, and she was given in custody on the present charge. The Tuesday previous the house was per- fectly secure, and the fastenings must have been broken to effect an entrance.—The Chairman (Mr. Pilkington) said this practice must be stopped, and fined the prisoner ss. and costs, or in default, seven days' hard labour. Ho hoped • hie sentence would be a warning to others as well as herself.

HOLY TRINITY DAY SCHOOLS, RTJNCOR,N.—The Government report of the condition of this school, which has just been received, is a most satisfactory one, and shows that the school is in a state of great efficiency. In several standards as high as a hundred per cent. of the scholars have passed the examination, and the money grant exceeds that of any previous year. Altogether the school is in a very flourishing condition.

THE SCHOOL BOAkD AT WORK AT WIDNES.—Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the Widnes School Bcard, appeared before the magistrates, on Wednesday, to prosecute the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school, and a tine of 5s was imposed in each case :—John Spooston, James Carr, Pstrick Duffev, James Griffiths, Stephen White, Thomas Hayes, John McCann, Anriie Whalley, and Michael Price. The cases were of the ordi- nary character. A WIDNES BUTCIIER'S Ben PRICTICE.—Before Mr. G Pilkington and Mr. H. S. Hall, at Wines Petty Sessions on Wednesday, a butcher named William Bolton was sum- moned to answer a charge of obstructing the footpath in Waterloo-road, on the 26th ult. He pleaded guilty. P.C. Skinner said the defendant was standing outside his shop selling meat, causing a great crowd to assemble, in conse- quence of which no passenger could move along the foot- pith. Mr. Superintendent Barker observed that this was a very bad practice, and the Bench fined the-defendant I.os. and costs.

WIDNES DRUNKAIIDS.—A.t Widues Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. John Brock, the following persons were each charged with drunkenness and fined as follows :—John Cannon, ss. and costs; Bridget Campbell, ss. and costs, Samuel Howell, 7s. dd. and costs; Patrick Walsh, ss. and coats; Patrick Kork,., 7s. 6d. and costs.—On Wednesday the following persons were brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions charged with drunkenness, and a fine was inflicted in each case :—Patrick Whelan, John Redman, Patrick Burns,_Rose Kelly, John White, Henry Campbell, and Catherine Power.

• THE ROBBERY F Roar A WIDNES PAWASHOP.—The prisoners in this case, John Butler, eleven years of age, and Mary Cullen, his mother, were again brought before the magistrates at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday. They were charged with having, on Monday, the 28th ult., stolen a dress of the value of 19s. from the pawnshop of Mrs. Hannah Jameson, Anne-street, West: Mr. Husband defended. —The depositions of the witnesses were read over, and a resumd of which was published in Saturday's Examiner.— Mr. Husband referred to the fact of Mr. G. J. Nield, pawn- broker, Faruworth, taking the shawl from a boy eleven years of age, and remarked that Butler had no right to be in the box, and asked for his discharge.—The Bench, after some consideration, complied with this request: when Mr. Hus- band contended there was no case against Cullen, there was not a tittle of evidence against her.—The Bench were, how- ever, of opinion there was a prima facie case, and com- mitted the prisoner to the Sessions for trial.—Bail was granted. A WIDNES WIFE DESERTER SENT TO GAOL. Michael Schaffer, a German, was brought up on remand at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, charged with having on the 7th April, 1881, run away from Widnes, leaving his wife and four children chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union.—Mr. Hartley, clerk to the Guardian., appeared to prosecute, and stated that so long ago as the date mentioned in the information, the prisoner's wife made an application to the then relieving officer for relief on account of her husband's desertion. The Guardians granted her 4s. per week, which she received regularly up to a month ago, when it was increased 10.45. 6d. per week. The total amount she had received was £l3 6s. 10d. Until a month ago the prisoner had not been in Widnes, and a week ago he was apprehended at Wigan. He now denied that he was the woman's husband, but he should be able to show that he was her husband by repute, and a well-known character in the town, which would be sufficient to justify a conviction. —Mr. John Scannell, relieving officer, gave evidence, and P.S. Clarkson was Called. He said he had known the pri- soner for the last seven years, and the woman lived with him in Waterloo-road, and was hie wife by repute.—The prisoner asked for the marriage lines to be produced, but acknow- ledged that he was the "woman's husband in one sense."— Mr. Hartley pressed for the extreme penalty to be inflicted. The Bench said it was a bad case.end sentenced the prieoner- to two months' imprisonment with hard labour. A WIDNES PUBLICAN IN THE MESHES OF THE LAW.— Joseph Rogers, landlord of the Ivy Green, was charged at Widnes Petty Session, on Wednesday, with committing a breach of the Licensing Act by selling drink to a drunken person ; and Peter Lawton, a labourer, was charged with being drunk on licensed premises.—P.C. Skinner stated that on Saturday, the 26th ult.,he was on duty in Waterloo-road, when he saw a man dragging the defendant, who was very drunk, along Pitt-street in the direction of Wellington- street. They entered the Ivy Green Inn, and shortly after- wards the officer followed them. He found Lawton and his companion with a glass of beer before them, and thereupon j asked Mrs. Rogers, who was attending to the bar, why she bad served a drunken man with beer. She made no reply, but Lewton exclaimed," Me drunk! I have only just come out of the yard," and he drank the beer. He was so drunk that he could not stand still, and was aided home by his companion.—Mr. Husband, who defended, commented unon the conduct of the constable following Lawton in the ma- ner in which he had, characterising it as sneaking and no- English, and said it was the constable's duty to warn Mrs. Rogers not to serve him.—He called Lawton, who stated he j was perfectly sober when he entered .the Ivy Green, and denied that his companion had to help him home.—James ! McMullen said he was in the bar when Lawton entered. Lawton was perfectly sober.—Elizebeth Lawton, mistress of the house where the defendant and his wife lodged, also as- serted that the defendant was sober.—Defendant Rogers also stated Lawton was sober to look at.—Mr. Superintendent Barker said the defendant Rogers was last week convicted of a similar offeece.—The Bench fined Rogers £2 and cost., but declined to endorse his licensees requested by the Super- intendent.—Lawton was fined 10s. and costs. THEFT OF A HORSE: THE MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH AND TEE WIDNES HORSE DEALER —Edward • Hewitt, of Widnes, was charged at the Warrington Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. H. Bleckly and P. Stubs, with stealing a Cay mare, value £4, from a field at Penketh, the animal being the property of Dr. Gornall.— The evidence of Dr. Go:nail was to the effect that on Satur- day night, between seven and eight o'clock, he saw the mare perfectly safe grazing in a field adjoining his house. When he went into the field on the Sunday morning the mare was missing. The field on the east side is partially guarded with iron railings, which he examined, and found one of the railings, a loose one, had been removed. He went j to the gate, which opened into the main road, ard there he j noticed recent marks of the horse's shoes. He also looked round the district and made enquiries concerring the horse j in the neighbourhool, but cou:d learn nothing as to the animal's whereabouts. He then came to the con- clusion that the horse must have been removed by some one, and gave information to that effect to P.C. William Rogers.—The constable said that from the information he received, he succeeded in tracing the horse to Widnes, where he found it in the possession of the prisoner. He apprehended the prisoner on Tuesday morn- ing, and charged him with stealing the horse, to which charge the prisoner made no reply. He put the horse up at the Central Stables, Widnes, where it remained until the doctor's coachman fetched it. He took the prisoner to the Widnes police station, and Inspector Barnett advised him to bring the nun to Warrington for the county magistrates to deal with. The prisoner, when in the Widnes police office, made a statement to the effect that his b.other had come from Warrington and told him that he had brought the wrong horse, and that he was going to take it back again. P.C. Rogers, continuing, said that on Friday, August 25th,:the:prisoner's brother (Wm. Hewitt), who deals in old horses, came to Penketh and arranged to buy an old horse belonging to a coal dealer named Fisher. The man Fisher rents the stables at an old farm in Baker's- lane, Penketh, at which place a Iran named Henry Draper lives. Hewitt, after making the arrangement with Fisher to pay him 235. for the horse, gave him 31. on account of it, and Fisher told Mrs. Draper that the man was coming for the animal on the Saturday night, and that she must allow him to take it on payment of £1 and on presenting her with a paper. The man -did not turn up for the horse according to promise, but sent the prisoner and another man for it. They went to Mrs. Draper's house and said they had come for an old horse belonging to Fisher. They paid Mrs. Draper's sister, who was in the house at the time, the money, and took Dr. Gornall's horse out of the field.—James Houghton, a labourer, said that he was the man who accompanied the risoner to Penketh. Prisoner's brother had instructed them to go for a horse, on which he had paid 35., and desired them to pay the remaining £l. He directed them where to go for the horse, telling them it was at a farm near to the old brewery. They went to the farm house, and prisoner said he had come for the horse which his brother had bar- gained for. The young woman who was in charge told them that the horse was in a field near to the old brewery. They went to the field, which is situated betwixt Dr. 6r'ornall's house and the brewery, where they found the horse lying down. They got the animal up, and seeing it was lame, prisoner came to the conclusion th iat t was the horse they had been sent y for. BRUNSWICK SUNDAY SCHOOL 3117TUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, Rtrxcomv.—The weekly meeting of this class was held on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of Mr, Simister. Mr. Walter Millington read a paper on "diamonds," treating big subject in a scientific manner, and describing a number of experiments by which its various properties had been discovered. He also treated of the artificial production of the precious stone, in an interest- ing way, the reading of the paper occupying over half an hour. On the motion of Mr. Coventry, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the young essayist, for his thoughtful paper.

SUDDFI.I DEATH OF A CH11,13 AT WIDNES.—The Comity Coroner, Mr. C. E. Briffield, held an inquest at the Golden, Bow Inn, Moss Bank, Widnes. on Tuesday, to hiquire into the cause of the death of Frederick Boast, infant son of David Boast, foreman of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire goods station, and residing at 48, Davies-street. It appeared that on Saturday last, the child was in good health. At 11 o'clock the mother went to bed and took the child with her. During the night she awoke and found the deceased quite well. At 6.30 she again woke and found the child dead on her arm. After hearing the evidence, the coroner said it was evidently a case of over-lying, and a ver- dict of "Accidental death" was returned.

TEMPERANCE LECTURE AT WIDNES.—In connection with the Widnes Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, a lecture, entitled the "Red Lamp," was delivered in Waterloo-road School, by the Rev. G. Howell, of Liver- pool. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar of Widnes, pre- sided, and there was a large audience. The lecturer at the outset said the Red Lamp was a fit emblem of the publican's business, for it was a danger signal. Drinking was full of dangers. It was dangerous to us as a nation. Our national drink bill amounted to 290 million pounds per annem, and this immense sum of money was spent in a manner entirely unproductive of benefit. It was dangerous also to us as in- dividuals; dangerous to our health and dangerous to our sanity. It filled our gaols and peopled our ltenatic asylums; and total abstinence was our only remedy. He urged those who could take drink in moderation without becoming ad- dicted to a craving for it, to give their adherence to total abstinence principles for the sake of the good which might be the result of their example. A REFRACTORY WITNESS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and H. S. Hall, Lawrence Kenny.was placed in the dock to answer a charge of unlawfully and maliciously wounding Ann Rawlinson, his sister-in-law, on the 31st July, by breaking her jaw.—Mr. Husband defended.—The prosecotrix showed great reluctance to entering the witness box, and commenced to cry in a rather noisy fashion. She refused to take the oath, raying she did not wish to give evidence, and when informed by Mr. Lewin that she had taken the oath , on the previous day, she replied that she did not know what she was doing on that day.—Mr. Lewin remarked that the prosecutrix had said she was "afraid to death" of the , prisoner, and Mr. Superintendent Barker said he should ask that she should be committed to gaol if she would not be sworn. Witness expressed her willingness to go to prison, but refused . emphatically to take the oath.—Mr, Husband said the breaking of the jaw was quite accidental. There were times when the prosecutrix was not responsi- ble for what she said.—The prosecutrix was ordered to stand down until the conclusion of the court. At that time she took the oath with a little hesitation, and stated that on the 31st July herself and the prisoner had a few words, and he injured her jaw so badly that she had to go to the Liver- pool Infirmary, where she remained ten days.—On this evidence Mr. Superistendentßarker asked for a remand for a week, which was granted.

TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WIDNES.—Comma Icing on Sunday afternoon, a temperance mission organised by the Sunbeam Juvenile Temple and the Star of Widnes Lodge LO.G.T. has been continued each evening during the past week. On Sunday afternoon Bro. T. It. Waine gave an address on "Temperance Topics," and in the evening Mr. Win. Hunt delivered an address, relating some of the inci- dents of his life during his fifty years' connection with tem- perance societies. An open air meeting was held on the promenade on Monday evening, when addresses were delivered by Bro. Bald, Bro. H. Raton, and others, whilst on Tuesday evening a miscellaneous entertainment was given, under the presidency of Mr. W. Bray, who gave an interesting address, and during the evening contributed a suitable reading. s.ongs were given by Bros. Wendt, Evans, and Kenyon; and recitations were given by Sister Wendt, Collins, Bradburn, M. Gough, E. Gough, and Bros. Kenyon and Kirkham. On liveduesday evening another meeting IN as held on the promenade. Bro. H. Hutton spoke on "Juvenile Templary," and addresses bearing on the subject of temperance were given by Messrs. Overton and Rout- ledge, ar.d Bros. Harrison and Turton. Thursday's pro- ceedings consisted of an entertainment, over which Bro. T. Reav presided. Bros. iarkinson and Johnson took part in the entertainment. Each meeting has been very well at- tended, and the mission is regarded as a success.

IMPOTITAIiT TO LIBERALS.—Wa would again direct the attention of our Liberal friends to the advertisement which appears in another column respecting objections which may have been taken to their right to be detained on the regis- ter of voters. All Liberals who have received notice of such objection should at once communicate with the Liberal agent (Mr. 11. Rob,rts), at the Liberal Club, this (Satur- dAy) evening, bArveen the hours of seven and nine o'clock, when by mAking a fleclaration in the presence of a magis- trate who will :We'd for the purpose, the trouble and an- noyance of attending at the Revision Court may be saved.

Mr. F. S. Mitoht-11, of Clitheroe, has for some years been working at the subject of Lancashire birds, and is at- tempting to bring togeth,!r in a collected form the ornitho- logical data of the county. Lancashire ornitbologists, though numerous and intelligent, have, unfortunately. seldom published their observations, and the quantity of printed material ready to !lewd is much smaller than is posctssed by some other counties. Mr. Mitchell is, therefore, appeal- ing for information to all who have given attention to this branch of stmly. In additicn to the information gained in the course of his own personal observations, Mr. Mitchell has analysed many important zoological books and periodicals, so that his work when completed, promises to be full and satisfactory.

WARRtNOTON FREEMASONS AT PRESTON.—The Warring- ton Freemasons turned out great in force to join their brethren in the great carnival at Preston on Tuesday last. Headed by the W.M's. of the two lodges (Bro. Jas. Paterson, W.M., 148, and Bro. T. Hutchinson, W.M., 1,250), and ac- companied by their officers, they left Bank Quay Station at 9.35 a.m. and arrived at Preston amid a downpour of rain , about 11 o'clock. Provincial Grand Officers assembled at the Town Hall and other brethren at Christ Church Schools, really - -r e-tl°u -EreoNnnr rer et in Bow-lane, where the general peoceesion was marshalled. Provincial Grand Lodge joined the procession at the Town Hall, headed by Lord Lathom and Col. F. Stanley (Grand Master and District Grand Master of the county), and thence, something like 2,000 strong, they marched through the principal street to the site of the foundation of the Harris Free Library. Here were assembled many well-known lords and noble ladies, who were shortly afterwards joined on the principal platform by H.R.H. the Duke of Cambridge an i his brilliant suit. The ceremonial was masonic throughout, and was gracefully performed by the Earl of Lathom, order returned to the assisted by his provincial grani officers. The sight was Town Hall, where Provincial Grand Lodge was duly closed. div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.

It would be unpardonable egotism were I to conclude that Mr. Shaw, in certain remarks he =cleat the Commissioners' meeting the other day, had been following the lead of "Flaccus," but there did seem a "wonderful kind o' con- ' nation," and I am sure all the resideats of Higher Runcoru will heartily thank him for showing the necessity for being better prepared with a water supply in cAse of fire happen- ing again in that neighbourhood. If I might offer a further suggestion it would be that the next drill of the fire brigade should take place at Higher Runcorn, and that they should test both the supply from the hydrant and the pressure that could be obtained by using the engine.

I saw a paragraph the other day to the effect that the pre- moters of the Manchester Tidal Navigation Scheme might find It necessary to buy up the Marsey and Irwell Naviga- tion Company; so we may possibly before long hear quoted as one of the contingent advantages of buying shares, the power of appointing a member on the Board of the RuncOrn Improvement Commissioners, as that anomalous Act vests the power of appointing a member, with or without the qualification, as required from elected members, in the com- pany of proprietors of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation on the owners for the time being. There was a sensation in the Commissioners' Board. room last Monday, I hear; and it arose in this way: A memorial against the proposed removal of the Library to Waterloo House was presented, and amongst the influential gentlemen who had signed it was mentioned the name of the Rev. Canon Barclay, whose support could not fail to be of great weight. In casually scanning the list, the Chairman saw the supposed signature of the Rev. Canon. Amid no little perturbation among the assembled Commissioners, he declared the writing was not genuine, and the memorial was handed round, and with eagerness inspected. With features in a state of solemn portent, all were ready with the answer —" that's not the Vicar's hand-writing." Perhaps he had authorised some one to write tLe name for him? Perhaps! Bet though a feasible explanation, scarcely likely. Was it a forgery? The idea was rejected unhesitatingly—an easy explanation, it was said, would be forthcoming. And with this reflection, business was proceeded with. Like many a greater difficulty, the explanation was easy; for subsequent inquiry revealed that it was not the signature of our worthy Vicar, but that of a young man bearing the same patrony- mic—John Barclay. "What's in a name " Uncom- fortable complications sometimes, and if I might offer a suggestion to the Rev. Canon, it would be that he should distinguish himself by adding to his name M.A., R.D., which, besides being useful, will be no less ornamental.

Whatever opinions may be held with regard to the elec- tion of last Thursday, there will, I think, only be one feeling with regard to the retirement of Mr. Wm. Handley, and that of profound regret. That he is a gentleman thoroughly acquainted with all matters relating to the government of the town he has frequently shown during his six years of office, and his knowledge has always been consistently used to forward the material interests of the inhabitants. It is a solacing thought that his services are not wholly lost to the town. He is a valuable member of the Library Committee, fulfils the office of overseer, and is one of the most promi- nent members of the Board of Guardians; and in these positions the town will yet receive the benefit of his ex- perience.

I observe that Mr. Bradlaugh has notiaed his intention of again presenting himsalf at the table of the House of Commons to take the oath whenever the interest of North- ampton will be best served by his taking such action. This step will undoubtedly open the question whether the Parliamentary oath is to be retained or not. For an insight into the value of the oath, to a Roman Catholic, I would refer my readers to a very able. article which appears in the Nineteenth century, for September, written by His Eminence the Cardinal Archbishop of Westminster, in reply to a paper by Lord 6herbrooke, which hart a place in the same maga-

div.p: LATEST_ NEWS. THE CAMPAIGN IN EGYPT.
THE ADVANCE ON IEL-EL-KEBIR.

_ A telegram from Ismailia on Thursday night says :—To- day we have positive information that Arabi Pasha is at Tel-el-Kebir, but is not in military command there. He is, however, regarded as the general commanding in chief. The enemy is resorting to strategies, not only using soldiers . peasants' garb to obtain infortration, but also as skirmishers to pick off our officers 1-rho may be seen reconnoitring. Fortenately their aim is not good, but more than one casualty had occurred, and there nave been many narrow escapes. Orders have been issued by Sir Garnet Wolseley, cautioning officers and men against.exposing themselves to fire except,. when doing duty requiring it. No forward movement is now expected till the beginning of next week, and when made it will be simultaneous upon four pointsnot yet indicated. The heat has moderated somewhat but sick- ness is on the increase both afloat and ashore. '

RECONNOITRING THE ENEMY'S OUTPOSTS. A telegram from Alexandria, dated Friday 1-4,5 p.m., says :—Lieut. Dornier's Corps of Mounted Infantry made a reconnaissance early this morning in the direction of the Palm Groves at Mandara and engaged the outposts of the enemy. There are no casualties on our side. The enemy, however, had two killed and four wounded. The Caspian, which gronuded in the channel of the harbour yesterday was got off a few hours afterwards. All quiet at Meks and Ramleh. AFFAIRS AT PORT SAID.

A Port Said telegram says: An understanding having been arrived at between the British military authorities and the Water Company, Port Said will receive a supply of 500 tons, and Ismailia sufficient to meet the daily requirements. There is no foundation for the statement published by a Paris newspaper that the Governor of El Arish and some Bedouin tribes at that place had declared for Arabi. The governor is faithful to the Khedive, and Bedouins and in- habitants of the town take no part in Arabi's movements.
IRELAND. THE DUBLIN POLICE STRIKE.

_ The metropolitan police, re-instated by the Lord-Lien- tenant, have expressed their gratitude for his having per- sonally examined the evidence concerning their grievances. The 17 men rejected are those whom the committee con- sidered the instigators of the strike.

THE CONVICT HYNES. The report that the convict Hynes is in a dying state bas no foundation whatever. On the contrary, Chong!) broken down in spirit, he is in excellent health, has a good appetite, and sleeps soundly. On Thursday he bad another interview with his relatives. He has no hope of a respite' and will be executed on Monday. A fund has been sttrted for the mur- dered man's family. STARTLING INCIDENT IN DUBLIN.

On Thursday evening, as Earl Spencer, attended by an aide-de-camp an and escort of cavalry, was riding up Grafton- street, Dublin, a birdcage, suspended at an upper window, suddenly fell within a few inches of the Lord-Lieutenant. The noise made by its smasking on the street, created a momentary sensation, and a number of persons ran to the spot. His Excellency promptly reined up his horse, which appeared to be somewhat frightened, and seeing at once the nature of the incident, rode off amid the cheering of the people who hathassemblecl. The occurrence was accidental.
THE INSURRECTION IN COREA.

The difficulty between Japan and Corea has been arranged. The latter has agreed to pay compensation to the Japanese Government to the amount of £500,000, and to the relatives of the Japanese subjects who were killed in the insurrection in July £50,000. REWARD FOR GALLANT CONDUCT. At the Coins Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before com- mencing the business of the court, the chairman presented a medal from the Royal Humane Society to Mr. George E. Robson, who recently rescued Mrs. Clapham from drown- ing in the Foulridge Reservoir at the risk of his own life. The gift was suitably acknowledged. THE SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC AT ACCRINGTON. Since the meeting of school managers, last Friday, there have been no fewer than eight deaths from scarlet fever at Accrington, and a large number of new cases are reported. The opening of the schools has not realised the anticipa- tions of those in authority, and the medical men seem powerless under existing circumstances to grapple with the epidemic, there being no infectious diseases hospital. The erection of a hospital is strongly urged by the medical officer of health.

A BURGLAR COMMITTED FOR TRIAL. William Garner, 35, carter, known to the police as a thief, was charged at Blackburn yesterday morning with burglary, and was committed to the Manchester Assizes for trial. He p'cked the lock of a dwelling-house, No. 23, number-street, about midnight on Wednesday, and although the occupier and his two grown-up sons had only just retired to bed, he succeeded in stealing a large quantity of food and clothing without being heard. SPONTANEOUS COMBUSTION.

The effect- of hurriedly harvesting hay in an unfit condition ws.s illustrated at Caester on Thursday night, when a stack of It .y containing forty tons, lon the farm of Mr. Lee, Cop House, took fire from spontaneous combustion, and was entirely consumed. The rick was built in the centre of fifteen other stacks, and it was only with great difficulty and by working all night that the firemen kept the flames from spreading. MINERS' WAGES AGI FATION. Yesterday in accordance with a resolution of the council of the Yotkshire Miners' Association, a circular was issued calling a large representative conference at Rotherham on the 25th September of all miners in the country whether connected with existing unions or otherwise, to consider the best means of cirrying out the motion passed at the Man- chester conference recommending colliers to give notice for 15 per cent. advance on the first pay day in October, or leave work throughout the whole of the mining districts. At a large representative meeting of miners held at Lower Gornal yesterday, it was resolved to ask the Federation I Board to take steps to obtain an advance in wages. It was contended (last in consequence of low wages miners were ' scarcely able to obtain the necessaries of life. The meeting also considered that an advance in wages might be conceded without the price of coal being increased. t' FOUNDERING OF A GLASGOW SRI ; 20 LIVES LOST - Intelligence received from Liverpool yesterday morning, states that the tine iron ship Canoma, Captain Mayer, 586 tons register. bound from Sunderland to Java, has foundered at sea, and that her crew of 20 men have all perished. A large iron ship has been discovered sunk off Yarmouth, and a quantity of wreckage has washed ashore belonging to the Canoma, and the sunken vessel is supposed to be the one named. The Channel pilotowhich went on board when she sailed, has never returned to Sunderland, so he is also given up as lost. SHOCKING DEATH. An insane hawker, named John MacErlain, who lived with his son in Cowgate, Dundee, met his death in a horrible manner yesterday morning. He had been in an unsound state of mind for the past six months, and early yesterday morning he raised the lower sash of the window of his room, three storeys high, and leaped out. He fell into the back court, fracturing his skull and breaking his right arm, and died immediately. THE MAYORALTY OF BACUP.

A desire having been generally expressed that Dr. Wor- rail, J.P, should be the first Mayor of Bacup, the doctor has complied with a numerously signed requisition and consented to be nominite.l as a councillor at the election in November. Dr. Worrall, who has been chairman of the Local Board for a number of years, bad decided to retire from public life. He is a Liberal, but has not taken a prominent part in politics. SALVATION ARMY DISTURBANCES IN THE POTTERIES. Charles James and Thomas Podmore, the young men who were the ringleaders in the disturbances- of the Salvation Army meeting at Hanley on Thursday, were brought up yes- terday morning before the magistrates of that borough. Whilst the Salvationists were speaking and singing, defend- ants and some score& of others howled, groaned, hissed, cockerowed, and created other disturbing noises, completely stopping the service several times. They were fined ICls. each and costs. PRESTON GUILD.

Yesterday was held the grand fete of the temperance organisations. Their procession was made more interesting by the fact that it is just 50 years ago since the first tee- total pledge was signed in Preston by Joseph Livesey and others. The British Temperance League a few days ago presented an illuminated address to Mr. Livesey on the jubilee. The procession was large and most effective, start- ing at nine o'clock. There was again a large body of visitors. At eleven o'clock there was a large reception by the Mayoress at the Town Hall. Among those present were Lord and Lady Lathom, the Earl and Countess Derby, Lord Winmarleigh, Lord Norreys, hir R. A. Cross, Sir C. it. Houg,'lton, Major-General Fieltien, M.P., Colonel Stanley and Lady Constance, the Rizht Hon. H. C. &likes, and Mr. Eckroyd, M.P. In the afternoon the Earl and Countess of Lathorn left for Knowsley Park, having spent almost the whole of the week at the ceremonies and festivities. Lady Constance Stanley presented the prizes won at the Guild amateur athletic sports in the afternoon. In the evening there was a grand pyrotechnic display and Guild ball. RAILWAY ACCIDEN AT WIGAN. Part of a luggage train proceeding north on the London and North-Western Railway yesterday mm.ning broke loose about two miles beyond Wigan, and rushed back down the etoep ireiire. The pointsman seeing the runaway waggons turnl them on the up line, and they dashed into an empty, en.ll-tr.ain which was standing in the Wigan station. The I;rlkesman was much shaken, and several waggons, broken, hut tie other damage was done. a A PERFECT DISGRACE.' At the Whitchurch Sessions, yesterday, a *person name Isaiah Lea, in a comparatively good position in the town, and two women named Eliabeth Humphreys and Harriet EtTerton, were charged with drunken and disorderly conduct i;Cthe public streets. It appears that Lea had lost his horse, ,ic,l bad collected subscriptions frorn the -rector, Major Lee, 'the magistrates, and the principal residents, all of which VCS spent in carousing. The bench said the parties were a !perfect disgrace, and sentenced ttte:n to fourteen day's h-ind abour.
