div.p: geittrO to the editor.

RECHABITES' DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES. Sir,—On reading your report of the Rechabite demon- stration I find Mr. Roper msde some remarks respecting the Oddfellows, Druids, and other societies, &c. He said that some of the societies had net increased during the past year, and that it was a bad sign when a society that num- bered over 500,000 had only increased something like 58; but he did not name the society, as I think he ought to have done. As the Druids have not that number of members some of those present at the meeting left it under the im- pression that the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows was the nnfortunate one. In fact, one of the gentlemen who was present on the platform has since asked me if such was the case. For the information of such persons I may say that the increase of memUers in the Manchester Unity during the past year was 10,096; but, by disobedience to the law of registration, that number was lessened by the suspension of 5,672, reducing the increase to 4,424. With respect to Mr. Roper's other remarks on the death rate and wealth, it is quite plain that he is a better temperance advocate than an authority on friendly societies. ROYAL OAK. Widnes, September 4th, 1882.

HAYDOCK COLLIERS AND THE STRIKE. Sir,—We, a portion of the miners in the employ of Messrs. R. Evans, and Co., now out on strike, beg to thank you for inserting in your last week's issue a report of our potatoe pie dinner and entertainment, and desire to again ask your kindness in allowing the following report to be inserted in your next issue. According to our former letter you will see that we had a small balance in hand left from the pro- ceeds of the potatoe pie dinner, with which we deter mined to have a tea meeting, and also to olicit private subscrip- tions. A number of friends heartily responded, which enabled us, with the assistance of two or three ladies, to have a right down good tea, c)mprising ham sandwiches, bread and butter, currant bread, and celery. Thirty-one sat down to the tea, which was thoroughly enjoyed. Afterwards a procession was formed consisting of about 20 of us, mostly smokers, wko had long pipes filled with tobacco, which was supplied by the generosity of three kind friends, thus adding another enjoyment to the evening's entertainment. After the tables were cleared, we adjourned to a kind friend's house to commence our entertainment which was opened by sing- ing the well-known hymn "Come let us join our cheerful song," accompanied by the harmonium. A chairman was afterwards appointed, and after giving us a short but pithy address he called upon several of the company to give rni- tations, songs, &c., accompanied on the harmonium, which were received with much applause. The recitations given were entitled "Temperance harvest," Temperance light," and "Lodgings for single gentlemen." The fallowing is a list of the melodies :—"'The old arm chair," "The fisher- man's daughter,"" Glorious news," "The barrel is a mighty foe, Jonathan Giles," "Stand like the brave," and "Try again," which were interspersed with several good hymns in which all took part. After a vote of thanks to the ladies for their generous services the meeting was brought to a close, thus adding another to the list of enjoyments with which we try to encourage each other in the present depres- sion which hangs over our neighbourhood.(Signed) THE MINERS OF HAYDOCK NOW ON STRIKE.

LICENSING MEETING AT WAR- RINGTON. A meeting of the Licensing Committee for hearing applications for new licenses was held at the Warrington Borough Court, on Tuesday; the magistrates present being Major Cartwright (chairman), Alderman Holmes, Council- lors Milner and Broadbent. Terse GROVE, BEWSRY-ROID : APPLICATION FOR rum. LicEersz.—Mr. Oswald H. Hardy, banister, of Liverpool, (instructed by Mr. Percy Davies) appeared on behalf of Mr. Elijah Lawton, liquor dealer, the Grove, Bewsey-road, for a victualler's license. Mr. J. E. Woreley (Messrs. Ridgway and Worsley) opposed the application on behalf of several residents in the neighbourhood.—Mr. Hardy said the license had been applied for on one or two occasions previously, but so far, Mr. Lawton had been unsuccessful in obtaining it. He would have, first of all, to prove that there was some necessity for the license, and if he could prove Mr. Lawton was a fit person, and that the house was a respectable house, he thought he might with some confidence ask for the license. He dared say the Bench were familiar with the neighbourhood in which the Grove was situated._ Ile stated that there was no public house for a complete radius of 660 . yards, the nearest being the Three Pigeons, in Tanners-lane. and that the district comprised 425 houses. He also pointed out that there was a large ironworks in the immediate , neighbourhood; and said supposing no license were granted, ,- the result would be a continuance of the drinking which had gone on outside the house, and which had been a nuisance to a great number of people. He presented a numerously- ' signed memorial, from residents in the neighbour- hood, in favour of the application ; but Major Cartwright observed that the metnorialists were nearly all workpeo-ple.—Mr. Burton, architect, Mill-street, produced plans of the house, and confirmed the statement of Mr. Hardy as to the member of houses in the district, and the distance of the nearest public-house. He decidedly thought a full licensed house was required in the neighbourhood of Bewsey.—Mr. Lawton. the applicant, was called, aud'he said there was often a good deal of neise through men taking too _ much drink from his house, and drinking it outside. The re noise would be prevented if the men who had been working during the night could go into his house instead of having to loiter outside until their wives arose and made things com- fortable at home.—Mr. Joseph Hall stated he had been in- sulted by the men who were drinking in the brick field opposite his house. In reply to Mr. Broadbent, he stated that the existence of an off-license was a nuisance, but he thought a full license would be the least of two evils.—Alder- man Holmes: To remove it altogether you would think better still ? Mr. Hall : Yes; I think so. (Laughter.)—The application was refused. OFF-LICENSES.—Applications for off licenses for beer only were made by J. Allcock, provision dealer, Green-st.; 11. Co- rney, provision dealer, 181, Orford-lane; John Mason, pro- vision dealer, 28, Tanners -lane ; Thomas Perrins, provision dealer, 26, Lovely-lane; and for transfer of beer license (off) from Samuel Budge to Mary Holloway.—The Clerk said if the Bench had made up their minds not to grant any new licenses it would be only a waste of time to hear the applications.—Major Cartwright : Have we full power to do so P—The Clerk : You have absolute control and power to refuse.—Major Cartwright : Are these new appli- cations P—The Clerk: I believe they are all entirely new. —Major Cartwright : The feeling of the Bench is that all new applications should be refused, and therefore it is use- less to proceed with them..

div.head: ORDINATION OF PRIESTS AT DITTON
div.p: ORDINATION OF PRIESTS AT DITTON
HALL.

On Sunday, at St. Michael's Roman Catholic Church Ditton, eleven ded.cons, who have passed through a course of training at the Ditton Hall Jesuit Seminary, were in the presence of a large concourse of people, ordained priests of the Society of Jesus. They were of German nationality, and their ages varied from twenty-eight to thirty-three. Their names are Jeseph Voiss, Julius Brinkmann, Louis Kaluza, Augustin Bringmann, C. de Beeselager, Christian Pesch, Clement Zarnitz, Guido Draves, Joseph Joye, Joseph Thuessing, and Theophilus Perrig. The ordaining bishop was the Right Rev. Dr. Cornthwait, Roman Catholic Bishop of Leeds, and he was assisted by the Very Rev. C. Hoevel, rector of Ditton Hall College, and the Revs. Chas. Wieden- mann, J. Knabenb tuer, H. Klene, and. F. Wernz. Mr. P. A.naetad acted as master of the ceremonies. The church had been artistically decorated with cheice plants from the col- lege conservatories. The high altar and also the altars of our Lady, the Sacred Heart, and St. Anthony were a mass of bright bloom and harmonious colour. The bishop entered the church at half-past nine, and proceeded to the altar. Mass having been said to the end of the gradual, the ordinaudi were presented to him by the rector of the col- lege. and the ordination service then commenced. The order of priesthood was conferred in the customary manner by the bishop solemnly laying his hands on the head of each of the deacons in turn. Subsequently the act of ordination was completed by Dr. Cornthwaite placing the chasuble over the shoulders of each of the younz priests. The service was concluded by the celebration of High Mass, in which those newly ordained took part. In the afternoon, a sermon on the Catholic Priesthood was preached by the Rev. Father Reitb. The priests ordained on Sunday will remain at Ditton Hall for twelve months, and at the expiration of that period will be sent to missions estab- lished by the Society of Jesus in both the old world and the sew.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Council was held in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. Present: Alderman Holmes (chairman), Aldermen Chand- Eurgess, Harrison; Councillors sairclough, Brown, Mackie, Sutton, Ashton, Jeans, Platt, Dixon, Barker, Whittle, VVoolfall, Burgess, Wright, Monks, Taylor, Messrs. W H. "Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), and C. Chorley (borough treasurer).

div.head: 'THE SMITE OF S-ANKHY-STREET ON SUNDAY NIGHT.
div.p: 'THE SMITE OF S-ANKHY-STREET ON SUNDAY NIGHT.

Councillor FAIRCLOUGH moved, and Alderman CHANDLEY seconded the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Com- mittee. Councillor Dutola' asked if the committee could not under- take to do something to regulate the traffic in Saakey-street on Sunday night. Last Sunday night, between half-past seven and half-past eight o'clock, he was sure it was most uncomfortable to walk down the street. Councillor FAIROLOUGH : Is it because people do not keep to the right side of the road? Councillor Dixon': They stand about. Councillor Strritorr : They take every side of the road. Councillor ASHTON : The question is, which is the right side. (Laughter). Councillor FAIRCLOUGH said he would bring the matter before tke Watch Committee at the next meeting. Councillor Su rroN : I expect all they can do is to make the street wider. ( Laughter). The minutes were passed. THE LAMP AT BRIDGE FOOT.

Councillor PLATT moved, and Councillor DIXON seconded the adoption of the minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH remarked that the committee had put a new lamp at Bridge Foot, but the captains of the vessels owned by his firm told him they experienced vcry great inconvenience from the strong light cast on the water,, and he thought it would be advisable if the side of the lamp facing the water could be darkened like the lamp at, Black Bear Bridge. Alderman BURGESS pointed out that the lamp not only , lighted the bridge, but the street leading to Arpley station, and if the lamp was darkened on the side suggested he thought a good deal of its usefulness would be lost. But it was a matter for the committee to consider, and he had no doubt they would do so. Councillor PIA= observed that it was not often they had a complaint that a lamp was giving too much light. How- ever, the matter should be brought before the committee. The minutes were agreed to. ATTENDANCE OF LADIES AT THE BATHS.

The confirmation of the minutes of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee was proposed by Councillor WHITTLE; seconded by Councillor SUTTON. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH asked whether the baths were very much used- by ladies on Thursday evenings when it was reserved for their use. It would be very interesting to the townspeople to know how the baths were being patron- ised by the ladies. Councillor WHITTLE replied that he had not enquired about the attendance of ladies lately. When he last en- quired he was informed a number of ladies did attend.
The minutes were then coafirmed. TILE PROPOSED REMOVAL OP TILE PIG MARKET.

Alderman CHANDLEY, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Markets Committee, said the only interesting item was the proposal to remove the pig market from Town Hill to the east end of the New Fair Ground. The com- mittee thought it very desirable the removal should take place, and they would be glad to have the opinion of the Council on the subject. Councillor Dlxox seconded the motion.

Councillor Surroer asked what provision would be made for the accommodation of the fair if the fair ground was taken for the purpose of a pig market. That was a matter that would have to be taken into consideration in deciding the question. Councillor MACKIE said he thought that subject of the pig market, which for the space of 20 years used to grieve the Town Council,was a very sore bone of contention, and men of "light and leading" in those days fought against its removal. The pigs and the fitth and all the filthy associationficonnected therewith were at that time victorious, and he did not think there had been any special cause since then of bringing the matter prominently before the Council. He thought the cause which the Government gave to them on that occasion was really a godsend in improving that part of Warrington, and getting them freed of a hot-bed of disease. They were indebted to Her Majesty's Government in the matter, and he could only say they deserved their very highest approval. They were all satisfied with the birth ' rate of Warrington, the marriage rate was very gratifying, and the death rate had certainly been coming down to a point that was extremely gratifying to them all. (Hear, hear.) He knew that Pig Hill Market was a most unpleasant place for any trader, and he thought it was in a most filthy, un- healthy, and unsatisfactory condition. With respect to the remarks of the last speaker he (Councillor Maede) had no doubt that he was not aware of the consultation that took place at the meeting of the Market Committee, but it was found that the small space of ground that was really needed for that improvement would in no sense interfere with the fair ground. If it did he candidly said he should be the last one to interfere with the comfort of pigs at the expense of the children and working men of Warrington, who enjoyed , the fairs as he himself had enjoyed their.. He u-nderstood their borough surveyor to have said that the only thing required was sufficient protection from the rain for the advantage of both man and beast, and that when the fair took place those having shows and the like would have to be informed that upon two Wednesdays they would more less likely be impeded by the pig market. He wished to draw the attention of the Council to the fact that War- , rington was getting a velar bad name indeed as a place of residence on the part. at any rate, of those in the middle walks of life. But they believed that Warrington was not n'y a place fee mak'n ; money in but also for living in, and some of them tried to get as near to the centre of it as they possibly could. The other day he received a letter from a gentleman who had promised to call upon him. He read the letter in question, which stated that the writer could not resist the conviction that the town's smoky atmosphere and consequent acid deposits and other depressing conditions, must inevitably affect the health of persoris who had always lived in pleasant London suburNasees The Clime:max observed that he thought that was a matter more for the Sanitary Committee. Councillor MACKIE said he thought it was one in connec- thee with Pig Hill. He wished te impress upon the Coun- cil that they had a bad name which they did not deserve. (A Member : Certainly not.) He thought it would be advisable if they followed the example of noted watering places and published the vital statistics about births, marriages, and deaths. It was a very nice place to live in, either in winter or summer. Here they had an opportunity of abating one of the most noxious nuisances that any one could possibly conceive of, and he hoped that now the Government had given them the necessary authority, or rather command, to abate that nuisance, that they would do so. He thought they should erect something equal for the traders in pigs that they had erected for those whotraded in hardware and millinery goods and the like, who certainly had not a tithe of the claim upon them that the pig dealers had. It was their duty to render them assistance and obey the reasonable request of the Government, as mani- fested in the letter which had just been read. Alderman BURGESS said that so far as he was concerned, and so far as the committee were concerned, he did nOt know that they were responsible for bringing about the in- quiry or representations as to the condition of the town's pig market. So far as he knew, too, the Medici Officer of Health was not responsible ; but he was glad to find, as stated in the letter of Mr. Peel, that there was such a thing as a travelling inspector going about the country from place to place, and if he could find out a nuisance such as that at Pig Hill and call public attention to it, he though he was doing good service. (Hear, hear.) With reference to the proposed change he was quite willing to leave it to the committee. It was not an easy matter to remove a market, and he thought they might safely leave it with them. If they found that they could conveniently remove the market from Town-hill to some more convenient place he thought it was well that something was done. Councillor WooaraLn, as a member of the Market Com— mittee, said he did not believe the statement made that the committee proposed erecting a covered market. Nothing of that sort had been discnseed in his presence at the commit- tee. If he might use the expression, where had the two annual show fairs in July and November to go? What provision were they going to make for them? Did they intend to abandon them? Where had the wholesale potato dealers—that was, the potato market—to go? They could not all be there; it was not possible. A covered pig market had never been entertained 17 the committee. Councillor Mame:: I think Mr. Alderman Chandley will be able to correct you there. You were doing double duty on that day, I think. Alderman CHANDLEY : That was so.

Councillor WOOLFA.LL : If -I was doing double duty the covering of the market was not entertained. (Laughter). Councillor 111A.CKIE : I assure you, Mr. Chairman, as it is a question of pervnal veracity, it was entertained. Pos- sibly in the absence of our friend, I don't say otherwise. He afterwards observed that if the minute book Was in the room it might mention the fact. It was entertained in the very humble sense that they should submit the matter to the Town Council, and the Surveyor undertook to give them the necessary particulars.

Councillor WHITTLE expressed the opinion that the pre- sent site of the pig market was a very good one, and he did not think a better one could be obtained. If anything was wrong with it he thought it was a reflection on the towns- people in not keeping it cleaner. Councillor JEANS thought the Market Committee should take into consideration whether they could not establish monthly, fortnightly, or weekly cattle marketsp.and provide a proper market for the purpose. He thaught it would be to the advantage and benefit of the town, if they could see their way to do so, and begged to suggest that they took the subject into consideration. Councillor PLATT was of opinion that the present site was not a suitable one, inasmuch as the gathering ngether of a quantity of pigs must be offensive in some degree, and it was not well to have that offensiveness in the centre of the borough. Whilst on the sqlaj,ct of the market he might say that be thought the suggestion of Councillor Jeans was a very good one, and be hoped if it was taken up it would : be the means of alAishing the present custom of holding the cattle fairs in the public streets to the great danger and inconvenience of the inhabitants. It was a subject of great importance, and be hoped to see the time when the cattle market held in the public streets was abolished and a suit- able place found. (Hear, hear.) Councillor FAIRCLOCGR thought the suggested site a very good one, and should support the committee in having a

covered market there not only for pigs, but for weekly and I monthly cattle sales. Councillor WRIGHT thought that the importance of the subject demanded their most careful consideration. He thought if they adopted the tesolution they would be com- mitting themselves to remove the cattle market from the present Town Hill to the new fair ground, and that was a point they ought to carefully consider. He remembered, as Dr. Mackie had said, that in the old Council Chamber they had a long discussion about the removal of the pig market to the preseßt fair ground, but they had such strong remon- strances, and opposition came from the town itself so mach that they were obliged to withdraw the pioposition. The pig dealers and the occupiers also remonstrated so strongly that they had to abandon the scheme. Councillor MACKIE remarked at the period to whick he had alluded the place to where it was proposed to remove it was quite as objectionable as Pig Hill. But it did not exist 110 W. _ _ _

Councillor TAYLOR thought the present site would do with very little expense, such as taking up the boulders and draining it. If it should be removed to the proposed site, the most of the pigs would be travelled up the princi- pal thoroughfares, and he thought that some of the members would want it again removing before very long. (Hear, hear, and laughter). Alderman CHANDLEY said that, with regard to the matter as to there being a covered market named at the committee meeting he did not think there were any minutes about it, but it was certainly named at the committee meeting. He believed it was during Mr. Woolfall's temporary absence, as ' he had gone to put in an appearance at another committee, and it was conversation that took place on the subject which was introduced by Councillor Taylor. The committee had considered the matter in all its bearings, and felt thoroughly satisfied that it would be very desirable indeed to remove the pig market to some other site. They had looked round, and come to the conclusion that the fair ground—one end of it only—(hear, hear)—was the most and best available space on their hand. The space required would not be any more than one-fourth of the whole space occupied at the time of the fair, and the fair was seldom so ' large that there was not sufficient room. At the time of the fairs all the shows and such things were got as much to the front as possible, and the owners objected to putting them in back places. The providing of a roadway through the fair, when they were held twice a year, would, of course, be a matter of detail. He had no doubt it could be arranged by its being known beforehand that certain roadways had to be kept. He thought that that should not come in the way of the market being placed there if they wanted it there. He did not want to enter into the subject of abolishing the fairs a'together, but as a member of the Market Committee, be would say that they must not let a pleasure fair or any- thing of that sort, which were being abolished throughout the country, stand in the way of really palpable and impor- tant improvements. (Hear, hear.) As to the suggestion of a cattle market, he would be very glad to introduce that sub- ject at the next meeting of the Committee. Then, if it was thouuht desirable to take any action in that matter,it would have to be considered whetter the fair ground would be sufficiently large enough to accommodate both the pig mar- ket and the cattle market. In point of fact the consideration of the cattle market would regulate their action with regard to the pig market, but the committee would take care to report progress before anything absolute was done. With regard to the covered market, from tbe conversation the committee had he gathered that it was their intention in their plans to sugtest that there be standing accommodation for the people purchasing and selling pigs, so as to be pro- tected from the weather. He thought it would be a very bad arrangement if any man had to stand outside. The CHAIRMAN asked if it was suggested that they might bring out a more improved scheme in a short time. Councillor SuTrox said it would be quite competent for the committee to bring in any amended scheme on giving notice of a resolution to the Council.
The CHAIRMAN was about to put the motion to the meet- ing, when Alderman HARRISON asked if they passed the minutes that it involved a necessity for them to remove the pig market?

The CHAIRMAN replied that he thought so. Alderman CHANDLEY : You will have plans and estimates before you, of course, before anything is absolutely settled. After some conversation, the CHAIRMAN remarked that it was impossible for any member to propose an amendment at that point, but it was quite within their lines to negative the proposition if they chose by voting against the motion. The motion for the confirmation of the minutes was then put, but the voting was so equal that the names were taken, the following being the result :—For: The Ex-Mayor (Cr. Fairclough), Aldermen Burgess and Chandley, Councillors Barker, Dixon, Burgess, Monks, Platt, and Mackie, nine. Against: Ald.Liolmes (chairman), Councillors Whittle, Brown, Jeans, Wright, Ashton, Taylor, Woolfall, and Sutton, nine. As the voting was thus equal the Chairman gave his cast- ing vote against the motion, remarking that he could only vote as he had dope before. SANITARY COMMVITEE : THE PIG MARKET, INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL, AND HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

Alderman BURGESS, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Sanitary Committee,said that the Government's letter and remarks were sent down to the Sanitary Committee, but they thought it was not within the province of the Com- mittee to deal with the question of the pig market, and so it was handed over to the Market Committee, and they had taken the matter up. He hoped the time would come before long when the question would be settled to the satis- faction of them all. Dr. Joseph had been appointed as deputy to the Medical Officer of Health at the Infectious Diseases Uospital. That appointment did not involve any particular outlay, the reason why Dr. Joseph had been appointed being the fact that their own medical officer had tone to reside three miles out of Warrington, and they thought it necessary in his absence that there should be some one in Warrington ready to be called upon to do any work that would devolve upon him. In reference to Warrington not being a desirable town to live, in he thought They could afford to let those gentlemen, who thought different, have their own opinion. They who had lived there, and some of them had lived there a very long time— ( hear,hear)—notwithstanding the smoky and acid vapours that had been alluded to, were still living in it. He might be pardoned for reminding Dr. Mackie that be thought he him- self gave an answer to what that gentleman had been saying, and that Warrington had not that bed character he repre- sented it to have. Dr. Mackie alluded to the fact that the birth-rate was a very high one, that the death-rate was very low, and that the marriage-rate was very satisfactory, and under those conditions he did not think they ought to weep very much. Gentlemen who had spent half an hour in Warrington and had then ,come to the conclusion that it was not a nice place to live in had not very much cause to grumble. Councillor MONKS seconded the motion.

Councillor MacKIE said, in reply to Alderman Burgess, that there was a difference between character and reputa- tion. Warrington had the reputation of being a very un- healthy town, but its character was very largely opposed to it. He thought, bowever, they ought to get rid of these abominable nuisances. The minutes were confirmed. NO COMMENT. The minutes of the following committees:—Finance,Pav- ing and Sewerage, School Attendance, Museum, &e., Ceme- tery, were confirmed without comment.
THE LIGHTING OF PARRER-STREET.-THE GAS STOVES.

The CHAIRMAN moved, and Councillor MONKS seconded, the confirmation of the proceedings of the Gas Committee. Councillor DIXON asked when the new lamp which was sanctioned was to be placed at the top of Parker-street. ' The CHAIRMAN said that was a matter for another com- mittee, the Gas Committee had nothing to do with it. He added that since the cominittee had commenced letting out gas stoves they had got about 100 customers. - __.
The minutes were confirmed. THE SUPPLY OF WATER TO THE CORPORATION.'

In ptoposing the confirmation of the General Purposes Committee's minutes, the CHAIRMAN said thePe was a rather elaborate statement as to the bargain which had been made with the directors of the Waterworks Company. The subject had claimed and received the serious attention of the Committee, and also that of the deputation who waited upon the Company and recommended the Council N adopt the report. He thought in the main the return was satis- factory. The Council would see that there were some recommendations on the minutes about tramways, which woull come under the notice of the Committee on the 12th inst.

Alderman HARRISON seconded. Councillor DIXON asked if the charge of £35 for the supply o! water to the markets was not a large amount. The CHAIRMAN said the deputation who waited upon the Waterworks Company's directors had a vast amount of bargaining with the directors as to the charges for the dif- ferent departments of the Corpration and these vrcre the best terms they could make. It was about £lO a year less than they had paid before.
The minutes were cwried and the Council rose, the pro- ceedings having only occupied one hour.
The fund now being raised at the Mansion House for the relief of the sufferers from the present famine in Iceland amounts to over £LOO.
Mr. Joseph Gregory, relieving officer of the Nantwich district of the Union, has been apPoiuted school attendance officer for the same district.

TIIROWING A POLICEMAN IN FRONT OF A RAILWAY TRAIN.—OR Monday morning, at Accrington, a rough- looking character, named John Rhodes, was charged with desperately assaulting a police-constable by throwing him in front of a passing train at Huncoat railway station, on Saturday night. The prisoner was brought to the station en route for Accrington, on a charge of drunkenness. A luggage train came along the line, and the prisoner rushed at the policeman, who was standing between him and the line, and knocked him on the metals in front of the train. Another policeman and a porter rushed to the spot, and succeeded in dragging him away just as the train passed by. Had it not been for their timely aid the constable would have been killed. The prisoner expressed a wish that be had killed the constable. The prisoner was fined and com- mitted for seven days for drunkenness, and was.also fined 20s. and costs for assaulting the police. THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 9, 1882. WARRINGTON CONSERVATIVES AT BELLE WE, From remarks made at the beginning of the year, the electors of Warrington were led to believe that henceforth there would be periodical floods of Tory oratory, in order that the constituency might be enlightened as to the Con- servative views of important imperial matters which from time to time presented themselves to Parliament. But, strange to say, since the soiree in January the men of "light and leading" amongst the Conservatives have not opened their mouths. It may be they have been depressed by the disappointment they experienced in the unfortunate illness of that extravagant statesman the leader of the Fourth Party—Lord Randolph Churchill—whose services were to be enlisted on behalf of the cause, but whatever be the reason of their reticence the Conservatives have at last found it necessary to demonstrate that the party still exists. This demonstration took place on Saturday last, when an attempt was made to give another political lesson to the supporters of Conservatism, who had rallied from miles round Warrington. But it is well knewn local upholders of the "Church and constitution" have an aversion to politics pure and simple, and means have to be adopted to lure them to the gatherings. The bait, which on Saturday in spite of the unfavourable weather proved irresistible to some 2,000 persons, was a journey by rail to one of the most popular pleasure places in Lancashire—Belle Vue, Manchester—where they were admitted and provided with a capital knife and fork tea at a low figure. The trippers left Warrington Central Station about two o'clock in three special trains, the last of which, conveying ir Gilbert Greenall and the committee, arrived at its destination immediately after four o'clock. On arrival at Belle Vise Gardens tea was provided in the magnificent ball room, which certainly presented a grand appearance when the large company sat down, but it was then noticeable that the majority of the visitors were young folks who are not on the register. After tea a short meeting was held, but the rising of the chairman was the signal fora general stampede. Vain calls were made for order, and, at length, amid the noise arising from the exodus of tea drinkers, the removal of crockery, the shifting of tables, the meeting was proceeded with. Captain r Reynolds occupied the chair, and he was supported by Sir G. Greenall, Captain Litton Mr. R. Pier- point, Councillors Pierpoint, Francomh, and Wright, Messrs. J. Smethurst, W. Porter, G. Seger, E. Auckland, J. L. Wil- son, C. Higginbothans, T. Hutchinson, J. Cawley, W. H. Kerr, J. Chadlaw, Hampson (agent), Sec. The CPUERMAN said they would be surprised to see that amongst those on the platform there were not many of the faces they were so familiar with, but he was asked to state that some of them would have been present if they possibly could. Alderman Davies would have been with them but for sickness, Mr. Robert Davies had been called away to some town in Yorkshire, and Colonel Greenall, who came with them, had to go to Blackburn on sime military matter. It gave them very great pleasure to see the Con- servatives of Warrington with their wives and their daughters there to enjoy an evening with them. (Elear, hear.) They bad come to a Conservative demon- Hon. (Applause.) They had come to demonstrate that they were sticking to their principles. (Applause.) They had come to demonstrate that night, that although they were not repre- sented in Warrington, they meant to be at the next election. (Applause.) They. had come to demonstrate that at the next eleetion they meant to return their esteemed friend, Sir Gilbert Greenall. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They also came to demonstrate that they considered the present Go- vernment, who went into office with certain cries, had not fulfilled the promises they gave to the country. (Hear, hear.) They were told that the Government went in for peace, retrenchment, and reform. Why, at the present moment we were at war; the Government now in power had been the most extravagant Government that had ever held the reins of office in this country—(hear, hear)—and they had passed a Bill of the most arbitrary character gagging freedom of speech in Parliament (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had come to ask every good Conservative in Warrington to do the most he could to carry out the principles he held so dear to his heart; he had come to ask them to help the party as far as they could in the registration court; and he had come to ask that, at the meetings the association intended to hold in Warrington every month, they would support them by their presence—(hear, hear)—and he assured them from what he knew, the Conservatives would not lo,e the next election as they did the last. (Applause.) Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who was loudly cheered, pro- posed the following resolution :—"That this meeting con- demns the policy of the present Government both at home and abroad—(hear, hear)--end pledges itself to use every endeavour to ensure the return of the Conservative party to power." He said he met them on that occasion with the greatest pleasure. They had been desirous of holding a meeting for some time, and they had a meeting that day worth seeing. (Hear, hear.) He thought the meeting was most valuable in this respect: it showed how well they agreed—(hear, hear)—and that their numbers were great. He looked upon the meeting with the greatest satisfaction, because it was an earnest of what they would do when the time of election came. (Applause.) The resolution said that the Government was good for nothing. He thoroughly agreed with, and endorsed the sentiment. If he were asked what the Government had done he would say decidedly it had done everything it said it would not do. (Hear, hear and applause, and a voice "Plenty of mischief.") The Government said they would please and pacify Ireland. Was Ireland pacified now, when the freedora of that country was trampled upon and Ireland was ruled almost at the point of the bayonet? Mr. Glade stone promised that he would abstain from war. Why, we were now engaged in a most uncomfortable and perilous war. He thought at one moment the Government had in Mr. Bright a fighting man, for he believed Mr. Bright was in the Cabinet when war was decided upon, but had he not better as a member of the Peace Society, have retired from the Governmentlong before be did, when he must have perceived that war was coming? (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone promised a remission of taxation, but was there a person present who could say that Mr. Gladstone had relieved him of any tax? (Cries of "No.") There were many persons present who were smarting under an increased income tax. (Hear, hear.) He would finish with the statement with which he began, that the present Government was a government the country, in his opinion, was tired of,—(hear, hear)—and had done little or nothing—(cries of" Nothing ") —except that which they said they never would do. (Ap- plause.) Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT, who was warmly applauded, said he had been asked to second the resolution, which con- demned, as every one of them must, the polcy which had been pursued by the present Government. The Govern- came into power with such a fanfare of trumpets as had seldom been heard in the country, and he ventured to say no trumpet was blown so loudly as that the Government blew themselves. (Hear, hear.) The Government was con- tinually preaching them peace, retrenchment, and reform. He asked bad we got peace now ? (Cries of " No.") Fled we got retrenchment now ? (Renewed cries of " No." The income tax was in process of being raised—that was splendid retrenchment, but it was not what they expected. They had got reform, but what was it ? It was reform of the most extraordinary and curious description, which affected not this land, but solely affected Ireland. He thought they would agree with him that the time had now almost come when they were tired of the cry of " Ireland for the Irish," and when they should raise that of "England for the Eng- lish." (Applause.) They did not want session after session to he spent in passing Mr. Gladetone's messages of peace. They could perhaps forgive those messages of p•ace if they did not turn out to be nothing but war. He found Mr. Gladstone said Ireland was more pacified than it had been for many years, and he Chen, like a doctor who thought it necessary to give medicine to everybody he came across, immediately proceeded to dose Ireland with one of his drastic remedies, and the dose had so affected the body politic of that country that murder walked rampant through the land, and rebellion was the object of the majority of the people. (Applause.) What better evidence had they of the meddling and muddling of the present Government—to quote the saying of that great man Lord Beacensfield— (applause)—when they read in the papers that day that the Dublin police were in what might be called a state of open mutiny, and that the soldiers were trying to keep the peace. There were ways of managing things and ways of mis- managing things, and it, appeared to him very evident when there were these two courses open, this happy Government we had, the members of which were so individually' clever and so collectively stupid, invariably chose the wrong way of doing a thing. Referring to the foreign policy of the Government, he said they were sending hack to Zululand one of the worst kings that ever reigned in that land, simply because they chose to think lie was a man to be pitied, when they knew a few years ago he was a man to be taken prisoner. But while the Government were doing that pacific action in Zululand, what were they doing in Egypt? He did not for a moment say the 'Government were wrong-now, but he did say that they had almost lost the ship for the sake of a half-penny worth of tar. (Hear, hear.) Had they only shown a proper bold front some time ago he felt fully convinced this terrible complication would never have happened, and the blood that was now dyeing the sands of Egypt would have been flow- ing freely in the veins of living men. (Applause.) It very often happened that the Liberal party, and especially the members of tho Government, had ranked as prophets. He would take an example of their prophecies. They knew, he dared say, from what they read in the newspapers at the time, that if there was one word which invariably brought the foolish laugh, whether said by that great man Mr. Gladstone, in Midlothian, or whether said in other parts of the country by that licensed buffoon Sir William Harcourt, Sir Wilfred Lawson, or Lord Hartington, that word was Cyprus. Mr. Gladstone referred to Cyprus in such words as these. " A worthless bribe," "A useless encumbrance,' "Cyprus is no use to us." What did they see now? Every morning they took up their newspapers, ships were going to Cyprus. troops were coming from Cyprus, or railway plant was going out there to be transhipped. But Mr. Gladstone said he could not think it was in ignorance, should he say it was from want of sincerity ?—what was the use of Cyprus; it was 300 miles from the route to India. But what was 300 miles' to the .ships of to-day ? A mere day's steam. They knew Cyprus was being used at this very moment, and now the wisdom of Lord Beaconsfield was endorsed. (Applause.) Then there was the purchase of the Suez Canal shares. What was so much scoffed at as that? Yet looked at merely as a commercial transaqiion. these shares were now worth nearly three times the amount of money we gave for them, and he ventured to think, being the chief owners of shares in the Canal, it was not unreasonable we should have a great voice in the management of it. (Hear, hear.) There was one thing he would like every man, woman, and child to raise their voices against, and that was a Bill brought for:.

ward but postponed until next session, a Bill, which he pro- posed to call, by its real name, the Cloture. He hoped they would do everything they could to stop it, though of course it would not affect the hon. member for Warrington, because they could not stop a man speaking when he never spoke. (Loud laughter and applause.) The resolution was carried.

Captain LITToN proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, and he remarked that the purchase of the Suez Canal shares was condemned all along by the present Government as the most suicidal piece of policy, but instead of that they saw from the great foresight of Lord Beaconsfield it had turned out one of the greatest political boons of this generation. Only a short time ago Lord Beaconsfield was ridiculed and pulled to pieces for the manner in which be brought Indian troops to Malta during the Turkish war, and now those who condemned that policy had adopted it themselves. (Ap- plause.) _

Mr. J. SMETHURST seconded the proposition. He said he felt convinced if they supported the chairman in this move- ment, and worked with him, they would navy their respected friend Sir Gilbert Greenall at the head of the poll at the next Parliamentary election in Warrington. (Applause.) Tkey might depend upon one thing, and that was if they wanted good government and good trade they must send to Parliament Conservatives to obtain them. (Hear, hear.) The proposition having been c irried, The CHAIRMiN, in reply, said if they wished to please him they must do so at the poll by returning their worthy friend, Sir Gilbert.

The few persons who had remained to hear the speeches then dispersed. Rain fell frequently during the evening, but the company seemed to find pleasure in the various attractions of the gardens—zoological, terpsichorean, and pyrotechnical—and returned home about twelve o'clock well ttisfied with their trip.
THE NEW CHURCH FOR WIDNES.

On Tuesday evening, a meeting of the parishioners of St. Mary's Parish Church, Widnes, was held in the National- schools, Waterloo-road, with the object of furthering the scheme for the erection of a new church at Anderson's- corner. The large number of persons present, and the practical interest they manifested, augured well for the com- plete carrying out of the scheme, which is earnestly desired by the Vicar, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, and, wo believe, the majority of the parishioners. The chief difficulty an the way of the complete realisation of the project is, of course, the money question, and the deliberations of the meeting were directed in the main to its solution. The church, the plans of which have been drawn by Mr. H. Shelmerdine, architect, Liverpool, is estimated to cost £3,000. It is to be built of bricks, with terracotta facings, in the Byzantine style, and will be a welcome addition to the architecture of a town which is lamentably deficient in public buildings of any description. The front will be in Widnes-road, facing "Kent's lamp," and entrance will be gained through two doors. The church will be 120 feet long, 70 feet broad across the transepts, and measure 50 feet across the nave, giving seating accommodation to 750 persons. The church will be divided into north and south aisles and nave. The font will be in the nave. There will be two vestries the choir vestry, 15 feet by eleven, and the clergy vestry. 11 feet ley twelve. It is proposed to have a roof of red tiles. Light will be obtained by nine clerestory windows ma the south side, and 7 windows in the aisle below. The ground upon which the church will be built is an acre in extent, and is the gift of the owner of the Leigh estate. The above brief description is of the church as a whole, but the money at present guranteed does not exceed £3,000, which is only snficient to build the nave and aisles,. The executive com- mittee recognising the imperative need of more church accom- modation,have decided to erect that part of the building,feel- ing it would not be wise to erect the whole, if the money is not forthcoming. But as the Vicar, who presided over the meeting, remarked sitting room would then only be provided for 450 persons, while there would be the extra expense of building at the end of the church where the chancel and tower should be, a wall which would have to be pulled down when the church was completed, so that on the ground of economy alone it was desirable they should exert themselves to erect the w'eole of the building at the prssent time. That this sentiment was in consonance with the wishes of those present was clear from the applause with which it was greeted. The Vicar threw out a namber of valuable suggestions as to raising the required sum, and a discussion of a very practical and encouraging nature took place. Offers of help, peceniary and otherwise, came from various parts of the building. Mr. Crawford described a method of collecting subscriptions which commenced a number of years ago, and said there had been paid into bank as a conseqffence about £4O. Eventually a collecting committee was formed of the following gentlemen :—Messrs. Imison, Matthews, Crabtree, Fowler, Crawford, Atherton, Haigh, Edwards, Brown, Kilcross, Jones, and McCollom. Messrs. Imison, Treacy, Brown, Crawford, and the clergy were appoisted a committee to develop an organised scheme of collecting, by mapping the town into districts, (!,-,c. The following subscriptions were promised in the meeting : Mrs. Deacon, £25; Mr. H. W. Deacon, £5O; the Vicar, .£2O ; Mr. linisonf £2O; Mr. Crabtree, £5; Mr. Kilcross. £5 (in addition to £l5 already promised) ; Mr. Edwards, £5; Mr. Lord, £5; Mrs.. Falkner, £3; Mr. Thomas, £2. Mr. Fowler, Mr. Haigh, and Mr. McCollom also promised pecuniary aid. As we have intimated, preciously there has been promised a sum sufficient to build the naive and aisles, and the sub- scriptions now promised will be devoted to erecting the transepts. It is to be hoped the collecting committee will be successful in raising a sum of money which will justify the eseautive in completing the church, or at least with the exception of the tower, and although, as the Chairman re- marked, the chemical trade is not in the most flourishing condition, if the parishioners will put their shoulders to the wheel its accomplishment is assured. The cause is a good one, and one which ought to receive the aid of all Christiass desirous for the spiritual welfare of the town. The church will be free and unappropriate4.

div.head: AGRICULTURAL NOTES IN LANCA-
div.p: AGRICULTURAL NOTES IN LANCA-
SHIRE AND CHESHIRE.

A correspondent writes :—" During the present year hay- making must be reckoned to have extended from May to September inclusive. On the 2nd of June I saw hay being carted, which must have been cut at least three days; and a few days ago in a run through Cheshire I was not a little astonished to find a large quantity of hay in every stage of progress, and there are old meadows still uncut. A very little over a week ago I found hay in the cock, in the swathe, abroad, and to cut in Cheshire, extending from near Wilms- low to Norton Bridge. Of course it was not the bulk of the crop, but the qaantity was larger than I was prepared to see. The uncut meadows, with their bleached and battered tal grase, wore a most chanceryfied', look. But I was still more astonished to find a day or two ago, in the district lying between Altrincham and Northwich, a large quantity of haycocks in the fields and old hay grass still to cut. In the neighbourhood of Mobberley little more than half the crop appeared to be got in. With such weather as we have recently had there is no telling how much longer it will be before the last of the crop is carted home. At Hale- wool I ern told they have had the worst haymaking season for many years, and a farmer on Chat Moss tells me he has never known root crops so bad to manage on account of the wet. When they have pulled up weeds there has not been sun to kill them and they have struck root again which will account for the great crop of weed in certain Places where the ground is heavy clay or ill-drained, and where the thunderstorms have broken with more than ordinary fre- quency. In the run from Manchester, via Crewe, 'through Cheshire, a little over a week ago, I found that rattler over half the grain crop was cut. Scarcely any of it was housed, but it was a good colour, and presented no signs of damage. The potato crop was generally light, and on wet land very poor. Where the land is dry turnips are very promising. There are many splendid herds of cattle in prime condition. Is the more recent visit to the district in Cheshire, etnbrac- ing Altrincham, Northwich, and Warrington, I found more traces of mischief by rain than in. are more southerly part of the county. The grain crops about Stretford. Brook- lands, and up to Bowdon were more than three-fourths cut, but now appear to have been housed. Oats have improved since I was last this way, and present the appearance in the haddock of a good crop. There is some poor wheat and some with plenty of straw but rather small heads. In the whole round it was surprising to observe how very close the stubbles are cut compared with what they used to be. Paper making from straw has given the farmer a source of income to which his father was a stranger. Some farmers tell me that they now calculate on paying their rent out of the straw, and this is perhaps one reason why they are taking more to the plough. Late potatoes are very heavy in the tops, but the disease is traceable in places. - Hay making and grain cutting were both in progress. The out- look west of Knutsford is not a bright one. The grain, which is mostly cut, is light and unhoused ; root crops are weedy, and second crops of clover are light. As we get upon the drier soils crops of all kinds are heavier, but fine weather is much wanted. I ascertained that the cutting of the grain crops. about Delamere Forest was well nigh finished, but none had been housed. As We near Warrington the grain has been nearly all cut. On the way from Warrington to Manchester there are some fields of oats, more than three-fourths of which are cut. Wheat cutting is also well advanced. Along this run are some 1 splendid second crops of clover lying abroad. In many places it has lost colour, and is taking harm for want of suitable weather. In this round I found the grain had suffered more from the weather than I noticed in a recent ride 200 miles from Manchester southward, and unless the weather takes up, and we get some good drying winds, We may expect to hear serious complaints of damage. It will take three weeks' fine weather to get the grain safely home. One thing is very noticeable and that is the very poor crops of eddish. The heavy yield of hay will be neutralised by the scarcity of eddish, and where land is wet second crops of clover will not be worth cutting. The turnip crop, however, is very heavy wherever the ground is dry. It has been stated that the harvest in Cheshire is suffering for want of labourers. There must be some error here, as over four fifths of the crops is cut."

Tun AUTUMN ASSIZE3.—The following are the cir- cuits chosen by the judges for the ensuing autumn assizes, viz. :—South-eastern circuit, L.rd Justice Lindley ; western circuit, Lord Justice Bowen; north-eastern circuit, Mr. Justice Hawkins; Oxford circuit, Mr. Justice Lopes; North and South Wales circuits, Mr. Justice Fry; midland circuit, Mr. Justice North ; and northern circuit, Mr. Justice Day. There will be no civil business taken at any place at these assizes, prisoners only being tried. The acsizes are expected to commence about the 24th of October next.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.

ALTRINCHAM. Mary Hardy was charged at Altrincham, on Wednesday, with assaulting her husband, James Hardy. The prisoner, while under the influence of liquor, &Inds several attempts to attack the complainant with a knife. She was in the habit of doing this when in drink. The bench committed her for a month's hard labour.

STEALING A MASONIC JEWEL.—John Thomas, a boy, was charged at Altrincham on Tuesday evening with stealing a masonic jewel, value ten guineas, from the exhibition re- cently held in the British school, Altrincham. During the presentation of prizes the jewel was removed from some masonic regalia, and was afterwards found in the prisoner's possession. On account of his previous good character the boy:was only ordered to be birched.

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

TRIPS PROM A sFrroN-AND -liisTurer.—A considerable number of persons left Ashton on Saturday and Monday, to visit the Belle Vue Gardens, Manchester, in connection with the London and North-Western Railway Company's trip thereto.

DISTURBANCE BrrvozErr FEMALES.— At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, before H. S. Woodcock and J. C. Eckersley, Emil., Elizabeth Atherton, a married woman, was charged with assaulting Hannah Evans, at Ashton, on the 23rd August. It appeared tint on the date named the children of the two women quarrelled, and a disturbance between the two women ensued in consequence. Complainant alleged that in the row the defendant hit her on the side of the head, knocked her down, and put her knee on her chest, and dragged her about "most shameful." The defendant said the complainant's children threw filth up the house front and threw stones at the door. When she remonstrated with complainant the latter spat in her face. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon the defendant.

div.head: GOLB ORNE.
div.p: GOLB ORNE.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—The chapel anniversary services in connection with the Gal- borne Primitive Methodist Chapel were preached on Sunday afternoon and evening last by Mr. Thomas Ball, of Gol- borne. There was a good attendance at each service. Le the afternoon the preacher selected as his text, John 21st chapter, 17th verse, and in the evening, Luke, Ist chapter, 78th and 79th verses. The collections were in aid of the trust fund, and the sum of a 6s. 9d. was realised. THE MINERS AT GOLIBORNE.—The settlement of the die. pate between the firm of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co. and their hands has been gladly welcomed in the district. Of the 230 hands employed by the firm previous to the strike at their Golborne pit, about 130 commenced work on Wednesday morning, it being assumed that the remainder have left the district. At the Edge Green and Bryn Pits the majority of the hands commenced working on Thurs- day morning.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

MESSRS. HARROP AND MOSSCROP'S FAT STOCii SALE.— This fortnightly sale was held at the auction mart on Tues- day, when 12 prime fat cows and heifers were sold at prices rangino•6 from £l5 to £2O each. Ten fat calves realised £1 15s. to £3 103. each. There were also about 70 sheep offered, which fetched good prices. The attendance of buyers was very large, and competition exceedingly good. TRH CaoPs.—The highly favourable change in the weather has raised the spirits of the farmers, and a good deal of corn has been safely harvested, and in some cases thrashed, yielding good. samples, for which fair prices have ban obtained.

FRODSHAM MusrcAL SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of the members of the Frodsham Musical Society was held in the girls' school, Church-street, Fredsham, on Wednesday evening, for the purpose of receiving a statement of accounts for the past year, also for appointing a committee of manage- ment and conductor for the ensuing year. Mr. Samuel Spencer, vice-president, was called to the chair, and there were about 40 persons present. The hon. secretary and treasurer—Mr. Thomas Riley—submitted a very complete and detailed report of the formation of the society and the work accomplished during the past year, from which we gathered that the number of subscribers during the season was 113, and 85 have more or less taken part in the practices. There were 21 rehearsals, and including two concerts, the attendance was taken on 23 occasions. The highest num- ber present taking part in the practices on any one evening was 65, and the lowest 44, the average being a little over 57. On one occasion only was the attendance under 52. The following is a summary of the financial statement, viz: Income : Subscriptions, £33 78. 6d.; two concerts, £:32 10s. 5d.; total, £36 6e. 11d. Expenditure: Disbursements at concerts, £29 3s. 11d. ; conductor's fee, 20; account books and printing, £1 is 6d.; hire and purchase of music, 14s. Bd.; tuning piano, 10e. ; rent of practice room, £1 10s.; improvement to artificial lighting for practice room, 155.; postages, carriage of parcels, arc., 13s. 61. ; total, £54 Bs. 7d.; balance in hand, £ll 18s. 41. The accounts have been audited by Messrs. C. E. Linaker and S. Davies, and the report and statements were unanimously adopted. Thd following officers were ap- pointed for the ensuing season, viz. :—President, Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar ; vice-presidents, Messrs. Alfred Thomas, Charles Reynolds, S. Spencer, and Thomas Had- field; hon. secretary and treasurer, Mr. Thomas Riley; com- mittee, Mrs. Collinson, Mrs. Heywood, Mrs. C. E. Linaker, Mr. T. Fairhurst, Mr. G. Riley, Mr. H. They, and Mr. J. S. Rimmer ; conductor. Mr. Argent; auditors. Mr. H. G. Lina- ker and S. Davies. It was resolved that Handel's oratorio Judas Maccaloaeus be next taken in hand, the practices to be resumed on the first Wednesday in October. A hearty vote of thanks to the hon. secretary and treasurer, and the pre- siding chairman, brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: HOLLINS GREEN.
div.p: HOLLINS GREEN.

ASSAULT AT HOLLINS GREEN.—At the Warrington Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. Henry Bleckly and Peter Stubs, three young men, named John Arstall, James Arstall, and John Perrin, were charged with it ssaul ting Chas. Keating, at Hollins Green, on the 12th August. —Mr. Percy Davies represented the defendants.—lt appeared that the complainant had on a previous occasion quarrelled with the defendant James Arstall. On the night of the Saturday in question complainant as proceeding home when he met the three defendants about 20 yards front Perrin's house. One of the defendants shouted out "there's Snig," and the three then called upon him to return to them. He would not do so, and pursued his way until he got to a place called the Pinfold, where he stayed to light his pipe. Defendants then overtook him, and James Arstall asked him "if he was going to have that fight out." Complainant replied that he was unfit, and would fight him any time when he was sober. John Arstall then said to his brother, "let him have it," whereupon Jas. Arstall commenced to beat complainant. The other defen- dants subsequently joined James, and dragged the complain- ant up and down the road.—Mr. Percy Davies,for the defence, said that defendants, along with their wives, and Ellen Perrin, sister of Perrin, were returning from the wakes, and when near to the police station at Hollins Green, they met the complainant, who came up to them and said to James Arstall, "I have lost a quarter through looking for you to- day, and I'll take it out of you." Complainant then made- a rush at him and struck him in the face. The defendant then " tussled " with complainant, and the only row that took place was between complainant and James Arstall. They rolled over each other on the ground, neither of the men at the time being sober. The whole assault, if any assault had taken place, was an assault on the first occasion by Keating, who brought it upon himself. The wives of John Arstall and Perrin gave evidence which went to show that the complainant caused the bother.—The Bench, how- ever, considered the case proved, and fined etch defendant 10s. and costs, with the alternative of 14 days' imprison- ment.

div.head: LEIGH.
div.p: LEIGH.

FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT.—On Sunday, a young man named James Bate, a collier, employed at Mr. Diggle's, Westleigh, died at the Wigan Infirmary. On the 28th Allg,lit deceased was working in the No. 3 pit belonging to Mr. Dig- glo when he met with a serious accident, his left arm and leg being injured. He was removed to the infirmary, and succumbed to his injuries, as stated, on Sunday.

LYM M. LOCAL BOARD.—The usual monthly meeting of this Board was convened for Thursday evening, but there not being stalicient members present to form a quorum it was postponed until Friday next. CHURCH OF ENGL AND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. OR Tuesday evening the monthly meeting and entertainment hi connection with this society took place in the National School. The Rector presided, and after recitations, songs, &c., by the members had been given, the Rev. W. G. Guest gave his usual reading. This, as at the other meetings, seemed to be the most appreciative event of the evening, the children listening with aTmost breathless silence. Temperance songs and hymns were now sung, and we may safely say that at the end of the programme, two hours of thorough enjoy- ment had been spent by those present. The attendance was pretty numerous, far more st than at the two preceding meet- ings. After the entertainment, a committee meeting was held, to receive the accounts, at which the treasurer (Mr. Bailey) showed'a balance in hand of over £7.

div.head: MIDDLEWICH.
div.p: MIDDLEWICH.

WINSFORD AND SANDBACTI Cmcji--r..—The quarterly meet- ing of the Free Methodist Church was held as usual at Middlewich, the centre of the circuit, on Monday last. There was a good attendance of stewards, leaders, and local preachers. The new superintendent, the Rev. W. T. Symons, was voted the chairman for the year at both preachers and stewards meetings, at the same salary as the late superintendent. The business arrangements were got over as speedily as consistently they could, in order to de- vise means for the spiritual improvement of the circuit. A most interesting meeting was held, and hopes were fostered of still better days for some parts of this circuit ; for though few have experienced the sunshine of success, others it was felt have been in the shade for a time back. After- wards a trustee and building committee meeting met in reference to the new chapel at Middlewich. It is expected before long that Middlewich will have one more improve- ment—a neat and comfortable place of worship in addition to those already there.

NANTIVICH. AgoTrrmn OUTRAGE ON IRISH LABOURERS IN CHESHIRE. —Fights between Irish and English labourers are becoming common in Cheshire. On Tuesday morning, seven English labourers were arrested and brought from Church Minshall, where they were in farm service, to Nantwich Police Station, charged with, assaulting three Irishmen. It appears that the F.olislin:en went to the place where the Irishmen were employed, broke open doors and fetched them out of bed. An Irishman named Lynn was severely injured. It is feared his ribs are broken, and the assault is said to be a most serious one.
