RUNCORN. BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS.

The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Tablic Offices, Runcorn, on Monday. Dr. Steele, the chair- man, presided, and there were present Messrs. Handley, allay', Briscoe, Rhodes, Meadowcroft, P. Speakman, J. J. Speakman, Norman, Whittaker, Williams, Fisher, G. S. liallehurst,W. IL Linaker (law clerk), Dr. Mouritz (medical officer), W. BrookesOecretary), and Barker (surveyor). THE liRALTU OF TILE TOWN. Dr. MOURITZ read his monthly report as follows: The 'number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amonnteti to -31. Of the above deaths 12 were dice •to diarrlecea, ,to marasmus, sto pulmonary diseases, 3to amain disease n.ad 2to abdominal diseases. Measles, scarla- tina, and eal;austion accounted for one each, representing a death rate of 24 per 1,000 per annum. Twenty-three deaths occurred among children of three years and under, and 20 one year end under. Three inquests were held; total deaths, 34.—The CHAIRMAN skid he was glad to learn scarlatina had abated in the town.—Dr. Mouszaz, in reply to a ques- tion, said the death rate compared unfavourably with last year, hut favourably with 1880, when there were 35 deaths, and only 15 last year.—Mr. HANDLEY observed that the in- fant mortality was very high, and the Sanitary Committee ought to take the report into their consideration and inquire as to the cause.—The matter then dropped. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the Hiehway and Sanitary Committee, on the 17th nlt, the Surveyor reported that the contractors • for the construction of-Ashridge-street and Percival-lane had exceeded the time allowed for the completion of the work, and the Secretary was instructed to write to Mr. 'Robinson and Mr. Jeffreys giving them notice that at the next meeting of the committee they will proceed to en- force the penalty. Complaints of the nuisance from the Glycerine Works was received, and it was resolved the Secre- tary write to Mr. Clolue informing him thereof, and giving him notice that unless the nuisance was abated prior to the 14th September the Commissioners would on that day cause a complaint to be made before a justice in rnannner pro- vided by the Public Health Act, 1875. A letter was read from the Liverpool Town Clerk asking whether the Commissioners had any objection to extend the period for the application to Parliament to ratify the agreement between the Commissioners and the Corporation of Liverpool with respect to the Vyrnwy water scheme to five years. It was recommended that the Law Clerk be instructed to reply that the Commissioners had no objection to the proposal. The Law Clerk was instructed to attend at the taxation of Mr. Beasley's solicitor's bill of costs, if the bill was taxed before the expiration of the long vacation.—Another meeting of the committee was held on the 31st ult., when the alleged nuisance from the Glycerine Works was further considered, and it was recommended that if proceedings were to be taken against Mr. Clolus, they should be taken for contravention of the 112th section of the Public Health Act, 1875.—Letters having been read from Mr. T. Robinson and Mr. R. Jeffreys, with reference to the time occupied in completing their con- tract for the construction of Ashridge-street and Percival- lane, it was recommended that the Board compound the penalty with Mr. Robinson for £1 and with Mr. Jeffreys for £2. Communications were read from the hon. secretary to the Association for Controlling the Escape ofNoxiousVaponrs and from the Warrington Union Rural Sanitary Authority, with reference to the appointment of an additional inspector under the Alkali, Je.e. , Works Regulation Act, 1881. Re- commended that replies be sent, stating that the Commis- sioners saw no reason to move in the matter. The plans of six houses in Greenwav-road, for Mr. H. White, were re- commended for approval. The Surveyor was instructed to write to Mr. W. Statham and Mr. Wilson, urging them to complete the work of constructing Portland-street and Cawdor—street as eequired by the notices served upon them on January 28th last.—On the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMS, the minutes were confirmed. THE 'E2ECTIOY.4 OF THE HOSPITAL—AN OBJECTION. Tbe Canal Boats and Hospital Committee's minutes contained a resolution appointing Mr. John Wilson clerk of the new hospital works at a salary of £2 per week. The Law Clerk reported that Mr. Statham declined to sign the hospital con- tract to complete the work within the time specified; and the committee recommended that the time be extended two months beyond the time fixed, and that he be reqaired to give satisfactory security to the amount of £2oo.—Mr. Wm. HANDLEY, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, ex- plained the reasons why the committee were granting an extension of time.—Mr. BRISCOE seconded the motion.— Mr. NORMAN said he was never more astonished in his life as when he saw that the Committee had recommended a man as clerk Of works at £2 per week, for a £5OO job.— .Mr. HANDLE/. rose to a point of order. The minute was passed at the last Board meeting, and not at the Committee, and the minutes of that meeting had been read that morn- ing, and allowed to be signed by the chairman without being challenged. Could the subject be re-opened except notice was given to rescind the resolution ?—The CHAIR- MAN : Certainly not. I bad forgotten that it was passed at the Board meeting.—Mr. Snaw observed that Mr. Norman could object to the person recommended, but not to the resolution.—Mr. NORMAN said he had no objection to Mr. Wilson, who was as nice a young man as they could got for the work, but he considered it money misspent so long as they had •a • surveyor of the town.—Mr. HANDLEY : He cannot manage it.—Mr. Noneteer:• If the surveyor of the town could not do the work, it would have been better to have engaged an architect to superintend the whole thing, and paid him at so much per cent.—Mr. HAELEURRsT remarked that £2 per week was a great amount.—Mr. Non- MAN :It is £4O or .£5O thrown away. It is a very serious matter.—Mr. HAZLEHETEST : I hope we shall find some- way out of the difficulty; £2 a week is too • much.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN agreed with Mr. Norman, and

gave notice of motion to rescind "The whole thing and • begin the thing over."—The CLERK observed that the Board • had virtually entered into the contract, and the contractor could claim if it were not fulfilled. If Mr. Speakman sue- needed .with his motion. the Board would be in a great diffi- .culty. . John Wilson was employed as clerk at works; it was .arranged at the committee meeting.—Mr. SIIAW pointed oat 'the necessity for the step which had been taken, and asked Mr. Speakman not to go forward with his motion in eattempting to interfere with the question, which had been delayed for so many.years.—The motion that the minutes do pass was then put, when six voted for, and six against. • —Mr. Slum asked that the names might be taken, so that .any expense and difficulty arising through this action might be-charged upon the people being the cause.—Mr. MEADOW- pcaorr seconded the proposal, and the names were taken.— The CHAIRMAN said he was bound to support the original •motion, and should vote for the proposition in favour of the anssiug of the minutes.—The minutes were then passed. ,THE 'IRE BRIGADE AND THE SUPPLY OF WATER. The minutes of the General Purposes Committee, which were passed on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seceeded by Mr. :BRISCQE, contained a recemmendation that a letter be sent to the IRuncorn Gas Company, inquiring as to the pos. Asibility of a reducq.m in the price of gas supplied to •estreet lamps. The Superintendent of the Fire Brigade '.reported that the brigade had attended fires at Mr. W. Webster's shop, High-street, August 2nd ; at Norton Manor farm' on August 7th and Bth; and at Mr. J. A. Ford's farm, aigher Runcorn, on August 20.—Mr. SHAW inquired vltether the Board had any control over the water in the 'tins for fire purposes, or whether, if not, it was possible to ob tam n such control from the Waterworks Company, so that a S apply might be got in certain districts of the town. In the Lower part of the town no difficulty was experienced, but . From what he saw at a fire on 'Mr. Ford's farm, he might say that the tire brigade was useless so far as Higher Rune, ern was concerned. There was no force of water. Of course the brigade could not stop the mains lower down, and the water, therefore, was rushing down into the town, and they co NM get no force. In any case they could not have a great de. al, but in this instance of which he was speaking, they con id not send the water on to the house or on a hay- stack, am I the men had to convey the pipe on the top and just allow it to run out at the end on to the stack.—Mr. P. SPEAKMA ' amerced that the brigade ought to have a fire • W _SHA thought the Waterworks Company ;them the privilege of stopping the water from the nOgut w .—er n arts of the town, whereby the brigade would Welndoe grant e have more essure.—Mr. HAZLEHURST thought it would be pi best to try an experiment, viz., to turn off the water and see to what heig 'lt A jet eould then throw.—Mr. HANDLEY . said they woe del have much more pressure. He thought there should be a good pit. One had been closed up which would have been very useful when the engine had to go in that direction, 1. us the engine could pump out of it.—A MEMBER recomm sieded that the committee should go into the matter; and t it subject dropped. THE PRICE OF GAS. Mr. MEADOWERk 'ivy asked for an explanation of the minute with referet Ice to the price of gas.—Mr. NORMAN said the company I tad always given a reduction without .ninittee thought there would be no asking for, and the co, harm in asking them to reduce it again.—Mr. J. J. SPEAK- MAN said the company had replied, stating that they had t already expended a gree many pounds in giving the town , improved lighting in the shape of Bray's lamps, for which they made no charge. H s did not think it was more than three months since that let ter was written: Fl HANCE. The Finance Committee's minutes stated the receipts for August were £5897s lid, a accounts amounting to .E-1:4 te_ 3s lid were recommended for payment. ft was reported that notices of the apportionmt vst of constructing Ashridge- street, amounting to £679 2s Bd, , had been served upon the owners. Rec,ommendition, that Vialication be made to the Guardians for payment of the cm of preparing the agree- ment between them and the Comt ii-e.-sioners for the admis- sion of pauper cases into the Conan iissioners' hospital 3 that is per night be charged to the Lib, Nery Committee for coal and gas for such nights as the Mart nr may be open to the public, from the lit September to 30 'Vk April.—Mr. FISHER moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded, t, beconfirnation of the minutes.—The CHAIRMAN explained that the committee had no right to find the library with gas and coals, and thought the charge suggested a reasonable one.—Mr. HAZLEHURST laughingly asked if they coteald not reduce it to 43d, but said he would not press the point. —The metion was carried.

div.head: BEASLEY T. COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: BEASLEY T. COMMISSIONERS.

The special committee appointed with respect to this action met on the 14th alt., when Dr. Steele was appointed chairman. The Law Clerk reported that judgment had been given against the Cramissioners with damage of £5 ss. and costs, as betweNl attorney and client, execution not to be put in under three months from the delivery of the taxed bill of costs. The meeting was then adjourned.
OFFICERS' DUTIES. Mr. T. Norman was appointed chairman of the committee formed to consider thii matter at their last meeting, which was adjourned LEH facer the election of Coramiasi:mers.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION.

The CHAIRMAN said he had had no less than four com- munications from the Library Committee and about the Library Committee, which he wished to lay before the Board. The first communication, signed by Mr. Brookes, secretary to the Library Committee, asked the Commis- sioners to allow the committee the use of the Board room every Thursday evening in consequence of the large number ef borrowers, there being over 500. The second was as follows :—" Dear Sire-The Library Committee deeply regret that their views with reference to moving to Waterloo House do not coincide with the views, of the Board. They think that after their own deliberations,' and the strong expression of approval on the part of the public with their selection of a position, it would be an act of injustice and discourtesy to have to remove before the present premises had been fairly tried. They will beeadad if the Commissioners will name the amount at which they will rent the building to the Library Committee." He'(the chairman) suggested that it would be better to 'refer the communications to the Highway and Sanitary ComMittee, which consisted of the whole Boand.—Me. Ileztararmsr ob- jected to this course. The Board meeting was the proper place to discuss the matter. The proceedings of the High- way and Sanitary Committee did net-come '-before the public.—The CHAIRMAN' said he had _in his pocket a news- paper dated the 19th August in which there 'was the second letter he had read. He thought it would have been more courteous on the part of the Library Committee to have sent the letter to the chairman of the Board instead of publishing it 12 days before they did so.—Mr. HAZLEHURST : 'I fully agree with you. I don't know why it has not been done; it ought to have been done.—Mr. P. SPEAICKAN expressed his surprise at a letter being published twelve days before the Board received it.—Mr. HAZLEUHRST said that was necessarily so, because the proceedings of the committee were published.—The CHAIRMAN said the discussion was out of order, and remarked that if the letter could not come before the members of the Board it might come before the chairman, so that he might take advantage of it.—Mr. HANDLEY suggested that a deputation from the -Board should meet a deputation from the Library Committee in order to ' consider the subject of the letters.—Mr. SHAW thought the matter should not be discussed now; the issue which arose out of those letters was not to be jumped at. Their meaning., as he understood it, was this: that the Library Committee desired the Board to rescind the resolution which the Board passed at the last meeting, because they thought that to occupy the Board-rooms for the Library alone, and to occupy Waterloo House for the purposes of the Board alone, was extravagant—(hear, hear.) —an extravagance which no ratepayer would justify, and which would not reflect credit upon any Commissioner. That lay at the very root of these letters, and, therefore, he thought the Library Committee had not come forward as they ought to have done. (Hear, hear.) He looked upon their action- as an unnecessary interference with the dis- charge of the duties of the Board, because the Board had underteken the responsibility, and were accountable to the ratepayers for their action. But it was not so with the Library Committee; they were not responsible to the rate- payers; and the Board had, therefore taken a proper and legitimate-course. The Board said that under all circum- stances of the case thee, did not consider it right and fair to saddle the ratepayera of the town with £9O a year additional expense for the purpose of a library, for he conteaded that until the library was formed the present offices were sufficient for the Board's requirements. Every member of the Board was willing and anxious (hear, hear) to get proper rooms for the.accommodation of the library, but they had to get it without unnecessarily causing excessive taxation. (Hear, hear.) He was satisfied that if the question were put on its merits it would be thus: The Commissioners were to leave thepresent roomsto make way for the library. Reverse the picture and it would be the Library in Waterloo House at a rent 0fX,90. And then what would the ratepayers say to that? That was the proper way to look at it. Whether the Commissioners moved from there, or whether the library occupied Waterloo House, the result was the same so far as the tax-payer was concerned. Would any man in his senses suggest that hr a population like Runcorn had they should occupy for the libiary a building that cost £2,000, and would cost £2OO, maintenance, when in towns where the population was five, ten, and twenty times as large, had not a building like it? He objected to what had been done hitherto in reference to this question. The public had been deceived, and many people had deceived themsflves as to the objects and desires and intentions of the Board. He firmly believed that there had been no member on the Board that had ever attempted to do anything but forward in every possible way the desires of the public in this matter. (Hear, hear.) MaShave went on to say that the Library Committee wished to accomplish the good of the Library one way and the Commissioners another, contending that the Library Committee had never properly grasped the situation since they were appointed. They had stated that one or two eveniegs in the week would be all that Was required for the Library: and he (Mr. Shaw) remembered saying they were doing the thing to stifle it by not giving proper facilities to the reading public when they opened it, and they were told it ought to be open every day and every evening. (Hear, hear.) But they got two nights a week, and now they slid they had not got time to carry on the work. He believed he was right in saying the every step the committee had taken they had had to move on, and he was confident if the committee had the Board's offices that before long, if the Library advanced, the accommodation would be insufficient. He maintained that it was insufficient for the carrying on of the Library and reading room, and never could be made to do without spending more money upon it than the place was worth.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN moved that the subject be referred to the committee.—Mr. &taw seconded.—Mr. HAZLEFIIIRST said the Library Committee asked the Board to say at what rent they could have the offices, and they looked to the Board for an answer to that simple question. They did not expect to have their communications referred to the Highway and Sanitary Committee, which was not a very suitable committee to consider questions, although it might be composed of the whole Board. The whole.ltoard was present that day in general meeting. With reference to Mr. Shaw's remarks as to the Library Committee interfering with the decisions of the Board in wiehing to claim those premises, it was decided months before the last Board meet- ing that those premises were the best for the Library, so that it was a case of the Board interfering with the resolutions of the Library Committee. Then Mr. Shaw had said that until the library was formed the present office afforded-suf- ficient accommodation for the Board. He (Mr. Hazlehurst) thought they were not suitable for the town's offices, and although they might afford sufficient accommodation for the Board meetings, they were the poorest rooms for the purpose they would find in the neighbourhood. With regard to ex- cessive taxation, it would be no heavier if the library re- mained in the present room or removed to Waterloo House. There was the rate of is. 9d. in the X and the Id. for the library, and it would be no more, simply for the reason that the property belonged to the Board. He had a deep and conscientious conviction that if the library were removed to Waterloo House it would inflict a heavy blow on the com- mittee by putting it in a retired part of the town, and into premises which were less than the present ones—that was undeniable—and he did not deny that he had on that ac- count thought it his duty to do everything he possibly could to retain the library in its present premises. That was why he (the chairman) had that memorial before him, which con- tained some of the most influential names of the town, and which showed that there was a large section of the commu- nity desirous of the library remaining in that building. He did not think he would say any more, but Michael Micha- velli said there were three orders of men. The first order was that which understood a matter intuitively; the second order was that which understood a matter when it was ex- plained to them; and the third order was that which could neither understand intuitively nor when it was explained to them by others. He was afraid the Commissioners had placed themselves beyond the first order, but he hoped they would not be put down under the third. (Loud laughter). The Chairman then stated that he had received a letter asking the Board that morning to receive a deputation from the Library Committee, and he had forwarded the following reply :—" Heath House, Runcorn, August 30th, 1882.—Rev. Canon Barclay.—Dear Sir,— Your letter of the 29th I received to-day only. I should have been happy to receive a deputation from the Library Committee, but as there is no minute authorising such deputation to wait upon the Chamber of the Commissioners, I must decline to receive them on the ground that they are quite out of order. I should be sorry to treat any body or person with discourtesy, but I do not think I should be justified in countenancing such irregular proceedings.—l ' remain, yours truly, MAT. STEELE." - -The Board would bear him (the chairman) out that he could hardly receive I t deputation when the committee had not authorised it. He saw the gentleman, who was the person alluded to, on Friday, and explained to him how thoroughly he was out of order. He saw the point, and he (the chairman) suggested that he should call a meeting of the committee to appoint a deputation, when he should be happy to receive them. He should not have troubled the Board with this explanation, but it might be implied that he had tried to stultify the committee, and throw opposition in the way of the chair- man. He had in his hand a memorial (previously presented by Mr. Hazlehurst), and he was surprised that so many as 175 people hat signed it, because out of the 533 borrowers only 105 lived to the east of the Library, and 433, or four times as many, at the west side. He should be sorry to throw cold water on any memorial, but he must aav the I number of signatures compared with the number of bor- rowers led him to the conclusion that it did cot represent the feeling of the community, and he thought there should be a counter memorial to test the feelings of the inhabitants. (Heae, hear.)—A little Conversation having taken place, the CHAILMAN suggested that a reply should be sent to the memorialists telling tbem that the Board would do what in Or& opinion they considered best for the Library.-e-Mr. HAZLENUEGT : I don't think that will satisfy the memorialist...,-Mr. SPEAKMAN proposed that the memorial be referred to the Sanitary Committee.— Mr. HAZLEIFZELST said he thought the spirit of conciliation which prompted the Vicar to write the letter asking that a deputation might wait upon the Board, was worth a great deal more than the point of order.—The CHAIRMA.N said it might he implied that be, as chairman, had, point blank, refused to receive the deputation ; tut he would read part of the Vicar's letter to him. It read, 4' I am in favour of Patience, believing that everything comes to him that waits, but I feel bound to traseamit the views .of some members of the committee." This showed that the feeling of the Vicar rthe matter was not to strong as represented.—Mr. .IEADOWCROFT asked if any application had been received for the offices 2.—Th e CHAIRMAN: NO.—The eO-.ODIUDiCatiOnS were then referred to the committee.

TARPORLE7 AGRICULTURAL SHOW. The CHAIRMAN announced that thc, Tarporley Agricul- tural Society had decided to hold their show at BRUM .at the commencement of October. The meeting wae then adjourned until the 14th inst.

corn but awaken a spirit that may lead to an improvement more in accord with present day requirements. On referenee to the Commissioners' Clauses Act,:we read that it was a consolidation or gathering up in one Act of provisions which had previously existed in older Acts; itself being passed in the 10th year of the present reign 1847. Although its clauses having reference to elections are admittedly im- perfect, they are interesting as an attempt to place smaller bodies than corporations in possession of a system somewhat in harmony with that existing in the municipal elections of that time; but, as years have gone by, and the" schoolmaster been abroad," corporations' elections of the "Eat an swill" type have long since been superseded by the ballot, and surely the time has come for improvement commissioners to follow in their wake. We believe there has been before Parliament for two or three sessions, backed by some of the foremost men in the House, some of whom are now mena- bars of the Government, a "Municipal Elections' Bill," and we think it would not be a difficult matter to agitate to have inclitded in its scope both Improvement Commissioners and Local Boards, as we are sure plenty of reasons could bs adduced showing its necessity. Even to go no further back than ths election of 1882, was it not the fact that the returning officer was a member of a firm which in itself and its connections employs a very large, if not the largest, number of workingmen ratepayers, and as returning officer inspected every voting paper brought by those men to the polling booth ? Add to this that there was extensively circulated what is known as the "works' list " of candidates, and voting papers with the names of those candidates printed in and given to the men, and they themselves brought in relays to the .polling booth, and it will not require an extraordinary amount of mental perception to fill in the rest. But, inadequate as the Commissioners Act is, there are provisions which in' Runcorn at least have been a dead letter, but which would if adopted go a long way in the direction of an improvement. We refer to the clauses which allow of a town being divided into wards or electoral divisions, and members being specially elected to represent those wards. If such were the case the smaller electorial area would almost necessitate a declaration of policy from those seeking the suffrages of the electors, and burning questions would come to the front and demand settlement. We imagine another effect would be the record- ing of a larger number of votes. The present method ir no sense, except an apathetic one, can be called the voice of the ratepayers, as the small number of votes recorded at a recent election and quoted last week will demonstrate. We believe the number of assessments on the rate book are considerably over three thousand, and as many of these have six or even twelve votes, the possible number of votes that could be re- corded would greatly exceed that number; so the pro- portion of actual votes recorded, seldom exceeding SOO as compared with the whole is very small indeed, and the abstentions correspondingly large. We take it to be an im- possibility for all to vote under the present system, as the number of hours during which the poll is open, with only one booth, would not allow of its being done, a calculation of three thousand voters, divided by six hours, giving over eight per minute. But to return, we think it time for the ballot, with its immunity from intimidation, its secresy, and the better opportunity it affords for a ratepayer expressing his honest opinion, is the only system which should rule all elections of a municipal character; and is it not time for workingmen, having respect for manliness and freedom of opinion and the untrammelled power of expressing it, to de- termine that nothing shall stand in the way of its accom- plishment? Such a resolve once arrived at—backed by.the unanimous power of workingmen—must carry all other con- iderations before it. THE ELECTION DAY. • Thursday, the day fixed for the election of six Com- missioners to fill the vacancies caused by the annual retire- ment of a like number, was as unlike an election day as could possibly be imagined. Beer and bustle are generally the accompaniments of elections, municipal or parliamen- tary, although beer does not play so great a part as it used to do, thanks to the efforts of the temperance societies; but Runcorn on Thursday departed not tram its usual hum- drum existence, and through a somewhat extraordinary cause. On the eve of the election it was thought, pretty extensively, that there would be a lively contest, and there were indications that bore out this view. A considerable _quantity of mural literature was to be seen in various parts of the town, urging the claims of this or that set of can- didates, or giving a "gentle rub" to their opponents. There was a "ratepayers'- catechism," all questions and no answers ; and a placard which attempted the satirical by likening the Commissioners' Board-room to a bear garden, and asking the suffrages of the ratepayers for six fletitious personages. The many "burning questions' Mae I had agitated the" local mind" during the past twelve months also made it extremely probable that the 3,000 "free and independent" who are on the voters' list, would wish to avert •their prerogative. Punctually at nine o'clock the poll was opened at the Public Offices, where a temporary wooden shed had been erected. A few minutes after nine o'clock two rate- payers recorded their votes. For an hour Dr. Steele, the returning officer, and his assistants waited to receive voting papers, but none came, and in accordance with the Act of Parliament, the poll was closed. The result was declared as follows at ten minutes past ten :—Messrs. Thomas Norman, 4; G. S. Hazlehurst,-4; Peter Briscoe, 4; Joseph Williams, 4: James Dobson, 4; and J. W. Lightbure,-2. When this list was posted up, it was soon surrounded by a number of men, who regarded it with much amusement. It will be seen that the composition of the Board is very little altered. Four of the old members are returned, the new members being Mr. JAMES Dobson and Mr. J. W. Lightburn. Mr. William Handley issued an address on Wednesday, in which he stated his reason for retiring was because he was unable to give that attention to the duties which he thought they demanded. It is not the first occasion that such con- tretemps has overtaken the election as that which occurred on Thursday. We believe that the election of 1880 had an ending of a somewhat similar nature. The abrupt and un- satisfactory (so far as the voting is concerned) termination of Thursday's election can scarcely 'be ascribed to a want of interest, but rather to causes which we describe above, and to a want of organisation, which certainly requires a remedy. About 11 o'clock several ratepayers, who went to record their votes, were greatly surprised to find the booth in pieces in the gutter, and the election decided; but the news quickly spread, and the voters stayed at home.

div.head: TNE AUDITOR AND THE NOARD.
div.p: TNE AUDITOR AND THE NOARD.

The CLERK said he had received accounts for the cabs which had been hired for the use of the Guardians during the recent revision. These expenses had formerly been allowed, but the present auditor expressed an opinion that they were I illegal, and would not allow them.—Mr. CHAMBHRS said he felt very strongly on the subject, and wished to have it tested. He, together with Mr. Penketh and Mr. Dobell, had recently been engaged in revising, and be intended to refuse to pay for the carriage which they htd to hire. He did this simply sea matter of principle, as t believed the ratepayers would have no objection whatever to pay these expenses, and yet because the auditor had chosen to say that it was not right they had been sur- charged. He thought if a gentlemen came there "clothed in a little brief authority," which authority he exercised for the. pnnishment of the Guardians, corporeally and finan- .cially, it was something which ought not to be submitted to. He would, therefore, more that the Clerk be instructed to write to the Local Government Board on the subject, and also at the same time to ask if those two Guardians appointed to attend the Poor Law Conference should not also have their expenses paid.—Mr. GERRARD seconded this proposi- tion.—The CHAIRMAN also suggested that the Clerk should bring under the notice of the Local Government Board the case of those Guardians who had to come a distance of eight or nine miles in conveyances, and had themselves to find all their horses food. Mr. CHAMBERS said he would be very glad to include that in his motion.—After some farther conversation, the CLERK said he had written to the Local Government Board bringing under their notice the fact that tie revisions carried out by the Guardians always resulted in a great saving to the Union, and asking that the expenses of the Guardians who undertook these revisions should be allowed. The answer from the Local Government Board was to the efect that they fully appreciated the labours of the Guardians, but stating that there was no authority for the payment for refreshments out of the poor rates, and therefore the Board could not sanction that it should be done. He (the Clerk) thought they would get exactly the same reply to the letter they intended to send.—Mr. CHAMBERS thought there was a difference between paying for refreshments and merely paying for a cab. If that were not allowed he should retire from the honourable post of Guardian.— Mr. FIDLER : So shall I.—After some further dis- cussion, Mr. CHAMBERS said he was perfectly prepared to go as one of a deputation to London at his own expense to represent the matter personally to the Local Government Board.—The CLERK said he would be wiling to accompany Mr. Chambers at his own expense.—lt was thereupon agreed that Mr. Chambers and the Clerk should go as a deputation to the Local Government Board.

div.head: IRE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES.
div.p: IRE REPRESENTATION OF WIDNES.

Mr. SADLER gave notice that at the next meeting he would propose that the Clerk be instructed to write to the Local Government Board with respect to an increase in the number of Guardians for Widnes on that Board.—This con- cluded the business of public interest.

div.head: YOUTHFUL DEPRAVITY AT -WIDNES.
div.p: YOUTHFUL DEPRAVITY AT -WIDNES.

Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Messrs. G. Pilkington (chairman) and John Brock, five raggedly dressed boys (whose ages varied from 11 to 14 years), named Thomas Feeley, Peter Mitchell, Joseph Carey, Thos. Devereaux, and William Lavin, were brdught up on remand charged with having, on Tuesday. stolen 6s. from the shop till of Mr. C. H. Smith, tobacconist, Widnes-road.—Mrs. Smith said that on Tuesday night she went into the kitchen, leaving no one in the shop. On her return she fond Mitchell behind the counter, and Lavin was kneeling upon it. Path of thorn had thoir hande In the till. Dever- eaux and Feeley were standing at the door of the shop, and Carey was in the road. Her husband ran after the boys and captured Feeley, who w..s taken to the shop. Mrs. Smith then examined the till, and found that 61. had bean abstracted.—P.C. Doodson deposed to apprehending the prisoners, and said he found 2s. 6d. In the trousers pocket of the prisoner Mitchell.--Feeley and Carey were then eiarged with stealing a geneva watch and chain from the house of Patrick McParklan, labourer, living at 19, Caroline- street; and Lavin, Mitchell, and Devereaux were further charged with stealing 61. from the person of a small boy named John Samuel Powlson, who lives with his parents in Lugsdale-road.—The prosecutor said the watch had been hanging up over the mantel piece in his house for three weeks, it being out of order. He missed it from its place on Tuesday night about nine o'clock, and he gave informa- tion to the police. The watch and chain were worth 153. William Darlington, a butcher's apprentice, stated that he was in Cow-lane, Ditton, on Monday morning, in charge of a horse and trap, when he saw the prisoners Feeley and Carey with a watch-and chain. He asked them to take a shilling for it, and finally they consented. Feeley told him he had found it.—With regard to the other charge against Lavin, Mitchell, and Devereaux, the prosecutor said when he was gong to school he met the prisoners. Lavin pat his arm round his neck, threw him to the ground, and put his hand into his pocket, taking out the 61. The other boys struck him, and then Lavin threw him into the ditch. They all then ran away.—P.S. Strickland having given evi- dence, the prisoners were committed to take their trial at the next Liverpool Sessions on each charge. Elizabeth A right, 11 years of age, was charged at the same court, with stealing, at half-past ten that morning, 4s. 6d. in silver, from the till of the Britannia public-house, the money of the landlady. Jas. Bogie, barman at the Britannia Vaults, Irwell - street. said about a quarter to ten the prisoner went to the bar and asked for threepenny worth of whiskey. He served her, and she gave him a two-shilling piece in payment. He gave her the proper change, and she took the whiskey away in a glass. While she was in he looked up the till, in which there was 4s. 61. in silver and 4s. in copper, and put the key is the top drawer of the lower counter, He believed the prisoner saw him do this. He then went into the kitchen leaving no person in the bar. He had his sus- picious about the prisoner, and consequently after the lapse of a few minutes he went back to the bar, when he found the prisoner on the connter. She was creeping back to the outside of the bar. The drawer was opened and 4s. 61 gone. The prisoner ran away. He pursued her, and on catching her, she gave up the 4s. 61. which she had stolen. She had left her clogs in the bar, where she had pulled them off, so that she would not make any noise.—The Bench fined her 10s. and costs; the chairman remarking that he hoped it would be a warning to her in the future.
PROSECUTION UNDER THE MINES REGULATION ACT AT PRESCOT,

At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Henry Potter, manager at the Cars Colliery Company's mine at Whiston, was charged with having neglected to comply with the Ist general rule, sec. 51, of the Coal Mines Regulation Act, which requirel that he should provide an adequate amount of ventilation constantly in the mine so as to dilute and reader harmless any noxious gases.—Mr. Collings prosecuted, and Mr. J. O. Swift defended.—Mr. Colling said he appeared on behalf of Mi. Hall, Her Majesty's Inspector of Mines for that district, in support of two informations, one against the owners of the mine, the Cars Colliery Company, and the other against Mr. Henry Potter, the manager of the colliery, for a breach of the Ist general rule, which they had before them: The non-observance of the rules laid down in that Act was the cause, in nine cases out of ten, of the most serious and fatal accidents which occurred in mines. In this case both the owners and the manager seem to have been guilty of culpable and flagrant breach of their duty, and there was no knowing how horrible the results might have been if an explosion had taken place. The circumstances of the case were very clear, he thought. Mr. Hall, the inspector, visited the colliery on the Ist August, and found no brattis- iug, which is used fer the purpose of carrying fresh air over the drift and:taking away the vitiated air. The brattising was altogether neglected, and in places there was practically no ventilation. It might be that the defeuce set up would be that there had been a sudden influx of gas. That was a very common excuse, but the Gth general rule provided that if the noxieus gases in any mine were in such quantities as to endanger the lives of persons in it, the workmen should be withdrawn. Consequently it would be the duty of the manager in this instance to have withdrawn the workmen. He (Mr. Collings) Geed scarcely say that the inspector had no personal feeling or interest in the matter, and in no single case did he commence a prosecution without submitting the case to the House Office, and without obtaining the sanction of the Home Secretary.al'air. Hall, Government Inspector, then spoke to having visited the mine and found dangerous gases in large quantities at various points at which colliers were working. Mr. Hall also statad that he had visited the mine in November, 1881, and on that occasion told the managing director that if be found the mine in such a state again he would proCeed against him. In April, 1882, he was again , down the pit, and, &though he found it in a little better condition, the brattising and several other things were neglected—The defence was that all practicable precautions tO Pecura floe safety of the workmen by the company and

the manager, in support of which several witnesses were called. The witnesses, who were chiefly colliers engaged at the mine, said that, in their opinion, there had not been sufficient gas to endanger the lives of the workmen, and that there had been sufficient ventilation. The Bench, however, considered the charge proved, but deferred sentence till the charge against the company, which was similar to that against the manager, had been gone into. On behalf of the company it was contended every method which could Bemire the safety of the mine had been taken by the direc- tors, and that if any were to blame it would be those who were on the spot and had charge of the workings. In sup- port of this contention he called Mr. R. Winstanley, mining engineer, Manchester, who said he was engaged by the directors to make a monthly report on the state of the mine, and be had always found them ready to adopt any means he might suggest for the improvement of the appliances, and to ensure the general safety of the mine. He considered the mine a very diftcult one to work, because it had a lifting floor and was liable to sudden falls of coal from the roof and was also liable to spontaneous oombustion.—ln the middle of the hearing the Bench said they had decided to dismisa the charge against the company, but would fine Potter, the manager, X 5 and costs.—Jas. Kenyon, the fireman, was then fined £2 and costs for having reported the mine to be in a safe and satisfactory condition on the morning of the day in question,

div.head: APPLICATION FOR AN
div.p: APPLICATION FOR AN

INCRHASS OT SALARY. The Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Bride) reported that there had been a considerable increase in the number of cases of scarlet fever in Weston. Thirteen were known to exist notwithstanding the measures which had been taken to prevent the-spread of the disease. On the occasion of his last visit to Weston the medical officer reported that several premises posses,ing defective sanitary arrangements were pointed out to him by the nuisance inspector. Under the conditions at present in existence upon certain premises there was little wonder if -scarlet fever became epidemic. The people had been apprised of the dangerous character of the disease, and warned against mixing with each other. He had nothing more to add to his previous statements respecting the need for the immediate drainage of Frodsharrt Lordship. Were he toalter his statements it would certainly be in favour of an extension of the scheme. In concluding the report, Dr. Bride said that in consequence of a largely increasing amount of sanitary work in the district of the union, he respectfully asked that his salary be increased from £l2O to £l5O a year from the 30th September. He *as at considerable expense in going from one part of the dis- trict to another, a disadvantage neither of his predecessors laboured under. In addition to this he was called upon to do other work never required of them. He was, therefore, doing more work for less salary, hence this application.— After a short discussion the authority decided that they could net increase Mr. Bride's salary, and he was accordingly reap- pointed at his former salary, £l2O per annum. FRODSHAM LORDSHIP SEWERAGE. In accordance with a resolution passed at the last meeting the Deputy-clerk read a financial statement with reference to the Frodsham sewerage scheme, from which it appeared that the total charge for works completed and proposed works. assuming that a further sum of £1,200 was expended, would be for the first half-year about 61. in the E on houses and lid. in the E on land, but the rate would be gradually re- duced as the principal was paid off. The mode of repayment was by 60 equal half-yearly payments of principal. This would mean a rate of us. 6d. on land for every £lOO of rental.—Mr. CHALLONER then rose to propose that the reso-* lotion passed a month ago with reference to the carrying outj of the Frodsham Lordship sewerage scheme be rescinded, a ' course which he justified on.the ground that extraordinary circumstances required extraordinary means. When the resolution was passed farmers were not present from Frodsham district, and he thought the Authority would have postponed the question. They had heard the Clerk's statement that, they were now paving a rate of 71d. in the £on household property, and it would yet be is. if not is. 2J., and perhaps is. 31. In Frodsham Lordship there were 2,500 acres of land. Was it reasonable that the owners of that land should pay the rate which would have to be levied, when they did not get any benefit from it? (Mr. Rigby: No it is not). The popula- tien was over 1,100 or 1,200 and when the proposed sewer was laid only about 300 could use it, and yet they were all to be saddled with the expense. The houses in the Lord-- ship numbered 225, and out of that number only about 80 could sewer into it, about a third of them; while it would not sewer above'loo acres erf farming land. Out of upwards of 30 farms, which would all have to pay, only three small farms and a lot of " rubbishly " cottages would receive any benefit. That part which the medictl officer of health had stated was much in want of sevrering, from Overton to Frodsham Smithy, was the cleanest part of the Lordship. He could not build a house in the whole length if he tried, nor any part that wanted -sewering. One member had pre- viously remarked that "those who pay the piper ought to choose the time," and he agreed with him. If a district had to be sewered, let that district pay for it.—Mr. ROBRRT ASHTON seconded the motion. He thought it would be very wrong indeed to allow the resolution to stand and carry out the scheme. Referring to the medical officer's state- ment on the subject, Mr. Ashton said be knew no more about that part of the township than the man in the moon. He had been over it and that was all, but, as Mr. Challener said, far from being the worst part, it was the best.—The Rey. J. LOCKWOOD explained his reasons for moving the re- solution it Was sought to rescind, which he said would never have been proposed had the members from the district been present. He strongly objected to Guardians who only attended the meeting once in ten or twelve weeks when there was some special cause affecting their district. He had known the medical officer for about seven years, and he thought the aspersions cast upon his character required mentioning. (Hear, hear.) He did not deserve in any possible degree any such insinuations, innetelos, or reflections as had been cast upon him. He was a conscientious man, and discharged his duty faithfully and without prejudice, and the remarks he bad made in reference to the scheme were such as be felt in his heart. They could not, Mr. Lockwood asserted, have a better medical officer if they appointed a man at double the salary. —The CHAIRMAN : It was a question of opinions.—Mr. DAREYSHIRE said Mr. rChalloner had said the doctor had stated a falsehood.—Mr. ASHTON : He is not well acquainted with the district.—Mr. CHALLOITER said the doctor's opinion was not correct.—The Cireartaux : You mean he is mistaken in his oninion.—Mr. .CIIALLONSR : Yes, sir.—The CHAIR- MAN: You don't mean to say that he had said one thing and means another.—Mr. CHALLONER : Oh no, sir.—After a little further conversation, Mr. WEIR remarked that he objected to the scheme being carried out a month ago, and he characterised their present method of doing business as "loose." With regard to the medical officer, two gentlemen said the place where he had -visited was not in the condition be represented. He (Mr. Weir) thought if they had to have a gentleman of this sort, and he did not give straightforward reports, the sooner they got "shut" of him and the better. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. DANSET then made a few remarks. He said Mr. Challoner bad not attempted to show that the scheme was not required, the most part of his speech being directed to pointing out the injustice of the whole parish contributing to works which they did not benefit by. The Sanitary Authority knew well enough that when it had been proved that part of a district had been proved to be in need of sewerage works, it was their duty to carry out these works. It was another question as to the area of the district that should pay for the works; whether a certain area should be carved out of the parish and made into a special drainage district. He remembered a long while aso suggesting to the Authority that perhaps it would be better if a special drainage district could he formed, but the Authority, after considering the matter, decided the two parishes should pay for it. If that was part of the griev- ance a special drainage district could now be formed. There was no doubt the works were admitted to be necessary, and would have to be done somehow or other.—Mr. CHALLONER said he was very glad to hear Mr. Dansey's remark, but when the question of a special d ainage district was con- Sidered FORM months ago the clerk told them point blank the Local Government Board would not allow it. He did not, however, admit for a moment that Frodsham Lordship required sewering. There were only a few paltry builditees, which it would almost pty the Authority to buy and pull I down. The sanitary inspector had not reported a nuisance !in the Lordship for a few years. If there were any why did he not report them ?—The proposition was then put, and carried without dissent. NOXIOUS VAPOURS. Letters were real from Mr. Sutton, clerk to Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority, and from the secretary of the society for controlling the escape of noxious vapours, with reference to the appointment of an additional inspector. They were ordered to lie on the table; and the meeting separated.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, at the Workhouse, Whiston, when there were present—Mr. Marsh (chairman), the Rev. T. Chambers, and Messrs. Fidler, Newsome, Hall, Gilbody, Sadler, Syder, Jackson, Griffiths, Dobell, Birchall, Penketh, Gerrard, and S. H. Hartley (clerk).

div.head: WORIEIIOI7SE MASTER'S RETORT.
div.p: WORIEIIOI7SE MASTER'S RETORT.

The Master of the Workhouse reported that there were at present 456 inmates in the workhouse, compared with the same number List week. and 452 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 122 children attending the schools ; and there had been four deaths in the Workhouse.

div.head: UNVACCINATED CHILDREN AT HUYTON.
div.p: UNVACCINATED CHILDREN AT HUYTON.

A letter was received from the Local Government Board calling attention to the fact that 14 children in the Huyton district were not accounted for as having been vaccinated. An explanation was requested.—The CLERK said he had written to the relieving officer for that district, who, in reply, said there were 11. of the children unfit for vaccination, and three had been successfully vaccinated, but certificates had not yet been received for them. He might say that this officer caused considerable trouble. and he believed did not look after the vaccination.—Mr. FIDLF,R : Who is he ?—The CLERK: Mr. Pendleton.— Mr. FIDLER : We will have to get somebody. else.—ln answer to Mr. NEWSOME, the CLERK said he would write to Mr. Pendleton and say his explanation was not satisfactory, because if a child was not vaccinated he ought to have got a certificate showing the reason why. He (Mr. Hartley) did not believe that the officer had those certificates. THE KALE YEAR'S EXPENDITURE. •

The following estimate of the probable amount of expen- diture in the relief of the poor and other charges by the Guardians on behalf of the Union for the half-year ending 25th March, 1883, was submitted, viz. :—ln maintenance, £2,600; paupers in schools, £1,200; out relief, £4,800 ; lunatics in asylum (less grant), £800; loan account, £1,080; county rate, £6,00; salaries of Union officers (less grant), £750 ; salaries of assistant overseers, £600; workhouse offi- cer's rations, £270; assesstsent committee expenses, £1,2C0; school attendance committee's expenses, £100; school fees (non-pauper), £200; vaccination expenses, £260; registra- tion expenses, £220; printinff, advertising, Are., £150; establishment charges, workhouse, dtc., £l,OOO ; total, £21.830; add 10 per cent, for contingencies, £2,183; grand £24,013.—The CLERK said the largeness of the sum for the assessment committee was because of the re- valuation of the railways throughout the Union.-11r. TrlxAnows : It vill be well spent.—The estimate was adopted.

div.head: PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday evening last, at the Board Offices, Prescot, when there were present, Messrs. Fogg (in the chair), Whit- field, and Preston, Mr. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Goldsworth (surveyor).

TIE BOARD AND THE GAS COMPANY. The CLERK read a letter from Mr. W. Prescet, secretary and manager to the Gas Company, which stated that the company would andertake to supply gas to the public lamps under the average meter system until the end of the present year at a rate of ss. 4d. per thousand cubic feet, the same being subject to a discount of 10 per cent. en pay- ment being made within one month from the delivery of the quarterly account. The directors. would at the end of the term mentioned send in another tender for the remainder of the lighting season, as they anticipated by that time to be be in a position to reduce the price of gas per 1000 cubic feet. —Mr. WHITFIELD: Has there been no other tender for light- ing the lamps ?—The CLERK: No.—Mr. WHITFIELD said he was disappointed to hear that, as he understood that the Wigan and Whiston Company were prepared to supply Prescot and Widnes with gas at 10d. per thousand feet if If the pipes were laid. It looked as if the Gas Company were going to bleed Prescot as long as ever they could. It was a mystery to him whys they should be compelled to knock under. The people of Prescot could do without gas for a while, and, for his part, if he had anybody to back him up, he would do without it till the company lowered its standard from ss. 4d. Mr. Petssrox thought it was a great shame for the Gas Company to charge ss. 4d., but there was no doubt the inhabi- tants of Prescot would have a turn after a while.—Mr. WHIT- FIELD said it was because the Gas Company had a monopoly, and they thought there would be no opposition, bat he really believed some one would come and break in on this monopoly. Mr. Whitfield then went on to say that at the last meeting but one, he had said that there were towns no larger than Prescot which were supplied with gas at 3s. 6d per thousand, but he was then pulled up. He no found that a small village like Rainhill paid only 4s. 63., and then if they went as far as Liverpool they found it to be so low as 2s. 101 He maintained that there was grievous extor- tion practised on the retepayers of Prescot, especially by the Gas Company. He had been speaking to a responsible person in connection with the gas woks, and asked him if ever there were any shares to let by the Gas Company, and he replied "No, but if there were you would net leave a chance." He asked him for what reason, and be said because he would have to pay £2OO for a £lOO share. That, Mr. Whitfield continued, spoke its own tale.—Mr. PsessTore I think you are wrongly infortned.—Mr. WHIT- ' FIELD said he bad been told so.—Mr. PRESTON said he did not think the Gas Ccmpany ought te want the last drop of blood, as it were, from the ratepayers of Prescot. It they did come a little lower it would be through fear and not love to them; it would be fear of the Wigan and Whiston Coal Company that would reduce the charges.— The CHAIRMAN said it was unfortunate that that matter had not been considered in the middle of summer. He did not think the Gas Company met the Board as they ought to do, and they treated them as if they were the smallest consumers in the district. For his part, he could not see why the Board could not sufficiently light the streets independently of the Gas Company, if they did net meet them in a more fair and equitable spirit than they had done. He thought ss. 4d. a very large figure indeed. He would, however, propose that in the meantime they accept the offer of the company.—Mr. PRESTON seconded this, as, he said, it was the only course left open to them ; but he EU sure the time would come when the inhabitants would have their revenge, for on the first opportunity they would get some other light. —The offer of the Gas Company was then accepted.—A number of nuisances were then submitted to the Board,which, having been disposed of, the Board some after adjourned.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER CORN, THURSDAY. —(From Messrs. William Warburton and Co.'s circular.)—Notwithstanding the con- tinuance of most unfavourable weather, the trade has been very dull since last market day, with prices tending down- wards. Large supplies of wheat and flour have been received at Liverpool. and full average quantities of other grain.—The weather was brilliant, the tone of the trade was without im- provement this morning, and transactions were on a limited scale. Foreign white wheat was without mate,dal altera- tion. New red American receded 2d to 3d per cental from the improvement noted last week. The few samples of new English offering were in poor condition and prices variable. Oats still dull at previous rates. Beans were firm. Canadian peas 4d to 60 per cental dearer. Mixed American maize was fully Id per cental lower. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FRIDAY. Sales of beef are small but no alteration in values is noted. Pork moves slowly at large figures, Bacon firm at the quotations. Hams are not inquired for. Shoulders :trove better. Lard 6,1 per cwt lower and dult at that. Cheese quiet but steady. Butter nominal. Tallow very firm. LONDON PROVISION, FRIDAY. Butter: Best descriptions of foreign meet with a steady sale: Friesland quoted at 1103 to 120 s; Normandy, 98s to 116 s; Jersey, 86s to 96s ; American merely nominal; Irish very quiet. Bacon: Moderate to light weights, 683 to 775; heavy and oversize, 663 to 755; Hams in- active, Lard steady at late values. Cheese: Finest new American; 56s to 58s. CLYDE CRUSHED SUGAR, FRIDAY.—A, large business was done at very steady prices. GLASGOW PIG IRON. FRIDAY.—First report: There was a quiet market and a moderate business done at 49311 d to 49s 8d cash, also at 50s to 49s 10Id one month; closing buyers 49s 80 cash and 493 100 one month; sellers a shade more. CORK BUTTER, FRIDAY. Ordinary: Firsts, ills; seconds, 1013 ; thirds, 94s ; fourths, 81s; fifths, —s. Kegs: Firsts, 1123 : seconds, 106 s ; thirds, 955; fourths, 81s; fifths,—s. Mild cured firkins: Superfine, 1265; fine mild, 118 s : mild, 1043. Mid cured kegs: Fine mild, —e; mild, —s. Firkins in the market, 1,910; kegs. 7; mild. 199, LONDON CORN, FRlDAY.—Market dull, and prices exhibit a downward tendency for wheat owing to the fine weather, and lower quotations from America. Flour also tending cheaper. Barley the turn lower; other articles very quiet. Arrivals— English : Wheat, 160 quarters; Irish oats, 700. Foreign : Wheat, 97.410 qrs ; barley, 2350; oats, 69,700; maize, 10,53 ; flour, 12,390 sacks.

STOCK AND SHARE MARKET. Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Sep. 7) :—ln the absence of any decisive news from Egypt the policy of waiting has been observed in most departments during the past week, and as a consequence the amount of business con- cluded is only moderate. Nevertheless, much confidence being felt as to the ultimate issue of the cunpaign lass caused a steady tone to prevail, and this feeling coupled with the late favour- able change in the weather has kept the market buoyant and induced a further general improvement in values, an improve- ment which, except in a few instances, is fairly well main- tained. Egyptian stocks have been comparatively quiet all through the week, during the early portion declining slowly, latterly, however, although with no great number of dealings marked they have turned upwards again, and to-day quota- tions show vary little change as compared with figures of a week ago. MO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- l. tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- couraging amongst their consumers the use of GAB FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Sell, Let out on Hire, or Purchase, Lease, GAS COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be selected from the beet makers for economy in consumption of gas, perfection in cooking, and constructed on the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee, in order to make cook- ing by gas a enemas, will lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, Manager. Gas Works, Warrington, 26th June, 1882.

To enable the governors to determine the number of assistant masters and mistresses required, intending pupils are requested t I apply for admission to the schools without delay. charged with assaulting Anderson. Both were remanded under bail. A special constable oil Sunday evening was seen, whilst under the influence of drink, to throw stones at some soldiers, and otherwise misconduct himself. He was sent to prison for six months, as was another "special," who had been guilty of drunken and riotous conduct, hav- ing assaulted several persons. On Monday night the city was quiet, there being nearly 500 special constables on duty. Perfect tranquility prevailed in Dublin on Tuesday, owing probably to the fact that a very large proportion of the con- stables who resigned returned to duty, with the permission of the Executive. In reply to the memorial addressed to Lord Spencer by about 200 of the discharged police officers, his Excellency has stated that after a careful inquiry into the character and conduct of each memorialist, such of them as appear deserving will be reinstated. The leaders of the mutiny—some fourteen in number—are excluded from this concession. To the large body of police the favourable decision of the Lord Lieutenant has given great satisfaction, and, except as regards the ringleaders, the whole affair may now be considered at an end. It is denied that the men who had resigned returned to duty on the conditien that the dis- missed ill€ll should be reinstated. The enrolment of special constables has ceased, and on Tuesday evening they were not called out for duty. It appears that the men were influenced in their action by the hope of obtaining assisted passages to Queensland, and an application was sent by 100 of the men to the agent of that colony in London. A reply was received on Saturday peremptorily declining to entertain any proposals from the na utineers. A late telegram says the Lord Lieutenant has reinstated all the dismissed Dublin police except 17, who remain per- manently expelled from the force.
